Let \(U\) be an open convex set of points with \(n\) coordinates and \(f\) a continuously differentiable function on \(U\) (definition 8.23, item 4).

  1. The function \(f\) is convex on \(U\) if and only if for every two points \(\vek x, \vek y \in U\) the graph lies above the tangent, that is,
    \[f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek x) + \nabla f(\vek x)\cdot(\vek y - \vek x) . \tag{29.14}\]
  2. If the strict inequality holds in (29.14) for every pair \(\vek x \ne \vek y\), then \(f\) is strictly convex.
Proof

We must show both directions of the first part. The direction from convexity to (29.14) follows from the chord lying above the graph with the same start, and the graph must lie below it also in the limit. Conversely we add two tangent inequalities.

  1. Let \(f\) be convex and \(\vek x, \vek y \in U\), \(\vek x \ne \vek y\), \(\vek d = \vek y - \vek x\). We define \(g(t) = f(\vek x + t\,\vek d)\). By lemma 8.29, \(g\) is differentiable at \(t = 0\) and \(g'(0) = \nabla f(\vek x)\cdot\vek d\).
  2. For \(0 < t \le 1\), by (29.12) (the graph below the chord), \(g(t) = f\big((1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\big) \le (1 - t)\,f(\vek x) + t\,f(\vek y) = g(0) + t\,\big(f(\vek y) - f(\vek x)\big)\). Hence \(\big(g(t) - g(0)\big)/t \le f(\vek y) - f(\vek x)\).
  3. As \(t \to 0\) from the right, the secant turns into the tangent and the left side has the limit \(g'(0)\), and the inequality is kept in the limit. So \(\nabla f(\vek x)\cdot\vek d \le f(\vek y) - f(\vek x)\), that is, (29.14).
  4. Conversely, let (29.14) hold for all pairs. For \(\vek x, \vek y \in U\) and \(0 < t < 1\) let \(\vek z = (1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\), which is in \(U\). Inequality (29.14) at the point \(\vek z\) (the tangent below the graph) for \(\vek x\) and for \(\vek y\) gives \(f(\vek x) \ge f(\vek z) + \nabla f(\vek z)\cdot(\vek x - \vek z)\) and \(f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek z) + \nabla f(\vek z)\cdot(\vek y - \vek z)\).
  5. We multiply the first by \(1 - t > 0\), the second by \(t > 0\) and add (the weighted sum on the chord): \((1 - t)\,f(\vek x) + t\,f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek z) + \nabla f(\vek z)\cdot\big((1 - t)(\vek x - \vek z) + t\,(\vek y - \vek z)\big)\). The vector in the bracket is \((1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y - \vek z = \vek 0\), so \((1 - t)\,f(\vek x) + t\,f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek z)\), that is, (29.12).
  6. Second part: if the inequality in step 4 is strict, which holds for \(\vek x \ne \vek z\) and \(\vek y \ne \vek z\), that is, for \(0 < t < 1\) and \(\vek x \ne \vek y\), the sum in step 5 is strict too.

Source: CHK §3.2 (PDF p. 47-48) states only the condition with a monotone gradient (theorem 3.1), without proof. The proof is not from the source.

The meaning of the right side of (29.14) is this: the function \(\vek y \mapsto f(\vek x) + \nabla f(\vek x)\cdot(\vek y - \vek x)\) is a plane (for one coordinate a line) that touches the graph at \(\vek x\) with the same gradient, and we call it the tangent plane (tangentna ravnina). The inequality says: a convex function lies above each of its tangent planes. The consequence for finding a minimum is immediate.

The corollary is shown in figure 29.29. On the left is the graph of a convex function with a horizontal tangent at the point \(\vek x^*\): the graph lies above the tangent, so \(\vek x^*\) is the lowest point. On the right, on the axis \(x\), the feasible set \(S\) lies only to the right of the point \(\vek x^*\), the tangent has a positive slope there, the graph is above it and is therefore on \(S\) above the value at \(\vek x^*\).

Corollary 29.21 Stationary point of a convex function (stacionarna točka konveksne funkcije)

Let \(U\) be an open convex set and \(f\) a continuously differentiable convex function on \(U\).

  1. If \(\nabla f(\vek x^*) = \vek 0\), then \(\vek x^*\) is a global minimum of \(f\) on \(U\).
  2. Let \(S \subset U\) be a convex set and \(\vek x^* \in S\). If \(\nabla f(\vek x^*)\cdot(\vek y - \vek x^*) \ge 0\) for every \(\vek y \in S\), then \(\vek x^*\) is a global minimum of \(f\) on \(S\).
Proof

We must show that both parts are a consequence of inequality (29.14), that is, of the graph lying above the tangent.

  1. By lemma 29.20, for every \(\vek y \in S\) we have (graph above the tangent) \(f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek x^*) + \nabla f(\vek x^*)\cdot(\vek y - \vek x^*)\).
  2. In the second part the scalar product in this inequality is nonnegative, so \(f(\vek y) \ge f(\vek x^*)\). The first part is a special case with \(S = U\), where the product is zero.

Source: For functionals: theorem 5.74 (CHK §3.2, PDF p. 46-48). The proof is not from the source.

The corollary says that for a convex function we have no peaks and saddles: every stationary point is a bottom. We need the second part of the corollary in the next section, when the feasible set is not the whole space. One more condition, which we check with derivatives and not with an inequality for every pair of points.

We follow the proof of the next lemma in figure 29.30. On the left is the convex set \(U\) with the points \(\vek x\) and \(\vek y\), the segment between them and the vector \(\vek d = \vek y - \vek x\). On the right, on the axis \(s\) and \(g\), is the graph of the function \(g(s)\) along the segment, the tangent at \(s = 0\) of slope \(g'(0)\) and the gap \(\tfrac12 g''(c)\) between the graph and the tangent at \(s = 1\), where \(c\) is some intermediate point. If the gap is not negative, the graph is above the tangent.

Lemma 29.22 Convexity by the Hessian matrix (konveksnost po Hessejevi matriki)

Let \(U\) be an open convex set of points with \(n\) coordinates and \(f\) a twice continuously differentiable function on \(U\) with the Hessian matrix \(\mat K(\vek x)\) (definition 8.69).

  1. If \(\mat K(\vek x)\) is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15) at every point \(\vek x \in U\), then \(f\) is convex on \(U\).
  2. If \(\mat K(\vek x)\) is positive definite (definition 6.27) at every point \(\vek x \in U\), then \(f\) is strictly convex on \(U\).
Proof

We must show the tangent inequality (29.14). We treat the values of \(f\) on the segment from \(\vek x\) to \(\vek y\) as a function of one variable and use theorem 8.68, and the second derivative of this function is the quadratic form of the Hessian matrix.

  1. Let \(\vek x, \vek y \in U\), \(\vek x \ne \vek y\) and \(\vek d = \vek y - \vek x\). We define \(g(s) = f(\vek x + s\,\vek d)\) for \(s \in [0, 1]\). The points \(\vek x + s\,\vek d\) are in \(U\), because \(U\) is convex.
  2. By lemma 8.29, applied to \(f\) and to every partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\), which is continuously differentiable, \(g'(s) = \nabla f(\vek x + s\,\vek d)\cdot\vek d\) is continuous and \(g''(s) = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} d_{\mathrm{i}}\,K_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek x + s\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek d^\T\mat K(\vek x + s\,\vek d)\,\vek d\) (as in step 4 of the proof of theorem 8.71). The first derivative is the slope of the graph, the second its curvature.
  3. By theorem 8.68 with \(x_0 = 0\) and \(x = 1\) there is \(c \in (0, 1)\) with \(g(1) = g(0) + g'(0) + \tfrac12 g''(c)\), that is, \(f(\vek y) = f(\vek x) + \nabla f(\vek x)\cdot\vek d + \tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\mat K(\vek x + c\,\vek d)\,\vek d\).
  4. In the first part the last term is \(\ge 0\) by the definition of positive semidefiniteness, so (29.14) holds and by lemma 29.20 \(f\) is convex.
  5. In the second part the last term is \(> 0\), because \(\vek d \ne \vek 0\). Inequality (29.14) is strict for every pair \(\vek x \ne \vek y\), and by the second part of lemma 29.20 \(f\) is strictly convex.

Source: CHK theorem 3.2 (PDF p. 48) (with the converse: a convex function has a positive semidefinite matrix), without proof. The proof is not from the source.

The lemma states only one direction. For a convex function the second derivative at a point cannot be negative, as it is at the peak, which CHK says (theorem 3.2, PDF p. 48), we do not prove this direction because we do not need it.

Example 29.23 The volume of the truss is convex in the height (prostornina paličja kot funkcija višine je konveksna)

Take \(V(h) = F\,(2a^2 + h^2)/(h\,\sigma_0)\) on the open convex set \(U = \{h > 0\}\) (an interval). The Hessian matrix of one variable is \(1 \times 1\) and equals \(V''(h)\), and positive semidefiniteness means \(d\,V''\,d \ge 0\) for every \(d\). We differentiate: \(V(h) = (F/\sigma_0)\,(2a^2/h + h)\), \(V'(h) = (F/\sigma_0)\,(1 - 2a^2/h^2)\) and \(V''(h) = 4F a^2/(h^3\,\sigma_0)\). This is positive at every \(h > 0\), so \(\mat K\) is positive definite and \(V\) is strictly convex on \(U\) by lemma 29.22. With the unit \(F a/\sigma_0 = 181{,}82\) cm\(^3\) we have \(V''/(F a/\sigma_0) = 4a/h^3 = 16/h^3\) per m\(^2\): \(4{,}7407\) at \(1{,}5\) m, \(0{,}5926\) at \(3\) m, \(0{,}0884\) at \(a\sqrt2 = 5{,}6569\) m and \(0{,}0312\) at \(8\) m (NumPy, num-03.py). The derivative is zero at \(h = a\sqrt2\), so by corollary 29.21 this is the global minimum on \(U\), not only a minimum nearby: \(V = 514{,}3\) cm\(^3\), the volume at \(h = 3\) m (\(621{,}2\) cm\(^3\)) and at \(h = 8\) m (\(545{,}5\) cm\(^3\)) is larger, as figure 29.21 shows. The small value of \(V''\) at large \(h\) says that the graph is almost flat there, and we cannot determine the minimum precisely: at \(h = 8\) m the volume is only \(6\) % above the least one (\(3{,}0000/2{,}8284 = 1{,}060\)).

Figure 29.18 is an example where the lemma does not hold. For the function \(f(x) = (x^2 - 1)^2 + 0{,}4\,x\) we have \(f''(x) = 12x^2 - 4\), and at the peak \(x_2 = 0{,}1010\) \(f'' = -3{,}88 < 0\), so the matrix \([f'']\) is not positive semidefinite and the lemma does not apply. That the function is indeed not convex is told by the tangent. The tangent at \(x_2\) is horizontal at \(1{,}0201\), and the graph goes below it at \(x_1\), down to \(-0{,}4095\). This is exactly the reverse of the tangent inequality (29.14), so by lemma 29.20 the function is not convex. The lemma is a sufficient condition: for \(f(x) = x^4\) we have \(f''(0) = 0\), yet the function is strictly convex (CHK, example 3.2, PDF p. 48), so the positive definiteness of the second part of the lemma is not necessary.

A convex function together with a convex feasible set is called a convex problem. The feasible set arises from constraints \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \le 0\) (the letter \(g\) here is a constraint function, not the gravitational acceleration of section 2.2), and for it the following holds.

The lemma is shown in figure 29.31. On the left is the feasible set \(S\) as the intersection of the regions bounded by the curves \(g_1 = 0\) and \(g_2 = 0\). In it are the admissible points \(\vek x\) and \(\vek y\) and the segment between them, and on it the point \(\vek z\). On the right is the value of one constraint \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) along the segment: the values at the endpoints are not above zero, the chord between them is therefore below zero and below it is the graph of \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Lemma 29.24 The feasible set of convex constraints is convex (dopustna množica konveksnih omejitev je konveksna)

Let \(X\) be a convex set of points with \(n\) coordinates and \(g_1, \dots, g_{\mathrm{m}}\) convex functions on \(X\). Then the set \(S = \{\vek x \in X : g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \le 0,\ i = 1, \dots, m\}\) is convex.

Proof

We must show that for two admissible points every point of the segment between them stays admissible.

  1. Let \(\vek x, \vek y \in S\), \(0 \le t \le 1\) and \(\vek z = (1 - t)\,\vek x + t\,\vek y\). The point \(\vek z\) is in \(X\), because \(X\) is convex.
  2. For every \(i\), by (29.12), the graph is below the chord, that is, \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek z) \le (1 - t)\,g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) + t\,g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek y)\). Both numbers \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x)\) and \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek y)\) are not positive, so the right side is not positive either, since \(1 - t\) and \(t\) are nonnegative.
  3. So \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek z) \le 0\) for every \(i\) and \(\vek z \in S\).

Source: CHK lemma 3.1 (i) (PDF p. 47), without proof. The proof is not from the source.

Definition 29.25 Convex problem (konveksna naloga)

An optimization problem (definition 29.1) with objective function \(f\) and feasible set \(S\) is convex (konveksna) if \(S\) is a convex set and \(f\) is convex on \(S\).

Source: CHK §3.2 (PDF p. 47): "If both the objective function and the feasible set of (P) are convex, the problem is said to be convex."

By lemma 29.18 every local minimum of a convex problem is therefore global, which is what we set out to show at the beginning of the section. We test all this on the truss where we limit the displacement of the joint.

Example 29.26 Wall truss with a deflection constraint (paličje na steni s pogojem na pomik)

The wall truss has \(\mathrm{A} = (-4;\ 0)\), \(\mathrm{B} = (-4;\ 3)\), \(\mathrm{C} = (0;\ 0)\) m and the force \(F = 10\) kN downward at \(\mathrm{C}\), bars \(\mathrm{AC}\) of length \(4\) m and \(\mathrm{BC}\) of \(5\) m and axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13{,}333\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16{,}667\) kN (section 4.1.4). Let the downward displacement of the point \(\mathrm{C}\) be at most \(\delta = 2\) mm. By theorem 4.96, in which \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\) are the axial forces for a unit force downward, that is, \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}}/F\), the downward displacement is

\[v_{\mathrm{C}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}\,\frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{E\,A_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{c_{\mathrm{AC}}}{A_{\mathrm{AC}}} + \frac{c_{\mathrm{BC}}}{A_{\mathrm{BC}}} , \qquad c_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}^2\,L_{\mathrm{k}}}{F\,E} , \tag{29.15}\]

with \(E = 196\) GPa and the numbers \(c_{\mathrm{AC}} = 3{,}628 \cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^3\) and \(c_{\mathrm{BC}} = 7{,}086 \cdot 10^{-7}\) m\(^3\) (NumPy, num-03.py). At areas of \(100\) mm\(^2\) we have \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 10{,}714\) mm, as in chapter 7. The constraint is \(g(\vek A) = c_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}} + c_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}} - \delta \le 0\) on the open convex set \(X = \{A_{\mathrm{AC}} > 0,\ A_{\mathrm{BC}} > 0\}\) (a quadrant).

The Hessian matrix of the function \(g\) is diagonal, because every term of the sum \(g\) contains only one area:

\[\mat K(\vek A) = \begin{pmatrix} 2c_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}}^3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2c_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}}^3 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = \frac{2c_{\mathrm{AC}}}{A_{\mathrm{AC}}^3}\,d_1^2 + \frac{2c_{\mathrm{BC}}}{A_{\mathrm{BC}}^3}\,d_2^2 > 0 \quad (\vek d \ne \vek 0) . \tag{29.16}\]

Both numbers on the diagonal are positive at every area \(> 0\), so \(g\) is strictly convex on \(X\) by lemma 29.22 and by lemma 29.24 the set of admissible areas is convex. The objective function \(V = 4\,A_{\mathrm{AC}} + 5\,A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) (in m\(\cdot\)m\(^2\), the bar lengths are \(4\) and \(5\) m) is linear, hence convex (inequality (29.12) holds with equality). The problem is convex.

In figure 29.33, in the plane \((A_{\mathrm{AC}}, A_{\mathrm{BC}})\) the blue curve is the boundary \(g = 0\) of the feasible set, the admissible areas are above it, where the grey arrows point. Two admissible designs with the same displacement \(2\) mm are the least volume \(P\) with areas \(464{,}85\) and \(581{,}07\) mm\(^2\) and \(V = 4764{,}7\) cm\(^3\), and the equal areas \(Q\) of \(535{,}71\) mm\(^2\) each with \(V = 4821{,}4\) cm\(^3\). The segment \(PQ\) has the midpoint \(M = (500{,}28;\ 558{,}39)\) mm\(^2\). Its displacement is \(1{,}9942\) mm, so \(g(M) = -0{,}0058\) mm, and it is below the average of the numbers \(g(P) = g(Q) = 0\), as convexity requires ((29.12)). The volume at \(M\) is the average, \(4793{,}1\) cm\(^3\), because \(V\) is linear. The dashed lines are the lines \(4\,A_{\mathrm{AC}} + 5\,A_{\mathrm{BC}} = \) const. through \(P\) and \(Q\), of slope \(-4/5\). The line through \(P\) touches the curve, because there the gradient of the constraint is parallel to the gradient of the volume, which we will test in the next section.

Lemma 29.24 requires a convex constraint function, and this is a sufficient condition. For the buckling of the bar \(\mathrm{AC}\) the constraint is \(g = N - c\,A^2 \le 0\) with \(N = 13\,333\) N, \(c = \pi E/(4 L^2) = 9{,}621 \cdot 10^9\) N/m\(^4\) for a full circular cross-section (derivation in section 29.2), and \(g\) is concave. The feasible set is nevertheless the interval \(A \ge 1177{,}2\) mm\(^2\), hence convex. The convexity of the constraint function is therefore a sufficient but not a necessary condition of the lemma. A counterexample is the region \(1 \le x_1^2 + x_2^2 \le 2\) (CHK, PDF p. 47). The constraint \(1 - x_1^2 - x_2^2 \le 0\) has a concave function and the set is not convex: the points \((1, 0)\) and \((-1, 0)\) are in it, but their midpoint, the origin, is not. The convex function \(x_1^2 + x_2^2\) has infinitely many global minima on this set, all points with \(x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 1\) (CHK, PDF p. 47), so also the uniqueness from the third part of lemma 29.18 fails without a convex set.

We now know convexity with everything we need for the next section. A local minimum of a convex problem is global (lemma 29.18), a convex function is recognized by the tangent plane (lemma 29.20) or by the Hessian matrix (lemma 29.22), a convex feasible set by convex constraints (lemma 29.24), and a stationary point of a convex function is a bottom (corollary 29.21). The nonconvex set that the choice of bars demands has several local minima (example 29.19). What remains is the question of how to recognize at a point that it is a local minimum when the feasible set is bounded by inequalities and the minimum is not a stationary point. These are the conditions that we state in the next section. The existence of a minimum is guaranteed by lemma 29.8, convexity does not guarantee it. Lagrangian duality (CHK §3.4, PDF p. 55-64) we only name, we do not prove it.

29.4 KKT optimality conditions (pogoji optimalnosti KKT)

In section 29.2 we minimized the wall truss (bars AC and BC, force \(F = 10\) kN at joint C) by an argument: each stress constraint bounds the area of one bar, the volume grows with every area, so the best choice of areas is the one where the stress in every bar is exactly \(\sigma_0\). The argument rests on each constraint concerning a single area. If we add a constraint that involves both areas at once, for example the largest allowed deflection of joint C, there is no such argument any more. How do we recognize the best choice when the constraints tie the variables together? And what does the number we get along the way tell us about a constraint? The answer is the KKT conditions. This section derives them, shows when they suffice and when they do not, and tests them on the truss.

The model is the same as before: the truss of chapter 4 with two steel bars (\(E = 196\) GPa), lengths \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m and \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m, forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13\,333\) N and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16\,667\) N, which are fixed by the equilibrium of joint C and therefore do not depend on the areas (section 4.1.4, the bars are statically determinate). The allowed stress is \(\sigma_0 = 220\) MPa, without a safety factor, which is our idealization: a factor would multiply all areas by one number.

29.4.1 The problem and the active constraints

For the general theorems we need the letter \(\vek x\) for a point with \(n\) coordinates (definition 8.23), as in chapter 8. For the truss the coordinates are the cross-section areas, \(\vek x = (A_{\mathrm{AC}}, A_{\mathrm{BC}})\), a point in the plane of areas of the figure further down. The letter \(x\) is therefore not a position coordinate here. The problem (definition 29.1) is

\[\text{minimize } f(\vek x) \quad \text{subject to} \quad g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \le 0 , \quad i = 1, \dots, m , \quad \vek x \in D , \tag{29.17}\]

where \(D\) is an open set of points with \(n\) coordinates, \(f\) is the objective function (ciljna funkcija) and \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) are the constraints (omejitve), all continuously differentiable on \(D\). A point \(\vek x\) of \(D\) that satisfies all \(m\) inequalities is feasible (definition 29.5). The equations of equilibrium do not appear in the problem: for the truss we solve them in advance, because the forces of the bars are known.

Let us draw the problem for the wall truss in the plane of the two areas (figure 29.35, left). Every point of the plane is one choice of both areas, so we draw the axes \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\). The volume is \(f = V = L_{\mathrm{AC}}A_{\mathrm{AC}} + L_{\mathrm{BC}}A_{\mathrm{BC}}\). Points of equal volume lie on a line of slope \(-L_{\mathrm{AC}}/L_{\mathrm{BC}} = -0{,}8\), so we draw two lines of constant volume, like the contour lines on a map (compare figure 4.251). The stress constraints are \(g_1 = |N_{\mathrm{AC}}| - \sigma_0A_{\mathrm{AC}} \le 0\) and \(g_2 = |N_{\mathrm{BC}}| - \sigma_0A_{\mathrm{BC}} \le 0\). The stress is the force of the bar per area, \(|N|/A \le \sigma_0\), and for \(A > 0\) this is the same requirement written without division. Both have a boundary, which is the line \(g_1 = 0\), that is \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 60{,}61\) mm², and the line \(g_2 = 0\), that is \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 75{,}76\) mm². The feasible set lies to the right and above. The contour lines of volume \(V_1 = 621{,}2\) cm³ and \(V_2 = 1000\) cm³ show that the volume decreases toward the lower left corner. The best point is therefore the corner \(P\), \(P = (60{,}61;\ 75{,}76)\) mm², in which both constraints hold with equality. We already reached this conclusion in section 29.2. Now we want to say the same with derivatives, because only that will work when the lines become curves.

We cannot improve the point \(P\), because every step in a feasible direction is a step toward larger volume. Let us say this with derivatives. For a move from \(P\) by \(h\,\vek d\) the volume changes by the chain rule (lemma 8.30) by \(h\,\nabla f\cdot\vek d\) to first order, where \(\nabla f = (L_{\mathrm{AC}}, L_{\mathrm{BC}}) = (4, 5)\) m. In both feasible directions along the sides, \(\vek d_1\) toward larger \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\vek d_2\) toward larger \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\), we have \(\nabla f\cdot\vek d_1 = 4\) m and \(\nabla f\cdot\vek d_2 = 5\) m, both positive. The same is said by writing the vector \(-\nabla f\) as the sum of vectors \(\mu_1\nabla g_1\) and \(\mu_2\nabla g_2\), which point out of the feasible set, with nonnegative numbers \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\). The vector \(-\nabla f\) is indeed the sum of these two at the corner.

The nonnegativity of the numbers \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\) has a physical reason that we know from section 8.3.7, where the multipliers are the forces of the constraints. Let us draw both boundaries as flat walls that the point must not cross. At the corner \(P\) we imagine a small ball. The vector \(-\nabla f = (-4, -5)\) m pulls it as a force toward smaller volume, just as weight pulls a ball down a slope. The walls push it back, the force of a wall is \(-\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}\): the first pushes in the direction of larger \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) with the vector \(-\mu_1\nabla g_1 = (4, 0)\) m, the second in the direction of larger \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) with the vector \(-\mu_2\nabla g_2 = (0, 5)\) m. Both point into the feasible set, because \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\). The three forces, laid one after another, close a triangle, so their sum is zero: \(-\nabla f - \mu_1\nabla g_1 - \mu_2\nabla g_2 = \vek 0\). A wall that does not touch the point has \(g_{\mathrm{i}} < 0\) and does not push, so \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). The force of a wall with \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} < 0\) would point out of the feasible set and the wall would pull the point. A one-sided constraint cannot do this, so this force is crossed out and always \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\).

Definition 29.27 Active constraint (aktivni pogoj)

Let \(\vek x^*\) be a feasible point of problem (29.17). The constraint \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) is active (aktivna) at \(\vek x^*\) if \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*) = 0\), and inactive (neaktivna) if \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*) < 0\). The set \(I(\vek x^*) = \{\,i : g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*) = 0\,\}\) is the set of active indices, and we denote its size by \(k\). In figure 29.35 both constraints are active at the corner \(P\), because both boundaries pass through \(P\).

The name has a reason. The neighbourhood of the point \(\vek x^*\) is a ball \(B\) and in it the coordinate directions through \(\vek x^*\). An active constraint at a point is working: its boundary \(g_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) passes through \(\vek x^*\), it holds the point at the boundary and forbids it to go further. An inactive one does nothing, because \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) has a negative value at \(\vek x^*\) and by continuity also at nearby points, so its boundary lies outside the ball and a move from \(\vek x^*\) cannot cross its boundary. At the corner \(P\) the active ones are \(g_1\) and \(g_2\), because the two boundaries pass through the corner. The constraints that the area is not negative, \(g_3 = -A_{\mathrm{AC}} \le 0\) and \(g_4 = -A_{\mathrm{BC}} \le 0\), are inactive, because \(-60{,}61 < 0\) and \(-75{,}76 < 0\).

We write the connection with section 8.3.5 in a function that collects the objective function and the constraints.

Definition 29.28 Lagrangian and KKT conditions (Lagrangeeva funkcija in pogoji KKT)

The Lagrangian (Lagrangeeva funkcija) of problem (29.17) is the function of the point \(\vek x\) of \(D\) and of the numbers \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_{\mathrm{m}}\),

\[\mathcal{L}(\vek x, \vek\mu) = f(\vek x) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{m}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\,g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) . \tag{29.18}\]

A feasible point \(\vek x^*\) and numbers \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_{\mathrm{m}}\) satisfy the KKT conditions (pogoji KKT) if

\[\nabla f(\vek x^*) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{m}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\,\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*) = \vek 0 , \qquad \mu_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0 , \qquad \mu_{\mathrm{i}}\,g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*) = 0 \quad (i = 1, \dots, m) . \tag{29.19}\]

The first equality is \(\nabla_{\vek{x}}\mathcal{L}(\vek x^*, \vek\mu) = \vek 0\), and at the corner \(P\) of the figure the \(\nabla f\) and the vectors \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}\) cancel. The numbers \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\) are the multipliers (množitelji) of the constraints. The last equality is the complementarity condition (pogoj komplementarnosti).

Source: CHK §3.3 (PDF pp. 50-51), equations (3.3) and (3.7): \(\mathcal{L}(\vek x, \vek\lambda) = g_0(\vek x) + \sum \lambda_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x)\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) = 0\), at the words "The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions". CHK writes \(g_0\) for the objective function and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{i}}\) for the multipliers. We write \(f\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\), because \(\lambda\) in chapter 10 is an eigenvalue and in chapter 8 the multiplier of equations, which equals \(-\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\) (theorem 8.37 has \(\nabla V = \sum\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\nabla f_{\mathrm{r}}\)).

The names. The function is named after the Lagrange multipliers, because its derivative with respect to \(\vek x\), set equal to zero, is exactly equation (8.23) of chapter 8, only that here the multipliers belong to inequalities and have a sign. A multiplier is the number by which we multiply a constraint before adding it to the objective function. The abbreviation KKT stands for Karush, Kuhn and Tucker, as the source says. The complementarity condition is named for the fact that the numbers \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(-g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\), both nonnegative, complement each other: for every \(i\) at least one of them is zero. An inactive constraint, in the figure the condition \(A \ge 0\), has \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), because a wall that is not in contact with the body does not push. A constraint with \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\), in the figure the stress boundary, is active, because a wall pushes only when it touches.

29.4.2 The necessary condition

Are the KKT conditions really satisfied at a local minimum? The idea of the proof follows the figure. We take the active constraints as equations and use theorem 8.37, which gives the multipliers without a sign. The sign comes from a curve that leaves the corner in the direction \(\vek d_1\) or \(\vek d_2\) of the figure: along it we leave the corner so that one active constraint becomes inactive and all the others stay at the boundary. Along this curve \(f\) must not decrease, hence \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\). For the construction of the curve we need theorem 8.35 and therefore the condition on pivots, as in section 8.3.5.

Theorem 29.29 KKT conditions are necessary at a regular local minimum (pogoji KKT so v regularnem lokalnem minimumu potrebni)

Let \(f\) and \(g_1, \dots, g_{\mathrm{m}}\) be continuously differentiable on an open set \(D\) of points with \(n\) coordinates and let problem (29.17) have a local minimum at the feasible point \(\vek x^*\): there is a ball \(B\) centred at \(\vek x^*\) such that \(f(\vek x) \ge f(\vek x^*)\) for every feasible point \(\vek x\) of \(B\) (definition 29.15). Let the matrix \(\mat G\) with \(k\) rows \(\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)^\T\) (the gradients of the active constraints), \(i \in I(\vek x^*)\) (definition 29.27), have \(k\) pivots (definition 8.21). Then there exist numbers \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_{\mathrm{m}}\) that together with \(\vek x^*\) satisfy the KKT conditions (29.19), and the numbers \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\) with \(i \in I(\vek x^*)\) are uniquely determined.

Proof

We must show the equation with the multipliers, the uniqueness and the sign \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\). The first two come from the theorem on Lagrange multipliers for the active constraints, the last from the curve along which we leave the feasible set across a single constraint.

  1. Let \(\vek x^*\) be a local minimum in the ball \(B\) and \(k = |I(\vek x^*)|\). For \(j \notin I(\vek x^*)\) we have \(g_{\mathrm{j}}(\vek x^*) < 0\), and since \(g_{\mathrm{j}}\) is continuous, there is a ball centred at \(\vek x^*\) in which \(g_{\mathrm{j}} < 0\) (the definition of continuity with \(\varepsilon = |g_{\mathrm{j}}(\vek x^*)|\)), so the boundary \(g_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) lies outside it. We therefore shrink the radius of \(B\) so that it lies in \(D\) and that all inactive constraints are negative in it. Every point of the ball on an active boundary, with \(g_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for \(i \in I(\vek x^*)\) is now feasible, so \(f \ge f(\vek x^*)\) there. The point \(\vek x^*\) is thus a local minimum of \(f\) on the set of solutions of the equations \(g_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), \(i \in I(\vek x^*)\).
  2. For \(k = 0\) all constraints are inactive in the ball, \(\vek x^*\) is a local minimum of \(f\) on the ball. For every \(i\) the function \(h \mapsto f(\vek x^* + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}})\) has along the coordinate direction its smallest value at \(h = 0\), so by lemma 1.83 its derivative is \(\partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*) = 0\). Hence \(\nabla f(\vek x^*) = \vek 0\), which is (29.19) with all \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). From here on \(k \ge 1\).
  3. For \(1 \le k < n\) we use theorem 8.37 with \(V = f\), equations \(g_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) (\(i \in I(\vek x^*)\)), \(m = k\) and the matrix \(\mat G\) with \(k\) pivots: there is exactly one \(k\)-tuple of numbers \(\lambda_{\mathrm{i}}\) such that \(\nabla f(\vek x^*) = \sum_{\mathrm{i} \in \mathrm{I}(\vek{x}^*)}\lambda_{\mathrm{i}}\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\), as at the corner \(P\) the vector \(\nabla f\) is a combination of the gradients. For \(k = n\) the matrix \(\mat G\) is square with \(n\) pivots, so by lemma 8.22 \(\mat G^\T\) is invertible and the equation \(\mat G^\T\vek\lambda = \nabla f(\vek x^*)\) has exactly one solution, the same equality. The number \(k\) cannot be larger than \(n\), because the matrix \(\mat G\) has \(n\) columns and every pivot has its own column.
  4. The sign. Choose \(r \in I(\vek x^*)\), the constraint that we shall leave. Figure 29.39 shows a general corner with the boundaries of two active constraints beside the feasible set, the gradients point out of it, and \(r = 1\). We number the coordinates so that the pivot columns of \(\mat G\) are the last ones, \(\vek x = (\vek y, \vek z)\) with \(\vek z\) of \(k\) coordinates, \(\vek x^* = (\vek y^*, \vek z^*)\) and \(\mat G = [\mat G_{\mathrm{y}}\ \mat G_{\mathrm{z}}]\). The matrix \(\mat G_{\mathrm{z}}\) has \(k\) pivots (section 8.3.1). We define \(k\) functions of the number \(t\) and the column \(\vek z\): \(h_{\mathrm{i}}(t, \vek z) = g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek y^*, \vek z)\) for \(i \ne r\) and \(h_{\mathrm{r}}(t, \vek z) = g_{\mathrm{r}}(\vek y^*, \vek z) + t\). They are continuously differentiable, \(h_{\mathrm{i}}(0, \vek z^*) = 0\) for all \(i \in I(\vek x^*)\) and \(\partial\vek h/\partial\vek z(0, \vek z^*) = \mat G_{\mathrm{z}}\). By theorem 8.35 (with \(N = k + 1\) unknowns and \(k < N\) equations) there exist an open interval \(Y\) around \(0\) and a continuously differentiable map \(\vek\zeta\) on \(Y\) with \(\vek\zeta(0) = \vek z^*\) such that \(\vek h(t, \vek\zeta(t)) = \vek 0\). Let \(\vek x(t) = (\vek y^*, \vek\zeta(t))\). Then \(g_{\mathrm{r}}(\vek x(t)) = -t\) and \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x(t)) = 0\) for the other \(i \in I(\vek x^*)\): the curve runs along the boundary \(g_2 = 0\) and with growing \(t\) moves away from the boundary \(g_1 = 0\).
  5. The map \(\vek x(t)\) is continuous and \(\vek x(0) = \vek x^*\), so there is \(\tau > 0\) such that \(\vek x(t)\) lies in the ball of step 1 for \(|t| < \tau\). For \(0 \le t < \tau\) we have \(g_{\mathrm{r}} = -t \le 0\), the other active ones are zero and the inactive ones are negative (step 1), so \(\vek x(t)\), a point on the curve, is a feasible point in \(B\). Hence \(\varphi(t) = f(\vek x(t)) \ge f(\vek x^*) = \varphi(0)\) for \(0 \le t < \tau\): the graph on the interval does not fall below the line \(\varphi(0)\).
  6. By the chain rule (lemma 8.30) \(\varphi\) is differentiable at \(0\) with \(\varphi'(0) = \nabla f(\vek x^*)\cdot\vek x'(0)\). If \(\varphi'(0) < 0\), then by the definition of the derivative the graph would fall below the line \(\varphi(0)\) and there would be a small \(t > 0\) with \((\varphi(t) - \varphi(0))/t < 0\), which contradicts step 5. Hence \(\nabla f(\vek x^*)\cdot\vek x'(0) \ge 0\).
  7. The vector \(\vek x'(0)\) is the tangent of the curve at \(\vek x^*\). We differentiate the equalities \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x(t)) = -\delta_{\mathrm{ir}}t\) for \(i \in I(\vek x^*)\) at \(0\) by the chain rule: \(\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\cdot\vek x'(0) = -\delta_{\mathrm{ir}}\) (Kronecker delta, \(1\) for \(i = r\), otherwise \(0\)). In the figure the tangent is perpendicular to \(\nabla g_2\), because the curve stays on the boundary \(g_2 = 0\), and the projection of the tangent on the direction \(\nabla g_1\) lies on the opposite side from \(\nabla g_1\), because \(g_1\) falls along the curve. By step 3, \(\nabla f(\vek x^*)\cdot\vek x'(0) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\lambda_{\mathrm{i}}\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\cdot\vek x'(0) = -\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). By step 6, \(-\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge 0\): the projection of the vector \(\nabla f\) on the tangent lies ahead of \(\vek x^*\), in the direction of the curve.
  8. We set \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\) for \(i \in I(\vek x^*)\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) for \(j \notin I(\vek x^*)\). Thus \(-\nabla f\) is the sum of the vectors \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}\) with nonnegative \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\). Step 3 gives the first equality in (29.19), and the number \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\) is zero for active \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) and, for inactive ones, because \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). The uniqueness of the numbers \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\) (\(i \in I\)) follows from the uniqueness of the numbers \(\lambda_{\mathrm{i}}\) in step 3.

Source: The proof is not from the source. CHK §3.3 (PDF p. 51) claims that the KKT conditions are necessary for "sufficiently regular nonconvex problems" and cites Theorem 3.4 for convex problems with Slater's condition, without proofs (PDF p. 44: "All theorems are presented without proofs"). The pivot condition is our choice of regularity condition, because we know it from chapter 8.

The proof showed that the multipliers exist where the matrix of active gradients is good enough for the implicit function theorem to give a curve. The sign came from one curve per multiplier, and this step will return for every constraint we treat in this chapter.

29.4.3 Example: the two stress constraints

Let us check the theorem at the corner \(P\) of figure 29.35, left. The problem has four constraints: \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) (the stresses) and \(g_3\) and \(g_4\) (the areas are not negative), all linear. At \(P\) the active ones are \(g_1 = |N_{\mathrm{AC}}| - \sigma_0A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(g_2 = |N_{\mathrm{BC}}| - \sigma_0A_{\mathrm{BC}}\), so \(I(P) = \{1, 2\}\) and \(k = 2\). The gradients are \(\nabla g_1 = (-\sigma_0, 0)\) and \(\nabla g_2 = (0, -\sigma_0)\), the matrix \(\mat G = -\sigma_0\mat I\) has two pivots, regularity holds. The first equality of (29.19) is \((L_{\mathrm{AC}}, L_{\mathrm{BC}}) + \mu_1(-\sigma_0, 0) + \mu_2(0, -\sigma_0) = \vek 0\), so

\[\mu_1 = \frac{L_{\mathrm{AC}}}{\sigma_0} = \frac{4\ \text{m}}{220\cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa}} = 1{,}818\cdot 10^{-8}\ \frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{N}} , \qquad \mu_2 = \frac{L_{\mathrm{BC}}}{\sigma_0} = 2{,}273\cdot 10^{-8}\ \frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{N}} . \tag{29.20}\]

Both are positive. The sum \(\mu_1\nabla g_1 + \mu_2\nabla g_2 = (-4, -5)\) m is the vector \(-\nabla f\) of the figure, and complementarity holds because the inactive constraints \(g_3\) and \(g_4\) get \(\mu_3 = \mu_4 = 0\). The point \(P\) is therefore a KKT point.

The multiplier has the meaning of a price. In figure 29.40 we enlarge the neighbourhood of the corner \(P\), so the axes do not start at zero. If the axial force \(|N_{\mathrm{AC}}|\) grows by 1 kN, the bar must carry more and the area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = |N_{\mathrm{AC}}|/\sigma_0\) grows. The boundary \(g_1 = 0\) before the change is grey dashed, the boundary after the change is orange, it has moved to the right by \(1000\ \text{N}/(220\ \text{MPa}) = 4{,}545\) mm². The boundary \(g_2 = 0\) stays in place, so the corner \(P\) moves to \(P'\). The contour line through the corner moves from \(621{,}2\) to \(639{,}4\) cm³: the volume increases by \(\mu_1 \cdot 1000\ \text{N} = 1{,}818\cdot 10^{-5}\) m³ \(= 18{,}18\) cm³, which is \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m times \(4{,}545\) mm². For \(|N_{\mathrm{BC}}|\) it is \(22{,}73\) cm³ per kN. We checked this directly: the least volume is \(V^* = (L_{\mathrm{AC}}|N_{\mathrm{AC}}| + L_{\mathrm{BC}}|N_{\mathrm{BC}}|)/\sigma_0 = 621{,}2\) cm³ and its derivative with respect to \(|N_{\mathrm{AC}}|\) is \(L_{\mathrm{AC}}/\sigma_0 = \mu_1\). That the multiplier of every constraint is such a derivative, we do not prove here in general. For this problem we saw it on a closed form, and for the deflection problem we will check it once more.

Is \(P\) really the best point? Theorem 29.29 says only that a regular local minimum is a KKT point. The converse must be said by another theorem. First, though, let us see what happens when regularity is missing.

29.4.4 An edge where the necessary condition fails

Theorem 29.29 demands that the matrix of active gradients have \(k\) pivots. Let us test whether the condition is really needed: we look for a problem where the minimum is clear, at the cusp of the set, and the pivot condition does not hold.

Let us minimize \(f = -x_1\) subject to \(g_1 = x_2 - (1 - x_1)^3 \le 0\) and \(g_2 = -x_2 \le 0\). The feasible set is \(0 \le x_2 \le (1 - x_1)^3\), so we need \((1 - x_1)^3 \ge 0\) and \(x_1 \le 1\) (figure 29.41). In the plane we draw the axes \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Because \(x_1 \le 1\), the smallest value of \(f\) is \(-1\), reached at the point \(S = (1, 0)\), which is a cusp (ost) of the set where the two curves touch. The set is a grey strip between the \(x_1\) axis and the curve \(x_2 = (1 - x_1)^3\), narrowed to a point at \(S\). The figure shows only its part with \(x_1 \ge 0\), to the left the strip goes on and widens. At \(S\) both constraints are active, the gradients \(\nabla g_1 = (0, 1)\) and \(\nabla g_2 = (0, -1)\) point in opposite directions, and \(\nabla f = (-1, 0)\) is perpendicular to them. Equation (29.19) would demand \((-1, 0) + \mu_1(0, 1) + \mu_2(0, -1) = \vek 0\), so \(-1 = 0\) in the first component. There are no multipliers. The vector \(-\nabla f = (1, 0)\) points out of the set, but is not a combination of the two gradients.

The proof of the theorem shows where it fails. The rows of \(\mat G\) are the two gradients, pointing in opposite directions. The matrix \(\mat G = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) has after elimination (add the first row to the second) only one pivot, in the second column, so \(1 < k = 2\). Step 4 would need a curve on which \(g_2 = 0\) and \(g_1 = -t\). From \(g_2 = 0\) we get \(x_2 = 0\), from \(g_1 = -t\) we get \((1 - x_1)^3 = t\), so \(x_1 = 1 - t^{1/3}\). The curve runs along the lower edge of the strip into the cusp \(S\) and exists, but its derivative at \(t = 0\) does not. In figure 29.42 we put \(t\) horizontally and the distance \(1 - x_1\) from the cusp vertically. The curve \(1 - x_1 = t^{1/3}\) leaves the origin straight up. The quotient \((1 - x_1)/t = t^{-2/3}\) is the slope of the secant from the origin to a point of the curve: \(1{,}59\) at \(t = 0{,}5\), \(4{,}64\) at \(t = 0{,}1\) and \(21{,}5\) at \(t = 0{,}01\), and outside the figure \(100\) at \(t = 10^{-3}\) and \(10^4\) at \(t = 10^{-6}\). With smaller \(t\) the secants turn toward the vertical, the slope grows beyond every bound, so \(x'(0)\) does not exist. Without it steps 6 and 7 are gone. The pivot condition is therefore not decoration: without it the theorem does not hold.

29.4.5 A sufficient condition for convex problems

The necessary condition finds candidates. Is a candidate really a minimum? For a function of one variable a zero derivative does not mean a minimum (the point \(x = 0\) of the parabola below has \(f' = 0\) and is a maximum), and so it is here. When, however, \(f\) and the set are convex, definitions 29.17 and 29.16, lemma 29.20 on the tangent plane gives us everything we need.

We shall follow the proof on a problem with one variable as well. On the axes we put \(x\) horizontally and the value of the functions vertically. Let us minimize \(f = (x - 2)^2\) subject to the condition \(g = x - 1 \le 0\). At \(x^* = 1\) we have \(f' = -2\) and \(g' = 1\), and the equation \(-2 + \mu = 0\) gives \(\mu = 2\). The function \(f + \mu g = (x - 1)^2 + 1\) has at \(x^*\) a horizontal tangent at the height \(f(x^*) = 1\). At the feasible point \(x = 0\) we have \(f = 4\) and \(f + \mu g = 2\).

Theorem 29.30 KKT conditions are sufficient for a convex problem (pogoji KKT so pri konveksni nalogi zadostni)

Let \(D\) be an open convex set of points with \(n\) coordinates and let \(f\) and \(g_1, \dots, g_{\mathrm{m}}\) be convex and continuously differentiable functions on \(D\) (the graph of a convex function lies above its tangent). Let a feasible point \(\vek x^*\) and numbers \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_{\mathrm{m}}\) satisfy the KKT conditions (29.19). Then \(f(\vek x) \ge f(\vek x^*)\) for every feasible point \(\vek x\), so \(\vek x^*\) is a global minimum of problem (29.17).

Proof

We must show that the sum of the tangent inequalities, multiplied by the multipliers, gives \(f(\vek x) \ge f(\vek x^*)\). We do not need the pivot condition.

  1. Let \(\vek x\) be a feasible point. By lemma 29.20 for a convex and continuously differentiable function the graph of \(f\) lies above its tangent, \(f(\vek x) \ge f(\vek x^*) + \nabla f(\vek x^*)\cdot(\vek x - \vek x^*)\), and the graph of \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) above its tangent, \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \ge g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*) + \nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\cdot(\vek x - \vek x^*)\) for every \(i\).
  2. We multiply the inequalities for \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) by \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\), which keeps the direction of the inequality, and add them to the inequality for \(f\): \(f(\vek x) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \ge f(\vek x^*) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*) + \big[\nabla f(\vek x^*) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\big]\cdot(\vek x - \vek x^*)\). On the left is the sum \(f + \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}g_{\mathrm{i}}\), on the right its tangent at \(\vek x^*\).
  3. By the first equality of (29.19) the square bracket is \(\vek 0\) (at the corner \(P\) the \(\nabla f\) and the \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}\) cancel). By the complementarity condition \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*) = 0\). The tangent of the sum is therefore horizontal at the height \(f(\vek x^*)\) and \(f(\vek x) + \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \ge f(\vek x^*)\): the lower bar is not negative.
  4. The point \(\vek x\) is feasible, \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \le 0\), and \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\), so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \le 0\). The upper bar, the difference \(-\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x)\) between \(f\) and the sum, is therefore not negative either. From step 3 it follows that \(f(\vek x) \ge f(\vek x^*) - \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\mu_{\mathrm{i}}g_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \ge f(\vek x^*)\): the difference \(f(\vek x) - f(\vek x^*)\) is the sum of both bars.

Source: CHK §3.3 (PDF p. 51), Theorem 3.5: "Let (P) be a convex problem, and let (x∗,λ∗) be a KKT point of (P). Then x∗ is a local (i.e. also global) minimum", without proof. The proof is not from the source.

The theorem says that \(P\) of the example of stress constraints is a global minimum: \(f\) (the contour lines are straight) and all \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) (the boundaries are straight) are linear functions, hence convex (a linear function lies on its tangent plane), \(D = \mathbb{R}^2\) is convex and \(\mu_1, \mu_2 > 0\). The matter is now proved with derivatives and no longer only by an argument of monotonicity. We also got the \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\), which the argument did not give.

Convexity is a condition we must not leave out, as the following problem shows. Let us minimize \(f = -x^2\) subject to \(g_1 = x - 1 \le 0\) and \(g_2 = -x - 1 \le 0\), that is on the interval \([-1, 1]\) (figure 29.45). On the axes we put \(x\) horizontally and the value of \(f\) vertically. We draw the parabola \(f = -x^2\) only between the grey dashed lines \(x = -1\) and \(x = 1\), which are the bounds \(g_2 = 0\) and \(g_1 = 0\). At the point \(x = 1\) the constraint \(g_1\) is active, \(f'(1) = -2\), \(g_1' = 1\) and the equation \(-2 + \mu_1 = 0\) gives \(\mu_1 = 2 \ge 0\), so it is a KKT point, and by symmetry so is \(x = -1\) with \(\mu_2 = 2\). At \(x = 0\) there is no active constraint and \(f'(0) = 0\), so the KKT conditions hold with all \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). The values of \(f\) are \(-1\) at \(x = \pm 1\) and \(0\) at \(x = 0\). The points \(x = \pm 1\) are minima, and the point \(x = 0\) is even a maximum. The gradients \(\nabla f\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{i}}\nabla g_{\mathrm{i}}\) cancel at all three points, but only at two of them is it a minimum. The function \(-x^2\) is not convex (its second derivative is \(-2 < 0\)), so theorem 29.30 does not apply. KKT points are candidates and nothing more, if the problem is not convex.

29.4.6 Example: the deflection constraint

Now a problem that thinking about each area separately does not solve. Let the wall truss have, besides the stress constraints, the requirement that joint C moves down under the force \(F\) by at most \(\Delta_0 = 2\) mm. This is the requirement of the designer, not a law. The deflection \(\Delta = -v_{\mathrm{C}}\) of bars with areas \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) is obtained by the unit force method (theorem 4.96). The forces in the bars for a unit vertical force are, because equilibrium is linear, \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}}/F\), so

\[\Delta(\vek x) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 L_{\mathrm{k}}}{F\,E\,A_{\mathrm{k}}} = \frac{c_{\mathrm{AC}}}{A_{\mathrm{AC}}} + \frac{c_{\mathrm{BC}}}{A_{\mathrm{BC}}} , \qquad c_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{k}}^2 L_{\mathrm{k}}}{F E} , \tag{29.21}\]

with \(c_{\mathrm{AC}} = 3{,}628\cdot 10^{-7}\) m³ and \(c_{\mathrm{BC}} = 7{,}086\cdot 10^{-7}\) m³. We check with the equilibrium of section 7.5.2: at \(100\) mm² per bar \(\Delta = (c_{\mathrm{AC}} + c_{\mathrm{BC}})/10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 = 10{,}714\) mm, which is the deflection \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -10{,}714\) mm found there. The additional constraint is \(g_{\mathrm{v}}(\vek x) = \Delta(\vek x) - \Delta_0 \le 0\) on \(D = \{A_{\mathrm{AC}} > 0,\ A_{\mathrm{BC}} > 0\}\), which is open and convex. The function \(1/A\) has on \(A > 0\) the second derivative \(2/A^3 > 0\), so it is convex (lemma 29.22), and \(g_{\mathrm{v}}\) is a sum of two convex functions with positive factors, so convex and continuously differentiable. The objective function \(V\) is linear. The problem is therefore convex and theorem 29.30 applies.

First we guess which constraint is active. In figure 29.47 the trusses before loading are grey dashed, the displacements are enlarged. The truss with the areas from the corner \(P\) deflects under the force by \(\Delta = 15{,}34\) mm by (29.21), which exceeds the limit \(\Delta_0 = 2\) mm more than seven times. The point \(P\) is therefore not feasible and the deflection constraint must be active. We guess that the stress constraints are inactive, and check this after the computation. The gradient is \(\nabla g_{\mathrm{v}} = (-c_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}}^2,\ -c_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}}^2)\), nonzero, so the matrix with one row has one pivot and regularity holds. The first equality of (29.19) with \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = 0\) for the stress constraints and \(\mu\) for the deflection is

\[L_{\mathrm{k}} - \mu\,\frac{c_{\mathrm{k}}}{A_{\mathrm{k}}^2} = 0 \quad (k = AC, BC) , \qquad\text{so}\qquad A_{\mathrm{k}} = \sqrt{\mu\,c_{\mathrm{k}}/L_{\mathrm{k}}} . \tag{29.22}\]

We insert this into the active constraint \(\Delta = \Delta_0\): \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} c_{\mathrm{k}}/A_{\mathrm{k}} = \mu^{-1/2}\sum_{\mathrm{k}}\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{k}}L_{\mathrm{k}}} = \Delta_0\). With \(S = \sum_{\mathrm{k}}\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{k}}L_{\mathrm{k}}} = 3{,}087\cdot 10^{-3}\) m² we have \(\sqrt\mu = S/\Delta_0\) and

\[A_{\mathrm{k}} = \sqrt{\frac{c_{\mathrm{k}}}{L_{\mathrm{k}}}}\,\frac{S}{\Delta_0} , \qquad \mu = \Big(\frac{S}{\Delta_0}\Big)^2 = 2{,}382\ \frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{m}} . \tag{29.23}\]

The numbers: \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 464{,}85\) mm², \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 581{,}07\) mm² and \(V^* = 4764{,}7\) cm³. The truss with these areas deflects by exactly \(\Delta_0\). We draw this in the same plane (figure 29.35, right, 1 cm is now 250 mm²). Because of the new scale the stress limits lie close to the axes, far from the point we seek. The contour line of volume has the same slope \(-0{,}8\) as before, and the deflection boundary is a curve, because \(\Delta\) is a sum of quotients \(c_{\mathrm{k}}/A_{\mathrm{k}}\). The optimum is the point \(Q\), where the contour line touches the curve. The vector \(\mu\nabla g_{\mathrm{v}}\) and the vector \(-\nabla f\) are equal: \(\mu\nabla g_{\mathrm{v}} = (-4{,}000, -5{,}000)\) m and \(-\nabla f = (-4, -5)\) m, because \(\mu\,c_{\mathrm{k}}/A_{\mathrm{k}}^2 = L_{\mathrm{k}}\) by (29.22). We had the same picture at the corner \(P\), only that the boundary curve is bent and a single constraint is active. CHK solves in example 3.5 (PDF pp. 52-54) a truss of two bars with a deflection and a stress constraint and obtains the same: only the multiplier of the deflection is nonzero.

We still check the guess for the inactive constraints. The stresses are \(|N_{\mathrm{k}}|/A_{\mathrm{k}} = 28{,}68\) MPa in both bars, far below \(220\) MPa, so the point \(Q\) lies far from the stress limits and \(g_1 = |N_{\mathrm{AC}}| - \sigma_0A_{\mathrm{AC}} = -88{,}9\) kN and \(g_2 = -111{,}2\) kN, both negative, and \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = 0\) agrees with complementarity. That the stresses are equal we did not assume, it came out of (29.22): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^2 = N_{\mathrm{k}}^2/A_{\mathrm{k}}^2 = N_{\mathrm{k}}^2L_{\mathrm{k}}/(\mu c_{\mathrm{k}}) = EF/\mu\), where we inserted \(c_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}}^2L_{\mathrm{k}}/(FE)\) from (29.21). Theorem 29.30 therefore says that \(Q\) is a global minimum: no choice of areas with a deflection up to \(2\) mm uses less material. Bars with equal areas \(535{,}71\) mm² (the same deflection) use \(4821{,}4\) cm³, which is \(1{,}2\) % more.

The multiplier has the same meaning of a price here. If we allow a larger deflection \(\Delta_0\), the least volume from (29.23) is \(V^*(\Delta_0) = L_{\mathrm{AC}}A_{\mathrm{AC}} + L_{\mathrm{BC}}A_{\mathrm{BC}} = S^2/\Delta_0\), so the slope of the tangent is \(\mathrm{d}V^*/\mathrm{d}\Delta_0 = -S^2/\Delta_0^2 = -\mu\). The multiplier \(\mu = 2{,}382\) m³ per metre, that is \(2382\) cm³ per millimetre, tells how much volume we save if we allow the deflection to be a millimetre larger, to first order. The estimate is good for small changes: at \(\Delta_0 = 2{,}1\) mm (5 % more) the exact volume is \(4537{,}8\) cm³, the estimate \(4764{,}7 - 238{,}2 = 4526{,}5\) cm³, a difference of \(0{,}25\) %, because \(V^* \propto 1/\Delta_0\): for \(\Delta_0' = (1 + \varepsilon)\Delta_0\) the estimate is \(V^*(1 - \varepsilon)\), the exact value is \(V^*/(1 + \varepsilon)\), and the relative error is exactly \(\varepsilon^2\), so \(0{,}0025\) for \(\varepsilon = 0{,}05\). At \(\Delta_0 = 3\) mm (\(50\) % more) the estimate fails: \(V^* = S^2/\Delta_0 = 3176{,}5\) cm³, while the estimate is \(4764{,}7 - 2382{,}4 = 2382{,}4\) cm³, which is \(25\) % too low.

The guess about the active constraints holds only in a certain range. The stress \(\sigma = \Delta_0\sqrt{EF}/S\) in both bars grows with the allowed deflection: \(71{,}7\) MPa at \(5\) mm, \(143{,}4\) MPa at \(10\) mm and \(220\) MPa at \(\Delta_0 = 15{,}34\) mm, when both stress limits are touched. That is exactly the deflection of the truss with areas \(60{,}61\) and \(75{,}76\) mm² from the corner \(P\). At a larger \(\Delta_0\) the deflection constraint at \(P\) is no longer violated, and by theorem 29.30 the optimum is again \(P\) (the horizontal part of the graph) with the deflection multiplier zero. Active are therefore either the stress constraints (point \(P\), \(\Delta_0 \ge 15{,}34\) mm) or the deflection constraint (point \(Q\), \(\Delta_0 \le 15{,}34\) mm), never both at once except at the limit that separates them. Complementarity said this without an additional computation.

Summary of the section. We derived the KKT conditions from the theorem on Lagrange multipliers and from a curve that leaves across one constraint, under the pivot condition (theorem 29.29), and showed that without the pivot condition they fail (the cusp). For convex problems they are sufficient (theorem 29.30, proved with tangent planes), for nonconvex ones they are not (\(f = -x^2\)). On the truss we saw both cases: two active constraints at a corner with multipliers \(L_{\mathrm{i}}/\sigma_0\), and one active curve with multiplier \(S^2/\Delta_0^2\). The multiplier is the price of a constraint. We will use these conditions in the following sections of this chapter, in least compliance and in sequential approximations. The Lagrange duality, which turns the KKT conditions into a second problem with the same optimum, we only name here: it is in CHK §3.4 (PDF pp. 55-64) and we do not prove it.

29.5 Minimum compliance (najmanjša podajnost)

We have \(300\ \text{cm}^3\) of steel and three places to put it. How much do we give to each place so that the structure under a given load is as stiff as possible? Take a wall and on it three points \(S_1\), \(S_2\) and \(S_3\) in a horizontal row, \(1\) m apart (supports). The letter \(S\) is the initial of the Slovenian word for support (podpora, in English support), since each of the points has that job. One metre below the middle point is the joint \(C\), free to move (joint \(C\)). We connect each point \(S_{\mathrm{e}}\) to the point \(C\) with a steel bar \(e\) (bars), \(e = 1, 2, 3\), and pull at \(C\) with the force \(F = 10\) kN (force), which makes the angle \(\theta\) with the downward direction (angle, figure 29.49). The bars need not all be equally thick. The thickness of a line is proportional to the cross-section of the bar, and a dashed thin line is a bar with cross-section zero, which is only still written down in the truss. Three directions of the force are drawn, \(\theta = 0^\circ\), \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\), each with the best cross-sections that we shall find.

Such a truss is the model of section 7.5.2: the bars are joined with pins (definition 4.4), forces act only at the joints, displacements are small and the material is linearly elastic with \(E = 196\) GPa (definition 3.1). The joints and their connections were chosen in advance. Such a net is called the ground structure (izhodiščno paličje), because we start from it and because optimization takes the whole cross-section from some bars. The unknowns are the cross-sections \(A_1\), \(A_2\), \(A_3\), which we write in the column \(\vek A\), these are the design variables (projektne spremenljivke) of definition 29.1. Each bar \(e\) has a length \(L_{\mathrm{e}}\), and both numbers \(L_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) determine the volume of material \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\). The weight of the bars is negligible, as definition 4.4 requires: \(300\ \text{cm}^3\) of steel has the mass \(2{,}34\) kg and the weight \(22{,}96\) N, which is \(0{,}23\ \%\) of the force \(F\). We therefore do not count the weight among the loads, and the load does not depend on the design.

Two of these assumptions have a cost, which we state here already. First, the displacements are small, because the calculation puts the equilibrium on the undeformed shape: at the optimum with \(\theta = 30^\circ\) the displacement is \(0{,}23\) mm against lengths of \(1\) m, a ratio of \(2{,}3\cdot 10^{-4}\), and the bar directions turn by about \(2{,}3\cdot 10^{-4}\) rad, and the forces in the bars change because of this by less than \(0{,}1\ \%\). For a truss that is near a mechanism and has a very small stiffness this no longer holds, and this section does not treat such a case. Second, there is a single load, the force \(F\) at the angle \(\theta\). The design is best only for it: the optimum at \(\theta = 0^\circ\) has one single vertical bar, and if a small horizontal force also acted at the joint \(C\), the joint would move without limit under it, since one bar alone is a mechanism. The model does not notice this because it has no horizontal force. Several loads at once are treated in section 29.10.1.

Before we ask which design is best, we must say what it means to be stiff. For one bar the answer is known. Bar \(e\) with length \(L_{\mathrm{e}}\) and cross-section \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) is fixed to the wall at one end, and at the other is the joint, which the force moves by the displacement \(\vek v\). Only the projection of the displacement on the direction of the bar extends the bar, under the force \(F\) along the bar it is \(F L/(EA)\), and the smaller this extension, the stiffer the bar. In a truss with several joints every joint has its own displacement, and we must choose one number.

29.5.1 Compliance of a truss (podajnost paličja)

First let us write how the cross-sections enter the stiffness. We collect the displacements of the free joints, in our case two numbers, the horizontal and the vertical displacement of the joint \(C\), in the column \(\vek u\), and the forces in their directions in the column \(\vek F\). The structure matrix \(\mat K\) in the free unknowns (theorem 7.18) is assembled from the bar matrices (theorem 7.13). The bar matrix in global axes (lemma 7.28) is multiplied by the cross-section \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\), and so the cross-section steps out of the assembly.

Lemma 29.31 Stiffness is linear in the areas (togost je linearna v presekih)

Let a truss have \(n\) bars with lengths \(L_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) and modulus \(E\), and supports that prescribe zero displacement of some joints. Let \(\mat K(\vek A)\) be the structure matrix in the free unknowns (theorem 7.18) at cross-sections \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{n}} \ge 0\). Let \(\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the unit vector of bar \(e\) from the end \(i\) towards the end \(j\) and

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek v) = \frac{\vek n_{\mathrm{e}} \cdot (\vek v_{\mathrm{j}} - \vek v_{\mathrm{i}})}{L_{\mathrm{e}}} \tag{29.24}\]

the extension of the bar per length at displacements \(\vek v\) of the free unknowns, where the displacement of a supported end is zero. Then

\[\mat K(\vek A) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{n} A_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}} , \qquad \vek v^\T \mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek v = E\,L_{\mathrm{e}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek v)^2 , \tag{29.25}\]

where \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) are symmetric matrices that do not depend on the cross-sections. The matrix \(\mat K(\vek A)\) is symmetric and \(\vek v^\T \mat K(\vek A)\,\vek v \ge 0\) for every \(\vek v\).

Proof

We must show that the bar matrix is linear in \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\), that the linearity carries over to the sum, and that the quadratic form of the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) gives the extension.

  1. By lemma 7.28, \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\mathrm{e}}\,\frac{E}{L_{\mathrm{e}}}\begin{bmatrix} \vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}^\T & -\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}^\T \\ -\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}^\T & \vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}^\T \end{bmatrix} = A_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^{0}\), where the matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^{0}\) does not contain the cross-section.
  2. By theorem 7.13, \(\mat K = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^{0}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\). We denote \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^{0}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) and obtain the first equation (29.25).
  3. By lemma 7.28, \(\tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,\frac{EA_{\mathrm{e}}}{L_{\mathrm{e}}}\,e^2\) with the elongation \(e = \vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot(\vek u_{\mathrm{j}} - \vek u_{\mathrm{i}})\). At \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = 1\) we therefore have \(\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek v = \frac{E}{L_{\mathrm{e}}}\,e^2 = E\,L_{\mathrm{e}}\,(e/L_{\mathrm{e}})^2 = E\,L_{\mathrm{e}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek v)^2\), where we used \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\vek v\) (point 2 of theorem 7.13).
  4. The symmetry and nonnegativity of the matrix \(\mat K(\vek A)\) are consequences of 7.14, since \(\vek v^\T \mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek v \ge 0\) by step 3 and \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\).

Source: The lemma is from ch7 and from CHK (5.7), (5.11), (5.12) (PDF p. 86-87), where \(\mat K = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} x_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{j}}^0\). The proof is ours, from chapter 7.

Here we also use that \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek v)\) is the extension of the bar per unit length, so the strain of bar \(e\) at displacements \(\vek v\), and that \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) is twice the strain energy density of the bar, since by lemma 4.5 the stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{e}} = E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}\) and the energy per volume of the bar is \(\tfrac12\,\sigma_{\mathrm{e}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\). This quantity will be at the centre of the section.

Let us draw this with one unknown, to see what the compliance is. On the axes of the left part are the displacement \(v\) and the force \(F\), and on the right the displacement \(v\) and \(\Pi\), while the labels \(u\) and \(F\) mark the point where the displacement and the force meet. On the left is the line of force against displacement, \(F = k\,v\), and at the load \(F\) we reach the point with the displacement \(u\). The work of a force that grows from zero is the area of the triangle, the strain energy \(U = \tfrac12 F u\), and the rectangle \(F\,u\) is twice as much, the compliance \(C\). On the right, for every displacement \(v\) there is the total potential energy, which has its lowest point at \(v = u\) with the value \(-C/2\), and the inverted parabola \(2Fv - kv^2\), which has its peak at the same \(u\) with the value \(C\). The gap between the peak and the parabola at a chosen \(v\) is \(k(v - u)^2\), never negative.

Definition 29.32 Compliance of a truss (podajnost paličja)

Let \(\mat K(\vek A)\) be the structure matrix of lemma 29.31 at cross-sections \(\vek A \ge 0\) and \(\vek F \ne \vek 0\) the column of loads in the directions of the free unknowns. If the system \(\mat K(\vek A)\,\vek u = \vek F\) has a solution, the compliance (podajnost) of the truss is the number

\[C(\vek A) = \vek F^\T\vek u , \tag{29.26}\]

where \(\vek u\) is any solution. If the system has no solution, that is if the load cannot be in equilibrium, we set \(C(\vek A) = +\infty\). The compliance is a number in joules, a function of the cross-sections \(\vek A\).

Source: CHK §5.1 (PDF p. 84): "the compliance \(C\) of the truss, i.e. \(F^T u\)". The comparison with \(C = +\infty\) and the independence of the solution are ours.

The name is from before: the compliance matrix (definition 4.139) gives displacements from forces, and for a positive definite matrix \(\mat K\) the number \(C = \vek F^\T\mat K^{-1}\vek F\) is its quadratic form, since \(\vek u = \mat K^{-1}\vek F\). For one bar \(C = F\cdot FL/(EA) = F^2/k\) with the stiffness \(k = EA/L\): the more a structure gives way under the force, the more compliant it is, and the smaller the compliance, the stiffer it is. In chapter 10 the letter \(C\) means the damping matrix, here it always means the number \(C(\vek A)\).

Why this number and not, for example, the horizontal displacement of the joint? The first reason is energy. By the lemma below, \(C\) is twice the strain energy, so what the structure stores. The second reason is that \(C\) is a convex function of the cross-sections (theorem 29.34), while the displacement of a joint in one direction is not (below with numbers), and the convexity from section 29.3 is what gives the optimum its reliability. The third reason is that in the best truss all bars with material have the same stress (corollary 29.38), which recalls the sizing by stresses of section 29.2.

Lemma 29.33 Compliance and energy (podajnost in energija)

Let \(\mat K = \mat K(\vek A)\) be the matrix of lemma 29.31 and \(\vek u\) a solution of the system \(\mat K\vek u = \vek F\). Then:

  1. the number \(\vek F^\T\vek u\) is the same for all solutions of the system,
  2. \(C = \vek F^\T\vek u = \vek u^\T\mat K\vek u = 2U\), where \(U = \tfrac12\,\vek u^\T\mat K\vek u\) is the strain energy of the truss,
  3. the total potential energy \(\Pi(\vek v) = \tfrac12\,\vek v^\T\mat K\vek v - \vek F^\T\vek v\) (definition 4.89) at \(\vek v = \vek u\) equals \(-\tfrac12\,C\) and \(\Pi(\vek v) \ge \Pi(\vek u)\) for every \(\vek v\),
  4. for every \(\vek v\)
    \[2\,\vek F^\T\vek v - \vek v^\T\mat K(\vek A)\,\vek v = C(\vek A) - (\vek v - \vek u)^\T\mat K(\vek A)\,(\vek v - \vek u) \le C(\vek A) , \tag{29.27}\]
    with equality at \(\vek v = \vek u\). So \(C(\vek A) = \max_{\vek{v}}\big[2\,\vek F^\T\vek v - \vek v^\T\mat K(\vek A)\,\vek v\big]\).
Proof

We must show four points, all from the symmetry of the matrix \(\mat K\) and from \(\vek w^\T\mat K\vek w \ge 0\) (lemma 29.31).

  1. Let \(\vek u\) and \(\vek u'\) be solutions. Then \(\mat K(\vek u' - \vek u) = \vek 0\), so \(\vek F^\T(\vek u' - \vek u) = (\mat K\vek u)^\T(\vek u' - \vek u) = \vek u^\T\mat K^\T(\vek u' - \vek u) = \vek u^\T\mat K(\vek u' - \vek u) = 0\), because \(\mat K\) is symmetric. In figure 29.52 this is the case \(\theta = 0^\circ\). The wall with the points \(S_1\), \(S_2\) and \(S_3\) is where the supports are, the two outer bars are dashed because their cross-section is zero, and the material is only in the middle bar, so \(\mat K\) is singular. The difference of the solutions is a horizontal displacement, at which the middle bar does not extend to first order and therefore gives no force. The force \(F\) is perpendicular to it and does no work on it, so \(\vek F^\T\vek u = \vek F^\T\vek u' = 1{,}7007\) J. In general \(\vek F = \mat K\vek u\) is the sum of the forces of the bars, and on a displacement that extends no bar, none of them does work. The scale \(1\,\mathrm{m}\) holds for the drawing only, the displacements are drawn \(3000\) times larger.
  2. From \(\vek F = \mat K\vek u\) we get \(\vek F^\T\vek u = \vek u^\T\mat K^\T\vek u = \vek u^\T\mat K\vek u\). By point 2 of theorem 7.13, \(\tfrac12\,\vek u^\T\mat K\vek u\) is the sum of the energies of the bars, that is \(U\).
  3. The value at \(\vek u\) is \(\Pi(\vek u) = \tfrac12\,\vek u^\T\mat K\vek u - \vek F^\T\vek u = \tfrac12\,C - C = -\tfrac12\,C\). From \(\vek F = \mat K\vek u\) it follows that \(\Pi(\vek v) - \Pi(\vek u) = \tfrac12\,\vek v^\T\mat K\vek v - \vek u^\T\mat K\vek v + \tfrac12\,\vek u^\T\mat K\vek u = \tfrac12\,(\vek v - \vek u)^\T\mat K(\vek v - \vek u) \ge 0\).
  4. With \(\vek F = \mat K\vek u\) we have \(2\,\vek F^\T\vek v - \vek v^\T\mat K\vek v = 2\,\vek u^\T\mat K\vek v - \vek v^\T\mat K\vek v\). We add and subtract \(\vek u^\T\mat K\vek u = C\) and obtain \(C - (\vek v - \vek u)^\T\mat K(\vek v - \vek u)\), which by \(\vek w^\T\mat K\vek w \ge 0\) is at most \(C\).

Source: CHK (5.16)-(5.18) (PDF p. 88) for the energy, CHK §5.1 (PDF p. 97) for \(C = \vek F^\T\vek u = \vek u^\T\mat K\vek u\). Point 3 is the same principle as theorem 4.91 and corollary 4.93. The proof is ours.

What did we get? The compliance is twice the energy that the load \(\vek F\) stores in the truss, and also minus twice the smallest total potential energy. This is Clapeyron's theorem (theorem 4.86) for a truss with numbers: the work of a force that grows from zero is half of \(\vek F^\T\vek u\). Point 4 is new and we shall use it twice. It says that \(C\) is the largest value of the family of functions \(2\,\vek F^\T\vek v - \vek v^\T\mat K(\vek A)\,\vek v\), where every displacement \(\vek v\) gives one function.

Let us look at the family for one bar, the middle bar of our net, which has \(L = 1\) m and carries \(F = 10\) kN (axes, figure 29.53). The compliance is \(C(A) = F^2 L/(EA) = 510{,}2/A\) in joules, if \(A\) is in mm² (blue curve). The displacement \(v\) gives the function \(2Fv - EAv^2/L\), which at a chosen \(v\) is a straight line in \(A\). At \(A_0 = 100\ \text{mm}^2\) we have \(v = FL/(EA_0) = 0{,}5102\) mm and the line \(10{,}204 - 0{,}05102\,A\) in joules (first line), at \(300\ \text{mm}^2\) we have \(v = 0{,}1701\) mm and the line \(3{,}401 - 0{,}005669\,A\) (second), at \(600\ \text{mm}^2\) we have \(v = 0{,}0850\) mm and the line \(1{,}701 - 0{,}001417\,A\) (third). Each line touches the curve at its \(A_0\) (dots) and lies below it elsewhere. The curve is the upper envelope of the lines, and the upper envelope of lines cannot bend downwards. This is the idea of the next theorem.

We see convexity on the segment between two designs. On the axes of the left part are the cross-sections \(A_1\) and \(A_2\), and on the axis of the right part the compliance \(C\). On the left, in the plane of two cross-sections, are the set \(\mathcal P\), the designs \(\vek A\) and \(\vek B\) and the segment between them, on which lies the design \(\vek M\). Around \(\vek A\) there is also a ball that stays in \(\mathcal P\). On the right the compliance along the segment is the curve, the chord between the values at \(\vek A\) and \(\vek B\) lies above it, and at the point \(\vek M\) a line of the family of the lemma touches the curve and is below it elsewhere. The gap between the chord and the curve at \(\vek M\) is what the theorem claims.

Theorem 29.34 Convexity of the compliance (konveksnost podajnosti)

Let a truss be as in lemma 29.31 and \(\mathcal P = \{\vek A \in \mathbb R^n : \mat K(\vek A)\ \text{is positive definite}\}\) (definition 6.27). On \(\mathcal P\) we have \(\mat K(\vek A) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\) also for cross-sections with negative components, and there the compliance is given by equation (29.26) with the same formula. Lemma 29.33 holds for them too, because its proof uses only the symmetry of the matrix \(\mat K\) and \(\vek w^\T\mat K\vek w \ge 0\). Then \(\mathcal P\) is a convex set and \(C\) is a convex function on \(\mathcal P\) (definitions 29.17 and 29.16), that is

\[C\big(t\vek A + (1 - t)\vek B\big) \le t\,C(\vek A) + (1 - t)\,C(\vek B) \qquad (\vek A, \vek B \in \mathcal P,\ 0 \le t \le 1) . \tag{29.28}\]
Idea

By point 4 of lemma 29.33, the compliance is the largest value of functions that are linear in the cross-sections. The largest value of linear functions is convex, as the upper envelope of lines in the figure.

Proof

We must show that \(\mathcal P\) is convex and that (29.28) holds for one function of the family of lemma 29.33.

  1. Let \(\vek A, \vek B \in \mathcal P\) and \(0 \le t \le 1\), \(\vek M = t\vek A + (1 - t)\vek B\). By lemma 29.31, \(\mat K(\vek M) = t\,\mat K(\vek A) + (1 - t)\,\mat K(\vek B)\).
  2. For \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\vek x^\T\mat K(\vek M)\,\vek x = t\,\vek x^\T\mat K(\vek A)\,\vek x + (1 - t)\,\vek x^\T\mat K(\vek B)\,\vek x > 0\), because both terms are positive or zero and at least one is positive (at least one of \(t\) and \(1 - t\) differs from zero). So \(\vek M \in \mathcal P\), and \(\mathcal P\) is convex.
  3. For \(\vek A \in \mathcal P\) the system \(\mat K(\vek A)\vek u = \vek F\) has a solution (theorem 6.29), so the compliance is a number. Let \(\vek w\) be the solution at \(\vek M\), that is \(\vek w = \vek u(\vek M)\).
  4. The function \(\varphi_{\vek{w}}(\vek X) = 2\,\vek F^\T\vek w - \vek w^\T\mat K(\vek X)\,\vek w\) at fixed \(\vek w\) is linear in \(\vek X\) with a constant term, because \(\mat K\) is linear by lemma 29.31. Therefore \(\varphi_{\vek{w}}(\vek M) = t\,\varphi_{\vek{w}}(\vek A) + (1 - t)\,\varphi_{\vek{w}}(\vek B)\).
  5. By point 4 of lemma 29.33, \(C(\vek M) = \varphi_{\vek{w}}(\vek M)\) (equality at \(\vek v = \vek w\)) and \(\varphi_{\vek{w}}(\vek A) \le C(\vek A)\), \(\varphi_{\vek{w}}(\vek B) \le C(\vek B)\) (inequality at other cross-sections). Together with step 4, \(C(\vek M) \le t\,C(\vek A) + (1 - t)\,C(\vek B)\).

Source: CHK §5.2.1 (PDF p. 92-93) proves the theorem with the second derivative: it shows that the Hessian \(\nabla^2 C\) is positive semidefinite and uses theorem 3.2 (i). Our proof from lemma 29.33 is not from the source.

The theorem holds on \(\mathcal P\), so at cross-sections with a nonsingular, positive definite matrix \(\mat K\). What happens outside? On the axes of the left part are the compliance \(C\) in joules and the cross-section \(a\) in mm², both on a logarithmic scale. Take \(\theta = 30^\circ\) and the cross-section \(1\) mm² in both outer bars next to the middle one with \(297{,}17\ \text{mm}^2\), which gives the same volume as above. The calculation gives \(C = 181{,}67\) J. At \(0{,}01\ \text{mm}^2\) of the outer bars it is \(18\,040\) J, and at \(10^{-4}\ \text{mm}^2\) it is \(1{,}80 \cdot 10^6\) J, always a hundred times more at a hundred times smaller cross-section. When the outer bars vanish, the middle one remains, and it cannot carry the horizontal force \(F\sin 30^\circ = 5\) kN. The matrix \(\mat K = \frac{EA_2}{L_2}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) is singular and \(\vek F\) is not in its column space, so the system has no solution and \(C = +\infty\) by definition 29.32. The theorem therefore speaks only about \(\mathcal P\). In the theorem on the optimum we shall prove the sufficient condition without inverting the matrix \(\mat K\), so that it also holds for a singular one.

The second reason for \(C\) was that the displacement of a joint is not convex. On the right part the horizontal axis is the parameter \(t\) of the segment, and the vertical axis with its marks \(-2\), \(-1\) and \(0\) mm carries the horizontal displacement \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the joint \(C\) at \(\theta = 30^\circ\) is \(-1{,}6404\) mm at the cross-sections \((512{,}9;\ 7{,}7;\ 2{,}0)\ \text{mm}^2\) and \(0{,}1258\) mm at the cross-sections \((135{,}3;\ 950{,}1;\ 674{,}5)\ \text{mm}^2\). At the average of the cross-sections it is \(0{,}1103\) mm, but the average of the displacements is \(-0{,}7573\) mm. Convexity ((29.28)) would require \(0{,}1103 \le -0{,}7573\), which does not hold. CHK §5.1 (PDF p. 84) states the same for \(\vek u^\T\vek u\). For the compliance we find no violation: with \(20\,000\) random pairs of cross-sections between \(1\) and \(1001\ \text{mm}^2\) there are \(0\) violations, which is a test, not a proof.

The compliance alone does not tell designs apart, because it decreases with larger cross-sections, so we compare designs at the same volume. How the compliance changes when all cross-sections are multiplied by the same number is told by this lemma.

Lemma 29.35 Scaling of the compliance (skaliranje podajnosti)

Let \(\vek A \ge \vek 0\) be a design with finite compliance \(C(\vek A)\) and \(\alpha > 0\). Then \(C(\alpha\vek A) = C(\vek A)/\alpha\) and \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}\,\alpha A_{\mathrm{e}} = \alpha\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\). If \(\vek F \ne \vek 0\), then \(C(\vek A) > 0\).

Proof

We must show that the solution changes with \(1/\alpha\) and that the compliance is positive.

  1. By lemma 29.31, \(\mat K(\alpha\vek A) = \alpha\,\mat K(\vek A)\). If \(\mat K(\vek A)\vek u = \vek F\), then \(\mat K(\alpha\vek A)\,(\vek u/\alpha) = \vek F\) and \(C(\alpha\vek A) = \vek F^\T\vek u/\alpha = C(\vek A)/\alpha\).
  2. The volume is linear in the cross-sections, \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}\,\alpha A_{\mathrm{e}} = \alpha\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  3. By point 2 of lemma 29.33, \(C = \vek u^\T\mat K\vek u \ge 0\). If \(C = 0\), then for every \(\vek w\) and number \(t\) we would have \(0 \le (\vek u + t\vek w)^\T\mat K(\vek u + t\vek w) = 2t\,\vek w^\T\mat K\vek u + t^2\,\vek w^\T\mat K\vek w\). On the axes are \(t\) and \(f\), in the left panel \(a = 1\), in the right panel \(a = 0\). The right side of the equation is a parabola in \(t\) (a line if \(\vek w^\T\mat K\vek w = 0\)) through the origin with the slope \(2\,\vek w^\T\mat K\vek u\) there. If the slope differs from zero, the parabola goes below zero on one side of the origin, because the term with \(t^2\) at small \(t\) does not catch up with the term with \(t\), and the inequality is violated. Only slope zero remains, \(\vek w^\T\mat K\vek u = 0\). So \(\vek w^\T\vek F = 0\) for every \(\vek w\) and \(\vek F = \vek 0\), which contradicts the assumption.

Source: CHK lemma 5.1 (PDF p. 96). The proof is ours.

At doubled cross-sections the compliance is halved: twice the steel is twice as stiff, and a comparison makes sense only at equal volume.

29.5.2 The condition for the best design (pogoj najboljšega projekta)

The task is therefore: find the cross-sections \(\vek A\) that at volume \(V_0 = 300\ \text{cm}^3\) minimize \(C(\vek A)\). We write it as
