Since \(0{,}7 \cdot 1{,}3 = 0{,}91\), the area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) is \(9\) % smaller after every pair of steps, so the designs in the figure creep up and to the left, and at point 8 bar \(AC\) is still the cheaper one. The displacement stays above \(2\) mm, because by lemma 29.48 the linearized constraint admits too much: the tangent plane of a convex function lies below it.

We do not prove the convergence of loops in this book. The test on this example is enough for the conclusion that SLP is not reliable without a rule for the move limit that shrinks with the rounds (CHK PDF p. 67 says that the choice of the move limits "affects the efficiency considerably").

29.7.3 Convex linearization (konveksna linearizacija)

Why does SLP describe the displacement so badly? Linearization in \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) would be exact if the displacement were a linear function of the areas, but by formula (29.44) the displacement is linear in \(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\). Figure 29.74 shows this on one bar: we choose the variable in which the function is closer to a straight line.

The axes show the displacement \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) of the joint as one area varies. The blue curve is \(c_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}} + c_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) and is convex and decreasing. The point \(\vek A^k\) is the current design. The grey line is the tangent, that is, the SLP linearization. At \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = 300\) mm² the difference is \(2{,}3904 - 2{,}0881 = 0{,}30\) mm: the tangent says \(2{,}088\) mm, but the true displacement is \(2{,}390\) mm. If we draw the same curve against \(1/A_{\mathrm{AC}}\), it is a straight line, and the tangent in this variable lies on the curve.

Definition 29.50 Convex linearization, CONLIN (konveksna linearizacija)

In the setting of definition 29.46 let all areas be strictly positive. An intervening variable is a function \(y_{\mathrm{e}}\) of the area \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) in which we expand the function linearly: \(y_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\mathrm{e}}\) or \(y_{\mathrm{e}} = 1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\). Let \(g\) be one of the functions \(f\), \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\Omega^+ = \{e : \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek A^k) > 0\}\), \(\Omega^- = \{e : \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek A^k) \le 0\}\). The CONLIN approximation of the function \(g\) at \(\vek A^k\) is

\[\tilde g^{\,k}(\vek A) = g(\vek A^k) + \sum_{\mathrm{e} \in \Omega^+} \frac{\partial g}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^k) + \sum_{\mathrm{e} \in \Omega^-} \frac{\partial g}{\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2\left(\frac{1}{A_{\mathrm{e}}^k} - \frac{1}{A_{\mathrm{e}}}\right) , \tag{29.45}\]

with the derivatives computed at \(\vek A^k\). The variables in which the derivative is positive are expanded in \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\), the others in \(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Source: CHK section 4.4 (PDF pp. 67-69): the choice between \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(1/x_{\mathrm{j}}\) by the sign of the derivative, equation (4.5) and the sets \(\Omega_+\), \(\Omega_-\) (PDF p. 69, read by hand from the crop of the equation). The term in \(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the expansion in \(y_{\mathrm{e}} = 1/A_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the derivative \(\partial g/\partial y_{\mathrm{e}} = -A_{\mathrm{e}}^2\,\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\) by the chain rule (lemma 8.30).

The name is short for "convex linearization" (CHK PDF p. 68), since the result is a convex function, which we prove at once.

Lemma 29.51 Properties of the CONLIN approximation (lastnosti približka CONLIN)

Let \(\tilde g^{\,k}\) be the CONLIN approximation of definition 29.50 for a continuously differentiable \(g\). Then:

  1. \(\tilde g^{\,k}(\vek A^k) = g(\vek A^k)\) and \(\partial\tilde g^{\,k}/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek A^k) = \partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}(\vek A^k)\) for every \(e\).
  2. \(\tilde g^{\,k}\) is a convex function on the set of designs with all \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\).
Proof

We must show that the approximation agrees with \(g\) in value and derivative and that it has a nonnegative Hessian matrix, so that by lemma 29.22 it is convex.

  1. At \(\vek A = \vek A^k\) all brackets \((A_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)\) and \((1/A_{\mathrm{e}}^k - 1/A_{\mathrm{e}})\) are zero, so \(\tilde g^{\,k}(\vek A^k) = g(\vek A^k)\).
  2. The derivative with respect to \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) for \(e \in \Omega^+\) is \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\). For \(e \in \Omega^-\) the derivative of the term \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2\,(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}^k - 1/A_{\mathrm{e}})\) with respect to \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) is \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k/A_{\mathrm{e}})^2\), because \(\mathrm{d}(-1/A_{\mathrm{e}})/\mathrm{d}A_{\mathrm{e}} = 1/A_{\mathrm{e}}^2\). At \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\) this is again \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\), which completes item 1.
  3. Every term of the sum is a function of one variable, so the Hessian matrix (definition 8.69) is diagonal. For \(e \in \Omega^+\) the second derivative is \(0\), a linear term. For \(e \in \Omega^-\) the second derivative by step 2 is \(-2\,\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}}\,(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2/A_{\mathrm{e}}^3\), and it is \(\ge 0\), because \(\partial g/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} \le 0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\).
  4. A diagonal matrix with nonnegative diagonal entries is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), so \(\tilde g^{\,k}\) is convex by lemma 29.22.

Source: CHK section 4.4 (PDF pp. 70-71): the first property and the proof that \(g^{C,k}_{\mathrm{i}}\) is convex, as a sum of terms \(C(x_{\mathrm{j}} - x_{\mathrm{j}}^k)\) and \(A + B/x_{\mathrm{j}}\). The proof with the Hessian matrix, step by step, is ours.

Why the choice by sign? Let us try the opposite, on the volume of bar \(AC\), which is linear in \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) (the derivative \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m is positive). If we expanded it in \(1/A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) we would get \(V_{\mathrm{R}}(A) = L(A^k + (A^k)^2(1/A^k - 1/A))\), that is, \(4\,(1200 - 360\,000/A)\) cm³ for \(A\) in mm² and \(A^k = 600\) mm². The right half of figure 29.74 has axes with the area \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) horizontal and the volume vertical, negative values included. The blue line is the true volume \(4A\) cm³, the orange curve is \(V_{\mathrm{R}}\), and both pass through the point at \(A^k = 600\) mm² with the same slope \(L = 4\) m. The orange curve is concave: the coefficient \(-L(A^k)^2\) in front of \(1/A\) is negative, so the second derivative is \(-2L(A^k)^2/A^3 < 0\), and at \(A = 1\) mm² the approximation gives the volume \(-1{,}435\cdot 10^{6}\) cm³, a negative one. The subproblem would push the objective toward \(-\infty\) as the area goes to zero, and every bar would vanish. The attempt fails precisely at the point where the lemma demands the sign of the derivative. With the right choice the volume remains a straight line.

Lemma 29.52 CONLIN is exact for a statically determinate truss (CONLIN je točen za statično določeno paličje)

For a statically determinate truss (definition 4.4) with axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\), unit forces \(n_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(c_{\mathrm{e}} = N_{\mathrm{e}} n_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}/E\), the displacement is \(v = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\), and its CONLIN approximation at every design with \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) is exact if every \(c_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\).

Proof

We must show that the approximation agrees with the function everywhere, not only at \(\vek A^k\).

  1. For a statically determinate truss the equilibrium alone determines \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{e}}\), and they do not depend on the areas, so by theorem 4.96 \(v = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  2. Every derivative is \(\partial v/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \le 0\), so all \(e\) lie in \(\Omega^-\).
  3. By formula (29.45), \(\tilde v^{\,k}(\vek A) = v(\vek A^k) + \sum_{\mathrm{e}} (-c_{\mathrm{e}}/(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2)(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2(1/A_{\mathrm{e}}^k - 1/A_{\mathrm{e}}) = v(\vek A^k) - \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^k + \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\), which is the true displacement curve.

Source: The proof is ours. CHK section 4.4 (PDF p. 68) states the same for a statically determinate truss: linearization in \(1/A_{\mathrm{i}}\) is exact, because displacements and stresses are functions of \(1/A_{\mathrm{i}}\).

By lemma 29.52 the displacement of the wall truss is covered by the exact curve, which is the blue curve in the figure. A consequence: the CONLIN subproblem is in this case equal to the true problem. The displacement is exact, and the volume is already linear in the areas (\(L_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\), so all areas are in \(\Omega^+\) for \(f\)). The subproblem is \(\min L_{\mathrm{AC}}A_{\mathrm{AC}} + L_{\mathrm{BC}}A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) subject to \(c_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}} + c_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}} \le \delta\).

Example 29.53 One CONLIN step on the wall truss (en korak CONLIN na stenskem paličju)

We solve the subproblem with the multiplier \(\mu\). The problem is convex, since \(V\) is linear and by lemma 29.51 the displacement is convex, so by theorem 29.30 the KKT conditions are sufficient.

  1. Stationarity in \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) for the Lagrangian \(V + \mu\,(v - \delta)\): \(L_{\mathrm{e}} - \mu\,c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = 0\), so \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = \sqrt{\mu\,c_{\mathrm{e}}/L_{\mathrm{e}}}\).
  2. The displacement in the constraint: \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \sqrt{c_{\mathrm{e}}L_{\mathrm{e}}/\mu} = \delta\), so \(\sqrt\mu = \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{j}}L_{\mathrm{j}}}/\delta\). The numbers are \(\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{AC}}L_{\mathrm{AC}}} = 1{,}205\cdot 10^{-3}\) m², \(\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{BC}}L_{\mathrm{BC}}} = 1{,}882\cdot 10^{-3}\) m², \(\sqrt\mu = 1{,}5435\) and \(\mu = 2{,}382\) m².
  3. The areas \(A_{\mathrm{AC}} = \sqrt{\mu c_{\mathrm{AC}}/L_{\mathrm{AC}}} = 464{,}85\) mm² and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 581{,}07\) mm², the volume \(4764{,}7\) cm³, the displacement \(2{,}0000\) mm. The multiplier is positive.

Since the subproblem at \(\vek A^0 = (600, 600)\) mm² equals the true problem, the result after one round is already the true optimum, and the starting design makes no difference to the areas from CONLIN. SLP did not settle in \(8\) rounds in the same circumstances. The stresses are \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}/A_{\mathrm{AC}} = -28{,}7\) MPa and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}}/A_{\mathrm{BC}} = 28{,}7\) MPa: both bars are equally loaded, which is a consequence, not an assumption.

The exactness is a property of static determinacy, not of CONLIN. In a statically indeterminate truss the forces \(N_{\mathrm{e}}\) themselves depend on the areas, so the formula \(v = \sum c_{\mathrm{e}}/A_{\mathrm{e}}\) does not hold and the CONLIN approximation only comes closer. An example is the truss with three bars: the joint \((0, 0)\), supports at \((-1, 1)\), \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 1)\) m, the force \(F = 10\) kN at \(30^\circ\) from the vertical, all areas equal to \(78{,}36\) mm² (volume \(300\) cm³).

Figure 29.75 shows the compliance \(C\) (section 29.5) as the area of the first bar varies. The axes carry the ratio \(x\) of the current to the starting area of the first bar horizontally and \(C\) in J vertically. The blue curve is the true calculation and falls, because more material makes the truss stiffer. The point \(x = 1\) is the starting design with \(C = 5{,}1625\) J. The grey line is the tangent, that is, the linear approximation in \(A_1\), and the orange curve is the CONLIN approximation, which is linear in \(1/A_1\). The derivatives with respect to the areas are \(-E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2L_{\mathrm{e}}\) (corollary 29.44), all negative, so all bars are in \(\Omega^-\).

When the area of the first bar is multiplied by \(1{,}5\), the true calculation gives \(C = 3{,}9084\) J, the linear approximation \(3{,}4650\) J (\(-11{,}3\) %) and the CONLIN approximation \(4{,}0308\) J (\(+3{,}1\) %), at half the area (\(\times 0{,}5\)) the true \(7{,}7883\) J, the linear \(6{,}8599\) J (\(-11{,}9\) %) and CONLIN \(8{,}5574\) J (\(+9{,}9\) %). CONLIN is not exact, but in both cases it is closer and above the true value. The linear approximation is below it, as it must be for a convex function: the tangent underestimates it (lemma 29.20). CHK (PDF pp. 69-70) proves that CONLIN is always at least as conservative as SLP.

29.7.4 Moving asymptotes (premikajoče se asimptote)

The method of moving asymptotes (MMA) uses the intervening variables \(1/(A_{\mathrm{e}} - L_{\mathrm{e}})\) and \(1/(U_{\mathrm{e}} - A_{\mathrm{e}})\), where \(L_{\mathrm{e}} < A_{\mathrm{e}} < U_{\mathrm{e}}\) are asymptotes that move between rounds (CHK section 4.5, PDF pp. 74-76). The first applies to variables with derivative \(\le 0\), the second to those with derivative \(> 0\). The closer the asymptotes lie to the current design, the more conservative the approximation, and the farther away, the more it resembles the tangent plane (PDF pp. 76 and 77). CONLIN is obtained at \(L_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) and \(U_{\mathrm{e}} \to +\infty\), SLP at \(L_{\mathrm{e}} \to -\infty\) and \(U_{\mathrm{e}} \to +\infty\) (PDF p. 77). The asymptotes move by a rule: if the signs of the successive changes \(A_{\mathrm{e}}^k - A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k-1}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k-1} - A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k-2}\) differ, the design variable oscillates and the asymptotes come closer (PDF p. 76), which is exactly the phenomenon of example 29.49. We only state the exact formulas and the proof of convexity, we do not prove them (CHK PDF pp. 74-76). CHK itself mentions that CONLIN sometimes converges slowly or not at all (PDF p. 74), so MMA is an improvement on it.

29.7.5 The optimality criteria update (posodobitev po merilu optimalnosti)

For the problem of the least compliance of a truss at a bounded volume from section 29.5 there is an even simpler loop, which needs no solution of a subproblem. Theorem 29.37 tells us what the optimum looks like: for bars with \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) we have \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = \lambda\), for bars without material \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \le \lambda\), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the relative elongation of the bar, and \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) is by theorem 4.3 twice the strain energy per volume of the bar, since \(U = EA\varepsilon^2L/2\). The quantity \(\lambda\) here is the multiplier of the volume constraint (in chapter 10 it means an eigenvalue). A bar that stores more energy per volume than the average is too thin, since it has a large elongation, so we thicken it, and conversely. We write this idea as a rule.

Definition 29.54 The optimality criteria update, OC (posodobitev po merilu optimalnosti)

Let the problem be the least compliance of a truss subject to \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}} \le V_0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge A_{\min} > 0\) (section 29.5). Let \(\vek A^k\) be a design with equilibrium \(\mat K(\vek A^k)\vek u^k = \vek F\) and relative elongations \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^k\), and let \(B_{\mathrm{e}}^k = E\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^2\). Let \(\eta \in (0, 1]\) be a number (the damping) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\) a move limit. The optimality criteria update is

\[A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1} = \min\Big\{\ \overline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k},\ \max\big\{\ \underline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k},\ A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\,(B_{\mathrm{e}}^k/\lambda)^{\eta}\ \big\}\Big\} , \tag{29.46}\]

with the bounds \(\underline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k} = \max\{A_{\min},\ (1 - \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\}\) and \(\overline A_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,k} = (1 + \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\), and with \(\lambda > 0\) chosen so that \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1} = V_0\).

Source: The form is after CHK section 9.1.2 (PDF p. 191, the equation with \(\eta\), there for a plate with thickness \(x_{\mathrm{e}}\) as the design variable) and SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 2, equations (2) and (3), \(\eta = 1/2\), "numerical damping coefficient"). The adaptation to a truss with \(B_{\mathrm{e}} = E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\) and volume \(L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}}\) is ours: for a bar \(\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^{\T}\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}} = E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2L_{\mathrm{e}}\), and dividing by \(a_{\mathrm{e}} = L_{\mathrm{e}}\) leaves \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2\).

The rule is easier to see on the graph of one bar (figure 29.76). In the left half the axes carry the quotient \(B_{\mathrm{e}}/\lambda\) horizontally and the ratio \(A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1}/A_{\mathrm{e}}^k\) vertically. The thin curve is \((B_{\mathrm{e}}/\lambda)^\eta\) and, because \(\eta < 1\), it bends more slowly than a straight line. It crosses the value \(1\) at the point \(B_{\mathrm{e}} = \lambda\): a bar with more energy per volume than \(\lambda\) thickens, one with less thins, and at \(B_{\mathrm{e}} = \lambda\) it does not change. The lower limit \(1 - \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) and the upper limit \(1 + \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) cut the curve off, so the thick line is the actual step. The right half has the same axes, but the bar is already at \(A_{\min}\): the lower limit is now \(1\), since \(\max\{A_{\min}, (1 - \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\min}\} = A_{\min}\), and the result is horizontal at \(1\) as long as \(B_{\mathrm{e}} \le \lambda\).

The name is "criteria" because the rule comes from the criterion of optimality \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = \lambda\) and not from an approximation of the whole problem.

We find the value \(\lambda\) by bisection (figure 29.77). The axes carry \(\lambda\) horizontally and the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1}\) vertically. The blue curve is this sum: every term in (29.46) is continuous and does not increase with increasing \(\lambda\), because \(\lambda^{-\eta}\) falls and min and max are not decreasing, so the sum is continuous and does not increase. The horizontal line is \(V_0\), and since the curve is continuous and falls, it crosses the line at the root. We enclose the root in an interval whose ends have the curve above and below the line, and in every step we halve it and keep the half that still encloses the crossing.

At \(\eta = 1/2\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}2\) we test the rule on the truss with three bars. Figure 29.78 shows the designs and the quotients through \(30\) rounds.

We start with equal areas \(78{,}36\) mm² (the axes show the area against the round). Then \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = 30{,}6\), \(21{,}4\) and \(0{,}83\) kJ/m³, so the first bar is the most overloaded and the third almost idle. The first bar thickens, the second stays near its start, the third thins toward zero. In the right half the quotients of the first and second bar approach each other and settle at the dashed value \(\lambda \approx 10{,}6\) kJ/m³, and the third falls to zero, that is, below \(\lambda\). After \(30\) rounds the areas are \((155{,}2;\ 80{,}3;\ 0{,}10)\) mm², against the boundary areas of the optimum \((155{,}29;\ 80{,}38;\ 0)\) mm² and the compliance \(3{,}1735\) J (section 29.5). The compliance falls from \(5{,}1625\) J at equal areas to \(3{,}1735\) J, the first six values are \(5{,}1625\), \(4{,}5785\), \(4{,}1905\), \(3{,}9268\), \(3{,}7433\), \(3{,}6115\) J. We are within \(10^{-3}\) of the final value at \(k = 27\), within \(10^{-6}\) at \(k = 56\). Without a move limit (\(\delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) unbounded) \(5\) rounds sufficed: \(5{,}1625\), \(3{,}6129\), \(3{,}2879\), \(3{,}1870\), \(3{,}1738\), \(3{,}1735\) J. If we put the lower bound at \(1\) mm² instead of nearly zero, the third bar stays at \(1\) mm² and the compliance is \(3{,}1885\) J, which is \(0{,}5\) % larger.

Lemma 29.55 Fixed points of the OC update (negibne točke posodobitve OC)

Let \(A_{\min} > 0\), \(\eta \in (0, 1]\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\) and let \(\vek A\) be a design with \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge A_{\min}\), \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} L_{\mathrm{e}}A_{\mathrm{e}} = V_0\) and nonsingular \(\mat K(\vek A)\). Then the following holds:

  1. If the update (29.46) leaves \(\vek A\) unchanged, \(\vek A^{k+1} = \vek A^k = \vek A\), with some \(\lambda > 0\), then for every \(e\): \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > A_{\min}\) implies \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 = \lambda\) and \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\min}\) implies \(E\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \le \lambda\).
  2. If for some \(\lambda > 0\) these two conditions hold, \(\vek A\) is a fixed point of the rule.
  3. Such an \(\vek A\) is a global minimum of the least compliance problem.
Proof

We must show that the fixed points are exactly the points with the criteria of theorem 29.37. We distinguish two cases by bar.

  1. Let \(A_{\mathrm{e}} > A_{\min}\). Then \(\underline A_{\mathrm{e}} < A_{\mathrm{e}} < \overline A_{\mathrm{e}}\), because \(A_{\min} < A_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \((1 - \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\mathrm{e}} < A_{\mathrm{e}} < (1 + \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\mathrm{e}}\). The result \(\min\{\overline A_{\mathrm{e}}, \max\{\underline A_{\mathrm{e}}, X\}\}\) equals \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) exactly when \(X = A_{\mathrm{e}}\): if \(X < \underline A_{\mathrm{e}}\) or \(X > \overline A_{\mathrm{e}}\), the result is one of the bounds, which differ from \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\), and if \(X\) lies between the bounds, the result is \(X\). So \(A_{\mathrm{e}}(B_{\mathrm{e}}/\lambda)^\eta = A_{\mathrm{e}}\), hence \(B_{\mathrm{e}} = \lambda\) (\(A_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\)).
  2. Let \(A_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\min}\). The lower bound is \(\max\{A_{\min}, (1 - \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\min}\} = A_{\min}\). The result is \(A_{\min}\) exactly when \(A_{\min}(B_{\mathrm{e}}/\lambda)^\eta \le A_{\min}\), that is, \(B_{\mathrm{e}} \le \lambda\).
  3. The conditions are reversible (steps 1 and 2 are equivalences), which is the second claim. The conditions are those of theorem 29.37 with the lower bound \(A_{\min}\), the problem is convex (theorem 29.34), so by theorem 29.30 a fixed point is a global minimum.

Source: The proof is ours. CHK section 9.1.2 (PDF p. 191) states that at convergence the specific strain energy is constant in every element, which is the first condition of the lemma.

A fixed point is therefore an optimum if all bars have \(A_{\mathrm{e}} \ge A_{\min} > 0\). The lemma does not say whether the loop reaches a fixed point: convergence is not proved, but in our tests the loop always converged. The lower bound is truly necessary.

Example 29.56 A bar with zero area never returns (palica z ničelno ploščino se ne vrne)

Take the same truss with three bars and the force at \(30^\circ\) and a starting design in which the middle bar is removed: \((106{,}07;\ 0;\ 106{,}07)\) mm², volume \(300\) cm³. The matrix \(\mat K\) is nonsingular, since bars \(1\) and \(3\) lie at \(\pm 45^\circ\). If the lower bound is \(A_{\min} = 0\), the right-hand side of (29.46) at \(A_2 = 0\) is \(0\cdot(B_2/\lambda)^\eta = 0\) for every \(B_2\), so the middle bar stays zero forever. The loop converges to the design \((167{,}30;\ 0;\ 44{,}83)\) mm² with compliance \(5{,}1020\) J, not to \(3{,}1735\) J. The condition of the lemma is violated there, as for the empty bar in the right graph of the figure of densities in section 29.5: \(E\varepsilon_2^2 = 68{,}03\) kJ/m³ is larger than \(\lambda = 17{,}007\) kJ/m³, the middle bar should receive material but cannot. With \(A_{\min} = 10^{-4}\) mm² (and a move limit) the same start converges to \((155{,}29;\ 80{,}38;\ 0)\) mm² and \(3{,}1735\) J, because the result of expression (29.46) at \(A_2 = A_{\min}\) can grow up to \((1 + \delta_{\mathrm{p}})A_{\min}\) and onward.

Programs therefore always use a positive lower bound, even for bars that should vanish. A consequence is that at \(A_{\min} = 1\) mm² the compliance is \(0{,}5\) % above the optimum, so we choose the lower bound small.

CHK (PDF pp. 186-191) shows that OC is a special case of sequential convex approximations: it linearizes the compliance in the intervening variable \(y_{\mathrm{e}} = A_{\mathrm{e}}^{-\alpha}\) with \(\alpha > 0\), at \(\alpha = 1\) this is CONLIN (PDF p. 186), and the damping is \(\eta = 1/(1 + \alpha)\) (PDF p. 191). Our \(\eta = 1/2\) is therefore CONLIN. We state this, we do not prove it.

Open questions. We tested the loops SLP and OC on small trusses with two and three bars, their convergence is not proved, and it is not proved for larger problems. How OC performs when the variable is the area of an element on a plate and the bars number in the thousands is shown by section 29.9, where the same rule solves a problem of topology.

29.8 The stiffest rod (najtogejša palica)

So far a design variable (projektna spremenljivka) was a list of numbers, for example the areas \(A_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{BC}}\) of two bars of a truss. Let us ask what happens when a single rod has its own area in every cross-section. Then the area is not a number but a function \(A(x)\) of the distance \(x\) from the support, measured along the \(x\) axis, and each of its infinitely many values may be chosen separately. When the design variable is a function, we speak of a distributed parameter system (sistem s porazdeljenimi parametri), because the decision is spread along the whole length and not collected in a few numbers. A truss is by nature a discrete system, because there are as many variables as there are bars (CHK §1.5, PDF p. 17). The stiffest (najtogejša) rod is the one with the greatest stiffness among all those with the same volume of material. We measure stiffness by compliance (podajnost, section 29.5): the more stiffness, the less compliance.

The model is this. A straight rod of length \(L\) is clamped into a wall at \(x = 0\), is free at \(x = L\), and on every unit of length of the rod acts a force \(b(x)\) in the direction of the \(x\) axis. We call such a force a distributed load (porazdeljena obtežba), because it is not concentrated at one point but spread over the whole rod. Its unit is N/m. In chapter 11 the letter \(b\) means force per unit volume, here it is force per unit length. There are three idealizations, and for each we say why it holds here, when it does not and what it does to the result. First: the material is linearly elastic with modulus \(E\) (definition 3.1). In the example below the stress nowhere exceeds \(100\) MPa (at the wall), while the allowed stress of the same steel in section 29.2 is \(220\) MPa. Above the limit up to which the straight-line law holds, the elongation would be larger than \(\sigma/E\) and the true displacements larger than the computed ones. Second: displacements are small. The free end will move by \(0{,}2551\) mm over a length of \(1\) m and the elongation per unit length will be at most \(0{,}05\) %, so we write equilibrium and the integrals over the undeformed length and make an error of that order in the lengths. For a rubber band that stretches by half its length we could not do so. Third: the load \(b\) does not depend on the area, as the weight of the rod would. The weight of a rod of volume \(100\) cm³ is \(7{,}65\) N, which is \(0{,}08\) % of the load \(10\) kN we shall take below, so we neglect it. If the load were the weight itself, every move of material would change the axial force too, and the theorem of this section would not hold in this form. For \(b\) we also assume that it is continuous and that there is a number \(m > 0\) with \(b(x) \ge m\) everywhere, so the rod is pulled everywhere (tension, section 2.1). We need continuity so that the axial force is differentiable. We need positivity so that the axial force is positive in every cross-section before the free end: where it were zero, as for a load that drops to zero before the end, the best rod would have area zero there and would be torn apart.

Let us draw the rod as on a board. The wall is on the left, because the rod is clamped there. The rod reaches from it to the free end. We draw the load as a row of arrows on the axis of the rod, because the axis is the line along which the forces act, and each arrow pulls in the direction of \(x\). The forces act along the axis, so in a cross-section only the axial force matters (definition 2.5). How large is it in the cross-section at \(x\)? We cut the rod in thought at \(x\), at the distance \(x\) from the wall, and look at the piece from the cut to the free end, which we draw separately. Only two forces act on it. The first is the load on the piece, whose sum is \(b\,(L - x)\) if \(b\) is constant. The second is the axial force across the cut. By definition 2.5 the part on the side of larger \(x\) acts on the part on the side of smaller \(x\) with the force \(N\), so the part on the side of smaller \(x\) acts on our piece with the force \(-N(x)\) in the direction of \(x\), that is, it pulls the piece to the left, and the arrow is drawn from the cut to the left. The piece is in equilibrium (definition 2.3), the sum of the forces on it is zero, and the load on the piece is the integral of the load over it. Therefore

\[N(x) = \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L b(s)\,\mathrm{d}s . \tag{29.47}\]

For a constant load \(b\) we have \(N(x) = b\,(L - x)\), from \(bL\) at the wall, where the piece is the whole rod, to \(0\) at the free end, where the piece shrinks to nothing. When the load is not constant, \(N(x)\) is by equation (29.47) the area under the graph of the load from \(x\) to \(L\) on the \(s\) axis. The graph nowhere falls below the level \(m\), so this area contains the rectangle of height \(m\) and width \(L - x\), and always \(N(x) \ge m\,(L - x) \ge 0\) (lemma 3.54, item 3). For the load \(b(s) = 10 + 3\cos(2\pi s/L)\) kN/m with \(m = 6\) kN/m, at the cut \(x = 0{,}4\) m the area is \(5{,}72\) kN and the rectangle \(3{,}6\) kN. If we do this at every \(x\), we get the graph of the axial force, which lies above the line \(m\,(L - x)\) and meets it only at the free end. So \(N(x) > 0\) in every cross-section before the free end. It matters that we obtained \(N\) from equilibrium alone, without the area and the material. We call such a rod statically determinate (statično določena): the forces in it are determined by statics, that is, by equilibrium, hence the name. What would be different is shown by the example of a rod clamped at both ends, at the end of the section.

Now we know where the force is large. At the wall the cross-section carries the whole load, at the free end almost nothing. Let us test what that means on a steel rod, clamped into a wall, with \(E = 196\) GPa (section 3.1.10), length \(L = 1\) m, load \(b = 10\) kN/m and constant area \(A_0 = 100\) mm². The volume is \(V = A_0 L = 100\) cm³. The stress (definition 2.6) is \(bL/A_0 = 100\) MPa at the wall, zero at the free end, and in between it falls linearly. The material near the free end hardly carries anything, and the material at the wall carries the most. How could we redistribute the same material so that the rod is as stiff as possible?

In section 29.5 the compliance is the number \(F\cdot u\), the force times its displacement. We cut the load into pieces, in figure 29.82 every arrow is one such piece. The piece at \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) of length \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\) has the force \(b(x_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\) and its displacement is \(u(x_{\mathrm{i}})\). The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} b(x_{\mathrm{i}})\,u(x_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\) is a Riemann sum (definition 3.47) and approaches an integral.

Definition 29.57 Compliance of a rod under a distributed load (podajnost palice pod porazdeljeno obtežbo)

Let a rod be clamped at \(x = 0\) (the wall), with the load \(b\) and the displacement \(u(x)\) of the cross-section at \(x\), continuously differentiable on \([0, L]\). The compliance (podajnost) of the rod is the number

\[C = \int_0^L b(x)\,u(x)\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{29.48}\]

Source: CHK §8.3 (PDF pp. 168 and 173): compliance is the value \(\ell(U)\) of the linear form of the load at the equilibrium displacement and by (8.26) equals \(a(U, U)\). For a rod \(\ell(v) = \int b\,v\,\mathrm{d}x\) (PDF p. 173). For point forces it is the \(F\cdot u\) of section 29.5.

Compliance depends on the area, because the displacement \(u\) depends on it, so we write \(C(A)\) when we stress this. Which areas may we choose? Let us draw four possibilities as bands above the \(x\) axis. The first area is continuous and positive everywhere before the end, so we may choose it. The second has a jump, which a continuous model does not allow. The third breaks at one point: the area is zero there and the elongation next to it would be infinite. Near the free end we must look more closely. The axial force falls to zero there, so an area that falls equally fast still allows a finite stress, and an area that falls faster does not. So we may choose areas that nowhere break the rod where there is force, and that near the free end, where there is hardly any force, may be arbitrarily small.

Definition 29.58 Admissible area function (dopustna funkcija ploščine)

Let a rod be as above, with the axial force \(N\) from equation (29.47). A function \(A : [0, L] \to [0, \infty)\) is an admissible area function (dopustna funkcija ploščine) if it satisfies three conditions:

  1. \(A\) is continuous on \([0, L]\),
  2. \(A(x) > 0\) for every \(x \in [0, L)\) (no break),
  3. the stress \(\sigma(x) = N(x)/A(x)\) on \([0, L)\) has a limit as \(x\) tends to \(L\) (definition 1.5).

We take the value of this limit as \(\sigma(L)\).

Source: The notion is not from the source. CHK §8.3 (PDF p. 169) requires only \(\rho \ge 0\) and a given volume.

The name admissible says that the function may take part in the contest for the best, like the elements of the feasible set in section 29.1. Condition 2 does not allow the rod to be broken anywhere, because the elongation there would be infinite. Condition 3 does not allow infinite stress at the free end. Two properties follow from it that we shall need. First, \(\sigma\) is continuous on \([0, L]\): on \([0, L)\) as a quotient of continuous functions with a denominator that is not zero (lemma](29.83:sigmaL) 4.109, item 2), and at \(L\) by the choice of [\(\sigma(L)\) (definition 1.59). Second, \(N = \sigma A\) on \([0, L]\): on \([0, L)\) by the definition of \(\sigma\), and at \(L\) the left side is zero, and so is the right, because either \(A(L) = 0\), or \(A(L) > 0\) and \(\sigma(L) = \lim N/A = 0/A(L) = 0\).

How do we compute the compliance without computing the displacement? Let us look where the displacement comes from. From the rod in figure 29.82 we cut out in thought a slice of length \(\Delta x\) at \(x\) and imagine that it alone stretches. Its elongation per unit length is \(\varepsilon(x)\), so it gets longer by \(\varepsilon\,\Delta x\). The part to its left stays in place, because the wall holds it. The whole part to its right moves from its earlier position to the right by the same \(\varepsilon\,\Delta x\), and with it all the load that acts on it. The sum of that load is exactly the axial force \(N(x)\) of equation (29.47). One slice therefore adds the amount \(N(x)\,\varepsilon(x)\,\Delta x\) to the sum of the products of force and displacement. The displacement of every arrow is the sum of the elongations of all slices to its left. So the same products can be added up in two ways, by arrows or by slices:

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} b(x_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}} \cdot u(x_{\mathrm{i}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} N(x_{\mathrm{j}}) \cdot \varepsilon(x_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{j}} .\]

On the left is the compliance, and on the right there are no displacements any more, only the axial force and the strain. The lemma shows this exactly for integrals. The changed order of adding is there integration by parts, which moves the derivative from \(u\) to \(N\).

Lemma 29.59 Compliance of a statically determinate rod (podajnost statično določene palice)

Let a rod be as above with an admissible area function \(A\) and displacement \(u\), \(u(0) = 0\) at the wall. Then

\[C(A) = \frac1E \int_0^L N(x)\,\sigma(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac1E \int_0^L \frac{N(x)^2}{A(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{29.49}\]

where \(N^2/A\) at \(x = L\) is taken as the limit \(N\sigma = 0\).

Proof

We must show that the integral of the work of the load on the displacements passes into the integral of the square of the axial force. We express the displacement through the strain of the slice and integrate by parts.

  1. In every slice the stress is \(\sigma = N/A\) by definition 2.6 and the strain is \(\varepsilon = \sigma/E\) by definition 3.1. The law measured on a specimen we apply in every cross-section separately, as for the hanging rod in section 3.1.10. With this we assume that the stress is uniform over the cross-section, which holds when the area changes slowly along the rod. What that costs for the best rod we compute after theorem 29.60. The function \(\varepsilon = \sigma/E\) is continuous on \([0, L]\).
  2. By definition 1.10 \(u' = \varepsilon\), that is the elongation of the slice \(\varepsilon\,\Delta x\) over its length \(\Delta x\), and \(u(0) = 0\), because the rod is clamped into the wall. The displacement is therefore continuously differentiable on \([0, L]\).
  3. The function \(N(x) = \int_0^L b\,\mathrm{d}s - \int_0^x b\,\mathrm{d}s\) is by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55, item 2, differentiable with continuous derivative \(N' = -b\). In figure 29.80 this means: when we move the cut by \(\Delta x\) to the right, the piece loses the load \(b\,\Delta x\). From equation (29.47), \(N(L) = 0\), because at the free end no piece is left.
  4. Corollary 3.56 with \(f = N\) and \(g = u\) on \([0, L]\) gives
    \[\int_0^L N\,u'\,\mathrm{d}x = N(L)\,u(L) - N(0)\,u(0) - \int_0^L N'\,u\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 - 0 + \int_0^L b\,u\,\mathrm{d}x = C .\]
    This is the changed order of figure 29.82: on the left the axial force times the elongation of the slice, on the right the load times the displacement.
  5. By step 2, on the slice \(N\,u' = N\varepsilon = N\sigma/E\), which is the first equality in equation (29.49). For \(x < L\), \(N\sigma = N^2/A\), which is the second.

Source: CHK (8.26) (PDF p. 168), \(a(U, U) = \ell(U)\), called Clapeyron's theorem. The proof by parts is not from the source.

So we compute compliance from the axial force and the area, without displacements. Because \(N = \sigma A\), we have \(N\sigma = \sigma^2 A\), and by definition 4.2 the strain energy of the rod, the sum of the energies of the slices, is \(U = \int_0^L \frac{\sigma^2}{2E}\,A\,\mathrm{d}x\), since the energy density is \(\tfrac12 E\varepsilon^2 = \sigma^2/(2E)\). Hence \(C = 2U\), as in theorem 4.3, where the work of the force is half the product of force and displacement. Let us check on the uniform rod, where the stress falls from \(100\) MPa to zero. By the fundamental theorem of calculus \(\frac{1}{EA_0}\int_0^L b^2 (L - x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{b^2 L^3}{3EA_0}\), and for our numbers \(1{,}7007\) J. With the displacement \(u(x) = \dfrac{b}{EA_0}\big(Lx - \tfrac12 x^2\big)\) and equation (29.48) we get the same number.

Now we set the problem. The material is as much as the volume \(V\), and the volume of the rod is \(\int_0^L A\,\mathrm{d}x\), like a Riemann sum of the volumes of pieces \(A(x_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\). In figure 29.84 we draw the area as the height of a strip, so the volume is the area of the strip, for the uniform rod of a rectangle of height \(A_0\). We look for an admissible function \(A\) with \(\int_0^L A\,\mathrm{d}x = V\) for which \(C(A)\) is smallest. Below the rod we draw the axial force \(N(x)\) and denote \(S = \int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x\), which is the area under its graph (unit N m, \(S\) as the sum of axial forces). In the uniform rod the cross-section at the wall is loaded the most, the cross-section at the end almost not at all, as the dashed stress line on the stress axis shows. We suspect that the area must be moved to where \(N\) is large.

Let us try with one bit. From the uniform rod we take away the area \(10\) mm² over a length of \(1\) cm around \(x = 0{,}9\) m and add it on the first centimetre at the wall. We have moved \(0{,}1\) cm³ of material, the volume is the same. The compliance (29.49) is the sum of the contributions \(N^2\,\Delta x/(EA)\) of the slices. The thinned slice stretches more and contributes more, the thickened one at the wall less. Which prevails? The stress at the wall is \(100\) MPa, at \(0{,}9\) m only \(10\) MPa. A slice whose area we increase by a small \(\Delta A\) lowers its contribution by about \(\sigma^2\,\Delta A\,\Delta x/E\), because the derivative of \(N^2/A\) with respect to \(A\) is \(-N^2/A^2 = -\sigma^2\). So the square of the stress counts. At the wall we gain \(0{,}0046\) J, at \(0{,}9\) m we lose only \(0{,}00006\) J, and the compliance falls from \(1{,}7007\) J to \(1{,}6961\) J. It therefore pays to move material from the smaller stress to the larger one as long as the stresses differ, and the move has nothing left to gain only when the stress is the same everywhere. This is a guess. The theorem proves it and says which area achieves it.

To prepare for the proof, let us draw a picture. At the top are the functions \(f\) and \(g\) above the \(x\) axis and the weight \(A\), a band. The inner product \((f, g)_{\mathrm{A}}\) is the area under the product \(f\,g\,A\). The middle shows why \((f, f)_{\mathrm{A}}\) is positive for every \(f \ne 0\): if \(f(x_0) \ne 0\), there is an interval around \(x_0\) where \(f\) is not zero, and there \(f^2 A\) has a bump with positive area. The bottom is the case of equality: the function \(\sigma\) is constant, parallel to the function \(1\).

Theorem 29.60 The stiffest statically determinate rod (najtogejša statično določena palica)

Let a rod with modulus \(E > 0\) and load \(b\) be as above, let \(N\) be from equation (29.47), \(S = \int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x\), the area under the graph of the axial force, and \(V > 0\), the area of the band. For every admissible area function \(A\) with \(\int_0^L A\,\mathrm{d}x = V\):

  1. the compliance, for example of the uniform rod, satisfies
    \[C(A) \ge \frac{S^2}{E\,V} , \tag{29.50}\]
  2. equality holds exactly for \(A^*(x) = V\,N(x)/S\), proportional to the axial force, which is an admissible area function with \(\int_0^L A^*\,\mathrm{d}x = V\),
  3. for \(A^*\) the stress in every cross-section equals \(S/V\).
Proof

We must show the bound for every admissible \(A\), for example the uniform one, that \(A^*\) reaches it and that no other function does. We get the bound from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the inner product with the weight \(A\).

  1. Let \(X\) be the vector space of continuous functions on \([0, L]\) and \((f, g)_{\mathrm{A}} = \int_0^L f\,g\,A\,\mathrm{d}x\), the area under the product of the functions \(f\) and \(g\) with the weight \(A\). The product of continuous functions is continuous (corollary 1.65), so the integral exists (theorem 3.53).
  2. Properties 1 to 3 of definition 6.16 follow from \(f g A = g f A\) (the area does not change when \(f\) and \(g\) are swapped), \((f + g)\,h A = f h A + g h A\) and \((k f)\,g A = k\,(f g A)\) at every \(x\) and from the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.54, item 1).
  3. Property 4: let \(f \ne 0\), that is \(f(x_0) \ne 0\). Since \(f\) is continuous, \(f \ne 0\) on an interval around \(x_0\), which contains a point \(x_1 < L\). There \(A(x_1) > 0\), and \(f^2 A\) is continuous, nonnegative and positive at \(x_1\). As in step 4 of the proof of lemma 6.17, item 1, we therefore have \((f, f)_{\mathrm{A}} > 0\).
  4. The function \(\sigma\) is continuous and \(N = \sigma A\) (by definition 29.58), so \((\sigma, 1)_{\mathrm{A}} = \int_0^L \sigma A\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x = S\), the area under the graph of the axial force. By lemma 29.59, \((\sigma, \sigma)_{\mathrm{A}} = \int_0^L \sigma^2 A\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L N\sigma\,\mathrm{d}x = E\,C(A)\). The volume is \((1, 1)_{\mathrm{A}} = \int_0^L A\,\mathrm{d}x = V\), the area of the strip.
  5. Lemma 6.19 gives \(|S| \le \sqrt{E\,C(A)}\,\sqrt{V}\), where \(S\) is the area under the axial force and \(V\) the area of the band. In figure 29.86 this inequality is a comparison of two lengths. By steps 2 and 3, \((\cdot, \cdot)_{\mathrm{A}}\) is an inner product, so every function \(f\) has the length \(\sqrt{(f, f)_{\mathrm{A}}}\), just like a vector in space. The function \(1\) has the length \(\sqrt{(1, 1)_{\mathrm{A}}} = \sqrt V\), and the stress \(\sigma\) by step 4 the length \(\sqrt{(\sigma, \sigma)_{\mathrm{A}}} = \sqrt{E\,C(A)}\). The shadow of the arrow \(\sigma\) on the line of the function \(1\) has the length \((\sigma, 1)_{\mathrm{A}}/\sqrt V = S/\sqrt V\). The inequality, divided by \(\sqrt V\), says exactly that the shadow is not longer than the arrow. The ratio of the shadow to the arrow is the cosine of the angle between the arrows. For the uniform rod \(S/\sqrt{E\,C(A_0)\,V} = 5000/5774 = 0{,}866\), which is \(30^\circ\), and the lengths, multiplied by \(\sqrt V\), are \(5000\) N m and \(5774\) N m. Both sides are nonnegative, so by lemma 1.29 \(S^2 \le E\,C(A)\,V\), and dividing by the positive number \(EV\) we get the bound (29.50). This is item 1.
  6. Let \(A^* = VN/S\), the area with the shape of the graph of the axial force, drawn in figure 29.84 as the wedge. From \(b \ge m > 0\) it follows by lemma 3.54, item 3, that \(N(x) \ge m\,(L - x) > 0\) for \(x < L\), so \(S > 0\) and \(A^* > 0\) on \([0, L)\). The function \(A^*\) is continuous, because \(N\) is continuous (step 3 of the proof of lemma](29.84:sklin) 29.59), and \(A^*(L) = 0\). The stress \(N/A^* = S/V\) is [constant, so it has a limit, and \(A^*\) is admissible. By the linearity of the integral \(\int_0^L A^*\,\mathrm{d}x = (V/S)\int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x = V\). The stress \(S/V\) is item 3.
  7. For the wedge, lemma 29.59 gives \(C(A^*) = \frac1E \int_0^L N\,\frac SV\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{S^2}{EV}\). So \(A^*\) reaches the bound. This is the direction "if" of item 2.
  8. Let \(A\) be admissible with \(\int_0^L A\,\mathrm{d}x = V\) and \(C(A) = S^2/(EV)\). By step 4, \((\sigma, 1)_{\mathrm{A}}^2 = S^2 = E\,C(A)\,V = (\sigma, \sigma)_{\mathrm{A}}\,(1, 1)_{\mathrm{A}}\), which is equality in lemma 6.19. By step 3, \((\cdot, \cdot)_{\mathrm{A}}\) is an inner product and \(1 \ne 0\), so \(\sigma\) is a multiple of the function \(1\), hence constant, \(\sigma = c\), like the stress in the wedge. In figure 29.86 the shadow is as long as the arrow exactly when the arrow \(\sigma\) lies on the line of the function \(1\), as in the wedge, where both lengths are \(5000\) N m. From \(N = \sigma A\) we get \(A = N/c\) for \(x < L\), where \(c \ne 0\), because \(N > 0\) for \(x < L\). The functions \(A\) and \(N/c\) are continuous and equal on \([0, L)\), so they have the same limit at \(L\) and are equal there as well (definition 1.59), hence \(A = N/c\) on \([0, L]\). The condition \(\int_0^L A\,\mathrm{d}x = V\) gives by the linearity of the integral \(S/c = V\), so \(c = S/V\) and \(A = VN/S = A^*\). This is the direction "only if" of item 2.

Source: CHK §8.3.2 (PDF pp. 173-174): from the condition of constant energy density \(E\,(u')^2 = \lambda\) (8.33), the volume (8.32) and equilibrium it derives the wedge \(\rho = 2V\,(1 - x)\) for constant \(b\) and \(L = 1\). The proof by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, general \(b\), the bound (29.50) and uniqueness are not from the source.

What does the theorem say? Among all admissible areas with volume \(V\) the compliance is at least \(S^2/(EV)\), and we reach it with exactly one, with the area \(A^*\) proportional to the axial force. In it the stress is everywhere equal, \(\sigma = S/V\). Such a rod is fully stressed (polno napeta), like the truss in section 29.2, and every bit of material is used equally. Equal stress means equal \(\varepsilon = \sigma/E\) everywhere, so the energy density \(\tfrac12 E\varepsilon^2\) is constant as well, and with it its double \(E\varepsilon^2 = E\,(u')^2\). This is the condition \(E\,(u')^2 = \lambda\) with a constant \(\lambda\) from CHK (8.33), PDF p. 173. The same condition is, in section 29.5, the condition of theorem 29.37 for the bars of a truss, here for infinitely many bars. Why the result is so, the proof tells: compliance is the sum \(\int \sigma\cdot N\), the volume is the sum \(\int A\), and the axial force is the product \(N = \sigma A\). The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is an equality exactly when the factors are proportional, that is, when \(\sigma\) is constant. The trial with one bit of material before the theorem says the same from the other side: at constant stress no move of material gains anything.

For our rod \(N = b\,(L - x)\), the area of the triangle under its graph is \(S = bL^2/2 = 5000\) N m and \(A^*(x) = V N/S = 2A_0\,(1 - x/L)\). The area is \(2A_0 = 200\) mm² at the wall and falls linearly to zero. Its shape is a wedge (klin), after the splitting wedge that narrows to an edge. Above it is the uniform rod with the area \(A_0\) everywhere. The axial force is the same for both rods, falling linearly from \(bL\) to zero, because it depends only on the load and not on the area. At the bottom is the stress \(\sigma = N/A\): in the uniform rod it falls from \(100\) to \(0\) MPa, in the wedge it is constant, \(S/V = 50\) MPa, as item 3 of the theorem says. The compliances are

\[C(A_0) = 1{,}7007\ \text{J} , \qquad C(A^*) = \frac{S^2}{EV} = \frac{5000^2}{196 \cdot 10^9 \cdot 10^{-4}} = 1{,}2755\ \text{J} . \tag{29.51}\]

The ratio is \(3/4\): the wedge is less compliant by a quarter. The uniform rod is a factor \(4/3\) above the lower bound of the theorem and the bound (29.50) is strict for it, because \(A_0\) is not proportional to \(N\). In figure 29.86 the shadow is therefore shorter than the arrow, and the square of the ratio of the lengths \(5000/5774\) is exactly \(3/4\). Where does the difference show on the rod itself? Let us look at the displacements.

We load the rod and its free end moves to the right, strongly exaggerated in the figure. The shift is the same for both rods, \(0{,}2551\) mm. Why the same? The displacement of the end is the sum of the elongations of all slices, \(u(L) = \frac1E\int_0^L \sigma\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the mean stress in figure 29.84 is \(50\) MPa for both rods, in the wedge everywhere, in the uniform rod as the middle between \(100\) and \(0\). The difference is in the interior. Let us draw the displacement \(u(x)\) of every cross-section above its position \(x\) (axes). In the wedge the strain is \(\varepsilon = \sigma/E = 0{,}2551 \cdot 10^{-3}\) everywhere, so \(u(x) = \varepsilon x\) is a straight line and \(u(L) = 0{,}2551\) mm. In the uniform rod \(u(x) = \varepsilon_0\,(x - x^2/(2L))\) with \(\varepsilon_0 = bL/(EA_0) = 0{,}5102 \cdot 10^{-3}\), a parabola, twice as steep as the line at the wall, because the stress there is \(100\) MPa instead of \(50\), and horizontal at the free end, because there is no stress there. It too ends at the same point, \(u(L) = \varepsilon_0 L/2 = 0{,}2551\) mm. The difference of displacements is \(\varepsilon_0\,x\,(L - x)/(2L) \ge 0\), in the interior the displacement of the wedge is smaller, in the middle by \(0{,}0638\) mm.

On this graph the compliance shows as an area. For a constant load, by equation (29.48), \(C = b\int_0^L u\,\mathrm{d}x\), so it is \(b\) times the area under the displacement curve. Under the line of the wedge is a triangle of area \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1\ \text{m} \cdot 0{,}2551\ \text{mm}\), which gives \(C = 1{,}2755\) J. Under the parabola there is in addition the lens between the parabola and the line, which adds a third, up to \(1{,}7007\) J. Compliance is the work of the load on the displacements of all points, not only of the free end, so it is smaller for the wedge. The displacement of the free end is therefore not a measure of stiffness under a distributed load.

Example 29.61 The wedge as the rod of least volume at an allowed stress (klin kot palica z najmanjšo prostornino pri dovoljeni napetosti)

Let us limit the stress by the allowed stress \(\sigma_0 = 220\) MPa, without a safety factor (the assumption of section 29.2), and ask how much material the cheapest rod needs. The condition \(N/A \le \sigma_0\) is the condition \(A(x) \ge N(x)/\sigma_0\) in every cross-section separately, because \(N\) is known from equilibrium. The volume \(\int A\,\mathrm{d}x\) is the smaller the smaller \(A\) is, so it is smallest when \(A = N/\sigma_0\) everywhere. This is a wedge, the area with the shape of the axial force, with \(\sigma = \sigma_0\), with the volume \(V = S/\sigma_0 = 5000/(220 \cdot 10^6) = 22{,}73\) cm³ and the area \(A(0) = bL/\sigma_0 = 45{,}45\) mm² at the wall. This is the area \(A^*\) from theorem 29.60 for \(V = S/\sigma_0\), since by item 3 the stress in it is \(S/V = \sigma_0\). A uniform rod with the same volume has \(A = 22{,}73\) mm² and at the wall the stress \(bL/A = 440\) MPa, twice what is allowed. The rod of least compliance at a given volume and the rod of least volume at a given stress are therefore the same rod, the wedge.

The wedge has area zero at the free end. This is an idealization. A real rod would have a smallest area \(A_{\min} > 0\) there, which we would have to add as the condition \(A \ge A_{\min}\), and with such a condition \(A^*\) is not admissible, so the theorem in this form does not hold. CHK requires only \(\rho \ge 0\) (PDF p. 169), and so do we, and we do not treat a rod with \(A_{\min}\). The rod is in tension everywhere (\(N \ge 0\)), so buckling does not threaten even at small area, while for compressed rods a condition would have to be added, as in section 29.2. The rod model requires that the area changes slowly, because in it the stress acts only along the axis, while the surface of the wedge is inclined to the axis. For a round cross-section of the wedge the radius at the wall is \(7{,}98\) mm and the slope of the surface is \(\mathrm{d}r/\mathrm{d}x = -0{,}0040\). From \(\pi r^2 = 2A_0\,(1 - x/L)\) the size of the slope is \(0{,}0040/\sqrt{1 - x/L}\), which grows towards the free end and reaches \(0{,}01\) at \(1 - x/L = 0{,}4^2 = 0{,}16\). Along the first \(84\) % of the length the slope is therefore smaller than \(0{,}01\). The last \(16\) % of the length contributes little to the compliance. In the wedge \(\sigma\) is constant, so the share of this piece in the compliance (29.49) equals its share in \(S = \int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x\), that is \(0{,}16^2 = 0{,}0256\), less than \(3\) %.

The theorem holds for a statically determinate rod, because the proof of lemma 29.59 and step 4 of the proof of the theorem used that \(N\) is known before we choose \(A\), as the axial force is the same for the uniform rod and for the wedge. What would happen if \(N\) depended on \(A\)? Let us look at a rod clamped at both ends.

Example 29.62 A rod fixed at both ends (palica, vpeta na obeh koncih)

A steel rod of length \(L = 1\) m with \(E = 196\) GPa and volume \(V = 100\) cm³ is clamped at \(x = 0\) and at \(x = L\) (supports). In the joint at the distance \(a = 0{,}3L\) from the left wall it is pulled by the force \(P = 10\) kN in the direction of \(x\) (force). The left piece has length \(a\) and constant area \(A_1\), the right piece length \(L - a\) and constant area \(A_2\), and \(s = A_1 a/V\) is the share of the volume in the left, shorter piece.

How much does each piece carry? The joint moves from its original position in the direction of the force by \(u\), exaggerated in the figure. The walls stand still, so the left piece stretches by \(u\) and the right one shortens by \(u\). For a rod, force \(=\) stiffness \(\times\) elongation with the stiffness \(EA/L\) (step 3 of the proof of theorem 4.3), so in the left piece the tension is \(k_1 u\) with \(k_1 = EA_1/a\) and in the right one the compression is \(k_2 u\) with \(k_2 = EA_2/(L - a)\). We cut the joint free in thought and draw the forces on it: the force \(P\) acts in the direction of \(x\), the left piece pulls it to the left with the force \(k_1 u\) and the right one pushes it to the left with the force \(k_2 u\). The joint is in equilibrium, so \(P = (k_1 + k_2)\,u\). The forces in the pieces are therefore

\[N_1 = P\,\frac{k_1}{k_1 + k_2} , \qquad |N_2| = P\,\frac{k_2}{k_1 + k_2} ,\]

and they depend on the areas. Equilibrium alone is one equation, \(N_1 + |N_2| = P\), for two unknowns, so the rod is statically indeterminate (statično nedoločena): we need Hooke's law as well. The stiffness of the rod as a whole, force over displacement of the joint, is \(k = k_1 + k_2 = (EV/L^2)\,\big(s/0{,}3^2 + (1 - s)/0{,}7^2\big)\) and the compliance \(C = P\,u = P^2/k\).

The graph shows \(k\) in the unit \(EV/L^2 = 19{,}60\) MN/m against \(s\). It runs from \(2{,}04\) at \(s = 0\) (all material in the longer piece) to \(11{,}11\) at \(s = 1\) (all material in the shorter piece). The uniform rod has \(s = a/L = 0{,}3\), \(k = 4{,}76\) units, \(93{,}33\) MN/m, and \(C = 1{,}0714\) J. At \(s = 1\), \(k = 217{,}8\) MN/m and \(C = 0{,}4592\) J. Then the right piece has in the limit area zero and carries nothing, \(N_2 = 0\), and the left piece is a statically determinate rod of length \(a\) with the axial force \(P\), constant along the piece, for which the proportional area is constant. Its compliance is \(P^2 a/(EA_1) = P^2 a^2/(EV) = 0{,}4592\) J, as the graph says.

We would like to use the theorem by taking the areas proportional to the forces. In the uniform rod the forces are \(N_1 = 0{,}7P\) and \(|N_2| = 0{,}3P\), so \(A_1 : A_2 = 7 : 3\), which gives \(A_1 a : A_2 (L - a) = 0{,}7 \cdot 0{,}3 : 0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}7 = 1 : 1\), so \(s = 0{,}5\). The stiffness is \(6{,}58\) units (the point at \(s = 0{,}5\)), \(C = 0{,}7759\) J, better than \(1{,}0714\) J, but worse than \(0{,}4592\) J at \(s = 1\). In this new rod the forces are no longer \(0{,}7P\) and \(0{,}3P\), but \(0{,}8448P\) and \(0{,}1552P\), the ratio is \(5{,}44\) instead of \(2{,}33\). The areas no longer follow the forces that these areas cause. Is there a plan in which the areas follow the forces in that same plan?

Lemma 29.63 The areas cannot be proportional to their own forces (ploščini ne moreta biti sorazmerni lastnima silama)

Let the rod be as in example 29.62 with the distance \(a \ne L/2\). There is no plan with positive areas \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) of the pieces in which \(A_1 : A_2 = N_1 : |N_2|\), where \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) are the forces in this plan.

Proof

We must show that proportionality of the pieces would put the joint in the middle, \(a = L/2\).

  1. By example 29.62 the forces in a plan are \(N_1 = P\,k_1/(k_1 + k_2)\) and \(|N_2| = P\,k_2/(k_1 + k_2)\), so \(N_1/|N_2| = k_1/k_2\).
  2. From the stiffness of the left piece \(k_1 = EA_1/a\) and of the right piece \(k_2 = EA_2/(L - a)\) we get \(k_1/k_2 = \dfrac{A_1}{A_2}\cdot\dfrac{L - a}{a}\).
  3. The requirement \(A_1/A_2 = N_1/|N_2|\) and steps 1 and 2 give \(\dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = \dfrac{A_1}{A_2}\cdot\dfrac{L - a}{a}\). Since \(A_1/A_2 > 0\), we must have \((L - a)/a = 1\), so the joint is in the middle, \(a = L/2\).

Source: The proof is not from the source.

The reason is Hooke's law. At full stress the elongation per unit length \(\varepsilon = \sigma/E\) would have to be equal in size in both pieces, but the left piece stretches by \(u\) over the length \(a\), the right one shortens by the same \(u\) over the length \(L - a\). Let us draw the displacement of every cross-section above its position, measured over the \(x\) axis. The graph is a broken line (lomljenka), which rises from zero at the left wall to \(u\) at the joint and falls to zero at the right wall. Its slope is the elongation per unit length, on the left \(u/a\) and on the right \(-u/(L - a)\). For the uniform rod \(u = 0{,}1071\) mm, the slopes are \(3{,}571 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(-1{,}531 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the stresses \(70\) MPa and \(-30\) MPa. The broken line has the same height \(u\) on both sides, so the slopes are equally steep only when the peak is in the middle, \(u/a = u/(L - a)\) only for \(a = L/2\). If we correct the areas by the rule "the new area is proportional to the present force", the ratio of the areas is multiplied in every step by \((L - a)/a = 7/3\) (step 2 of the lemma). The share \(s\) therefore goes from \(0{,}3\) through \(0{,}5\), \(0{,}7\), \(0{,}845\) and \(0{,}927\) towards \(1\), and all the material moves into the shorter piece, to which the computation has already brought us. Theorem 29.60 does not hold for a rod clamped at both ends, because the proof assumes that the axial force \(N\) is determined by the load alone. The best plan in the family \(s\) is \(s = 1\), but we do not know whether it is the best among all plans. The condition of constant energy density is derived by CHK for an abstract system with an energy that is linear in the design function, and it does not require static determinacy (§8.3.1, theorem 8.1, PDF pp. 168 and 172).

The same problem for a beam, where the variable is the width of the cross-section, is in CHK §8.3.3 (PDF pp. 175-178). First, for a given cross-section area, one looks for the shape that gives the largest second moment of area, and shows that the material must be put in the flanges (the I profile, PDF p. 176). Then, for a simply supported beam with constant load, the width along the beam is computed from the condition of constant energy density (PDF pp. 177-178). We do not repeat this here, because it needs the beam equation of chapter 5 and the calculus of variations with a second derivative.

A summary of how each claim is shown. Equation (29.47) is the equilibrium of the piece, with the sign from the definition of the axial force. Lemma 29.59 is derived by integration by parts from the definitions of stress and strain. Theorem 29.60 is proved by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the inner product with the area function as the weight. Example 29.62 is computed from the equilibrium of the joint and Hooke's law, and lemma 29.63 from the same two equations. Notation: \(C\) is compliance, and in chapter 10 the damping matrix. The stress \(\sigma_0\) is the allowed stress without a safety factor, which would only multiply all the areas by the same number. The letter \(S\) denotes the sum of axial forces, because \(I\) in chapter 5 is the second moment of area.

29.9 Topology of a sheet (topologija plošče)

In the truss of section 29.5.3 the optimum deleted a bar by itself: its area fell to zero, and the structure got a different connection of its joints. This is how the topology (topologija) changes, which is why we called it topology optimization already in section 29.1. With the truss we chose the bars in advance. But what if we have a piece of sheet instead of bars and ask where the material goes and where a hole stays? Then there is no list of bars to point at, and every small piece of the sheet can be solid or empty. In this section we write the task as a minimum compliance problem (naloga najmanjše podajnosti) of section 29.5, find out why intermediate values do not disappear without an extra rule, and add two rules used by programs: the power rule (SIMP) and the sensitivity filter (filter občutljivosti). For each we say what we prove and what we do not. In the figure of the domain below, every piece of the sheet is one square element that we can fill or empty.

29.9.1 The sheet of variable thickness (plošča s spremenljivo debelino)

Take a thin sheet of thickness \(t\) loaded in its own plane, that is, plane stress (definition 11.36). We divide the region of the sheet into \(N\) square elements, each of side \(1\) (the unit of length). An element has four nodes, each with two degrees of freedom, which is the four-node element of chapter 15. In every element \(e\) we take the thickness constant and write it as \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} t\), where \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} \in (0, 1]\) is the relative thickness (relativna debelina). The thickness is now the design variable, as the area \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\) was for a bar (CHK §9.1.1, PDF pp. 183-185). Elsewhere in the book the letter \(\rho\) means mass density, here it is always the number \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the element index. For a three-dimensional body, which we do not treat here, \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) would not be a thickness but a relative density of the material (PDF p. 192), and we use the same name for the sheet. In the figure below, each of the \(N = 300\) elements is such a square with its own thickness \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} t\).

The example we solve is a half beam, as used by SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 3, figure 1). A full beam, supported at both ends and loaded in the middle, is symmetric, so we compute only the left half. The region has \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 30\) elements in the horizontal and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = 10\) in the vertical direction (dimensions). The force \(F\) acts downwards at the top left node. The left edge lies on the plane of symmetry, so its nodes must not move horizontally, which we draw as rollers. The bottom right node is supported vertically (support). The supports prevent all three rigid motions of the sheet in its plane: the rollers together with the support prevent the horizontal translation and the rotation, the support prevents the vertical translation. Each element has its own relative thickness \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\).

We choose units so that the modulus is \(E = 1\), the thickness \(t = 1\), the side of an element \(1\) and the force \(F = 1\). The compliance \(C = \vek F^\T\vek u\) is then a number that gives the compliance in the unit \(F^2/(E t)\), because in a plane problem the displacement is proportional to \(F/(E t)\) and the length of the element cancels. The model assumes small displacements and a linear elastic material (the idealizations of section 29.5.1). For the full beam the displacement of the top left node, where the force acts, is \(123{,}07\,F/(E t)\), for a beam with compliance \(190{,}9\) it is \(190{,}9\,F/(E t)\) (for a unit force the compliance equals the displacement of its point of application). The quantity \(F/(E t)\) is a length, because \(E t\) has the unit of a force per length. If \(F/(E t)\) is at most \(10^{-4}\) of an element side, the displacement is at most \(190{,}9 \cdot 10^{-4} = 0{,}0191\) of a side, that is below \(2\,\%\), hence small, as the model assumes. A force at one point would in the continuous model give an infinite stress under the force, while the compliance stays finite on a finite mesh. So we take the force on a node as a model of the load and not as a prediction of the stress at that point.

The stiffness matrix of an element at full thickness is the matrix \(\mat k_0\) of chapter 15. Its size is \(8 \times 8\) (four nodes, two degrees of freedom each). For \(\nu = 0{,}3\) and \(2\times 2\) Gauss integration we computed and checked it (num-09.out, A). It is symmetric, has three zero eigenvalues, which are the three rigid motions of the element (two translations and a rotation), and five positive ones: \(0{,}4945\) (twice), \(0{,}7692\) (twice) and \(1{,}4286\). The first row begins with \(k_{11} = 0{,}4945\) and \(k_{12} = 0{,}1786\). The sum of its entries that belong to horizontal displacements is zero, as it must be: if all nodes move horizontally by the same number, the element is not deformed and there are no forces. It belongs to one of the elements of the mesh in the figure of the domain.

Why is the stiffness proportional to the thickness? Let us look at the sheet from its edge, so that we see its thickness (figure 29.91, (a)). Take two equal sheets of thickness \(t/2\), fixed to the same wall, and pull each with the force \(F/2\). Both get longer by the same \(u\): the grey dashed line shows the free end before loading, the orange outline the sheet after it. Since the neighbouring faces move by the same amount, there is no force between the sheets, even if we glue them. Glued, they are one sheet of thickness \(t\), which for the same \(u\) needs the force \(F\), the sum of the two. A sheet twice as thick is therefore twice as stiff, and the same holds for every share \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) of the thickness.

The conclusion rests on the assumption that the displacement is the same everywhere through the thickness, which is plane stress. It holds for a thin sheet loaded in its own plane. It does not hold when the sheet bends out of its plane: then the layers through the thickness stretch differently and the stiffness grows with the third power of the thickness (theorem 22.28, \(D = Eh^3/(12(1 - \nu^2))\)), so half the thickness would give one eighth of the stiffness and not one half. So the problem of this section holds only for loading in the plane. The displacement of the glued sheet is the same \(u\) over the whole thickness, so the stiffnesses add up across the thickness.

Lemma 29.64 The stiffness of the sheet is linear in the thickness (togost plošče je linearna v debelini)

Let the element \(e\) have thickness \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} t\) and let \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \rho_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat k_0\) be the stiffness matrix of the element, \(\mat K(\vek\rho) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{N}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^{0}\) the matrix of the structure, where \(\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^{0} = \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the placement of the matrix \(\mat k_0\) among the degrees of freedom of the structure (theorem 7.13). Then \(\mat K\) is linear in \(\vek\rho\) and \(\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek v \ge 0\) for every \(\vek v\). If the supports are such that \(\mat K(\vek 1)\) is not singular, then \(\mat K(\vek\rho)\) is positive definite for every \(\vek\rho\) with \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\) for all \(e\). In the figure of the sheet edge this means that the sheet of thickness \(t\) has the sum of the stiffnesses of the two sheets of thickness \(t/2\).

Proof

We have to show linearity, nonnegativity and positive definiteness.

  1. The stiffness matrix of a plane element is the integral over the element of the product of the matrices \(\mat B^\T\mat D\,\mat B\) and the thickness (chapter 15). The matrix \(\mat B\) (displacements to strains) depends only on the position of the nodes, the matrix \(\mat D\) only on the material (theorem 11.37), so at a constant thickness \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} t\) the matrix of the element is \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} t\int\mat B^\T\mat D\,\mat B\), that is \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat k_0\) with \(\mat k_0\) at thickness \(t\). This is the computation for figure 29.91: the sheet of thickness \(t\) has twice the stiffness of a sheet of thickness \(t/2\).
  2. By theorem 7.13, \(\mat K = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\mat k_0)\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\).
  3. For \(\vek v\) we have \(\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek v = (\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\vek v)^\T\mat k_0(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\vek v) \ge 0\), because \(\mat k_0\) is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15, the strain energy of the element is nonnegative).
  4. Let \(\rho_{\min} = \min_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\). By step 3, \(\vek v^\T\mat K(\vek\rho)\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek v \ge \rho_{\min}\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek v = \rho_{\min}\,\vek v^\T\mat K(\vek 1)\vek v > 0\) for \(\vek v \ne \vek 0\). The last inequality holds because \(\mat K(\vek 1) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\) is positive semidefinite by step 3 and nonsingular by hypothesis, hence positive definite: its eigenvalues are nonnegative and none is \(0\), so all are positive.

Source: CHK §9.1.1 (PDF pp. 184-185): \(\mat K(\vek x) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} x_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\), the same as for the truss (CHK §5.1, PDF pp. 86-87). The proof is ours.

The lemma is the same as lemma 29.31 for the truss, with \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) in place of the area \(A_{\mathrm{e}}\). So the whole section on the truss repeats for the sheet. CHK says that this is so (PDF p. 184), and therefore we write the problem anew only in a short form.

Definition 29.65 The variable thickness sheet problem (naloga plošče s spremenljivo debelino)

Let \(\mat K(\vek\rho)\) be as in lemma 29.64, \(\vek F \ne \vek 0\) a load, \(\rho_{\min} \in (0, 1)\) a lower bound, \(\varphi \in (\rho_{\min}, 1)\) the volume fraction (delež prostornine) and \(N\) the number of elements. The sheet problem is

\[\min_{\vek\rho}\ C(\vek\rho) = \vek F^\T\vek u \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mat K(\vek\rho)\,\vek u = \vek F , \quad \sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{N}\rho_{\mathrm{e}} \le \varphi N , \quad \rho_{\min} \le \rho_{\mathrm{e}} \le 1 . \tag{29.52}\]

It has \(N\) elements of variable thickness, the force \(F\) is given and the sum of the densities is bounded.

Source: CHK §9.1.1 (PDF pp. 183-185), the problems (P_s)_FE, where the volume is \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}} a_{\mathrm{e}} x_{\mathrm{e}}\) with element areas \(a_{\mathrm{e}}\). Here all elements are equal, \(a_{\mathrm{e}} = 1\). The name "volume fraction" and the letter \(\varphi\) are ours: SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 2, equation (1)) writes \(f\), which in this chapter is the objective function.

The feasible set is a box cut by a half-space, hence a convex set (definition 29.16). We look at it for two elements in figure 29.92, where the axes are the densities \(\rho_1\) and \(\rho_2\). The box \([\rho_{\min}, 1]^2\) is the square between the lower and the upper bound of the density. The half-space \(\rho_1 + \rho_2 \le \varphi N\) is the part of the plane below the line that cuts the square. The feasible set is their common part, the shaded triangle. With more elements it is the same, except that the box is higher dimensional.

Figure 29.93 shows why the compliance is convex. Take the segment from the design \(\vek\sigma\) to the design \(\vek\rho\) and on it the number \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\). For every chosen vector \(\vek v\) the expression \(2\vek F^\T\vek v - \vek v^\T\mat K\vek v\) is a linear function of \(t\), because \(\mat K\) is linear in \(\vek\rho\): these are the lines. At every \(t\) the compliance is the largest of them, so it is the envelope, which curves upward. The chord between the endpoints lies above the envelope, and this is convexity.

Corollary 29.66 The sheet problem is convex (naloga plošče je konveksna)

Problem (29.52) is a convex problem (definition 29.25): every local minimum is global (lemma 29.18). Convexity shows in the feasible set and in the envelope of the compliance: it curves only upward, so there is no second valley.

Proof

We have to show that the feasible set is convex and that \(C\) is convex on it.

  1. The feasible set is the intersection of the box \([\rho_{\min}, 1]^N\) and the half-space \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}} \le \varphi N\). The box and the half-space are convex, and an intersection of convex sets is convex: if \(\vek\rho\) and \(\vek\sigma\) lie in the intersection, then \(t\vek\rho + (1 - t)\vek\sigma\) lies in both sets (in the figure this is the segment between two feasible points, which stays in the triangle).
  2. By lemma 29.64, \(\mat K\) is linear in \(\vek\rho\) and positive definite on the box, because \(\rho_{\min} > 0\) (assumption: \(\mat K(\vek 1)\) nonsingular, which is a condition on the supports) (each of the lines in the envelope figure is linear along the segment).
  3. The proof of theorem 29.34 needs only these properties: the linearity of the matrix in the variables (step 1 there), positive definiteness (step 2) and item 4 of lemma 29.33, which holds for every symmetric positive definite matrix. So \(C\) is convex on the box, because it is the upper envelope of functions linear in \(\vek\rho\) (the envelope of the lines lies below the chord between the endpoints).

Source: CHK §9.1.1 (PDF p. 184): the problem is "mathematically equivalent to the truss problem", and §9.3.2 (PDF p. 196): "The variable thickness sheet problem is a convex problem." The proof is ours, following theorem 29.34.

A near miss for this corollary is \(\rho_{\min} = 0\). Then the feasible set contains designs in which the node where the force acts has only elements of zero thickness. Its row in the matrix \(\mat K\) is zero, the system \(\mat K\vek u = \vek F\) has no solution, and \(C = +\infty\) (definition 29.32, extended to this problem). The matrix is singular, the problem lies outside the range of the corollary, and the computation fails (CHK §9.2, PDF p. 192: "state problems that are singular and not uniquely solvable"). That is why programs always take \(\rho_{\min} > 0\), as for the truss: SIGMUND2001 takes \(\rho_{\min} = 0{,}001\) (PDF p. 2, "x_min"), and so do our computations.

Does such a convex problem give a beam that we can make from material and holes? The computation answers. We take \(\varphi = 0{,}5\), \(\rho_{\min} = 0{,}001\) and compute the optimum with the rule of section 29.9.3 at \(p = 1\). The compliance is \(162{,}4\), and more than two thirds of the elements (the share of elements with \(0{,}1 < \rho_{\mathrm{e}} < 0{,}9\) is \(0{,}703\)) have an intermediate thickness. Figure 29.99 shows it: the bottom picture is grey almost everywhere, without sharp edges. This is not an error of the computation but a property of the problem: at \(p = 1\) the stiffness is proportional to the thickness, and half the thickness gives half the stiffness, so nothing penalizes grey. What do we do? We must make intermediate values cost something.

29.9.2 Penalizing intermediate values (kaznovanje vmesnih vrednosti)

Instead of letting every element choose its thickness, we force it to choose between solid and empty. Penalization (kaznovanje) means that an intermediate value \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) gives less stiffness than its volume entitles it to. CHK §9.2.1 (PDF pp. 192-193) introduces the power rule that we call SIMP (solid isotropic material with penalization). In the figure the curve for \(p = 3\) lies below the line \(p = 1\) everywhere except at the full element: this is the penalty for an intermediate value.

Definition 29.67 The SIMP power rule (potenčno pravilo SIMP)

Let \(p > 1\) be a number, the penalization power (kaznovalna potenca), and \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} \in [\rho_{\min}, 1]\) the relative density (relativna gostota) of the element \(e\). The SIMP rule takes the modulus of the element

\[E(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}) = \rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p}\,E_0 , \tag{29.53}\]

where \(E_0\) is the modulus of the solid material, and the volume of the element proportional to \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\). The stiffness matrix of the element is \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p}\,\mat k_0\), that of the structure \(\mat K(\vek\rho) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\), and the compliance is

\[C(\vek\rho) = \vek F^\T\vek u = \sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{N}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p}\,\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\,\vek u_{\mathrm{e}} , \tag{29.54}\]

where \(\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the vector of nodal displacements of the element \(e\) at \(\mat K(\vek\rho)\vek u = \vek F\). The rule is shown by the curves for \(p = 1, 2, 3\) above the density axis.

Source: CHK §9.2.1 (PDF pp. 192-193), where the power is denoted \(q\), and SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 2, equation (1)), where it is \(p\), typically \(p = 3\). The step to \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\) in equation (29.54) is Clapeyron (theorem 4.86): \(\vek F^\T\vek u = \vek u^\T\mat K\vek u = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^p\mat k_0)\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}\).

The letter \(p\) means a pressure in chapters 2 and 11, here it is always the power, and the letter \(\lambda\) means an eigenvalue in chapter 10, here the multiplier of the volume constraint. For \(p = 1\) we get the sheet problem of the previous subsection.
