In figure 29.94 the horizontal axis carries the relative density \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) from \(0\) to \(1\), and the vertical one the relative stiffness \(E_{\mathrm{e}}/E_0 = \rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p}\). Which colour belongs to which power is told by the legend at the top left. The curves for \(p = 1\), \(p = 2\) and \(p = 3\) show what the power does: at half density the element has, at the marked points, only \(0{,}5\), \(0{,}25\) and \(0{,}125\) of the full stiffness.

A historical note, because it says why SIMP is in use and why the usual power is \(3\). The first approach to the topology problem (SIGMUND2001, PDF p. 1) was based on homogenization: material with microscopic holes, whose size and orientation have to be chosen. By the same source this approach has two weaknesses: determining and evaluating the optimal microstructures is cumbersome or unresolved for problems other than compliance, and the resulting structure cannot be built, because no definite length scale is associated with the microstructures. The power approach is simpler and was at first criticized, because no physical material was supposed to exist with such properties. It was later proved that the power form is physically permissible if \(p \ge 3\) at \(\nu = 1/3\) (PDF pp. 1-2). That proof is cited there, it is not ours, and so we cite it and do not prove it. This is why \(p = 3\) is the usual choice (SIGMUND2001, PDF p. 2: "typically p = 3"). Its curve is the one we use in this problem for the stiffness of an element.

Why the rule penalizes intermediate values we show for a case we can compute.

Lemma 29.68 Uniform density under SIMP (enakomerna gostota pri SIMP)

Let \(\mat K(\vek 1)\) be positive definite and \(\vek\rho = \rho\,\vek 1\) with the same density \(\rho \in (0, 1]\) in all elements. Then

\[C(\rho\,\vek 1) = \rho^{-p}\,C(\vek 1) . \tag{29.55}\]

The volume is \(\rho\) times the volume of the solid body, the stiffness is \(\rho^p\) times, so the stiffness per unit volume, measured as a ratio to the full value, equals \(\rho^{\,p-1}\). For \(p > 1\) this is less than \(1\) at every \(\rho \in (0, 1)\), for \(p = 1\) it is exactly \(1\). At \(\rho = 0{,}5\) and \(p = 3\) the point on the curve shows stiffness \(1/8\), so the compliance is eight times larger.

Proof

We have to show that the system of equations at uniform density reduces to the system of the solid body.

  1. By definition 29.67, \(\mat K(\rho\,\vek 1) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho^p\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0 = \rho^p\,\mat K(\vek 1)\).
  2. The system \(\rho^p\,\mat K(\vek 1)\,\vek u = \vek F\) has the solution \(\vek u = \rho^{-p}\vek u_1\), where \(\mat K(\vek 1)\,\vek u_1 = \vek F\), and \(C(\rho\vek 1) = \vek F^\T\vek u = \rho^{-p}\,\vek F^\T\vek u_1 = \rho^{-p}\,C(\vek 1)\).
  3. The volume is \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho = \rho N\), that is \(\rho\) times the volume \(N\), and the stiffness is \(\rho^p\) times. The ratio of the two is \(\rho^p/\rho = \rho^{\,p-1}\), which for \(0 < \rho < 1\) is less than \(1\) exactly when \(p > 1\) (the ratio of the heights of the curve and the line at the same density is \(\rho^{p-1}\) and is below \(1\)).

Source: The proof is not from the source. The meaning of the ratio is CHK §9.2.1 (PDF pp. 192-193): at \(q > 1\) "the obtained stiffness ... disproportionately low".

Let us look at the numbers, num-09.out (C). The solid beam with \(\rho = 1\) has \(C = 123{,}0694\). At uniform density \(\rho = 0{,}5\) the compliance at \(p = 3\) is \(984{,}5548\), which is \(8{,}000\) times more, and \(0{,}5^{-3} = 8\) is exactly this quotient: the point on the blue curve at \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}5\) shows the stiffness \(0{,}125 = 1/8\), and a stiffness eight times smaller gives a displacement eight times larger at the same force. At \(p = 1\) it is \(246{,}1387\), which is \(2{,}000\) times more, because the grey line gives the stiffness \(0{,}5\) at the same density. If we have half the material, then at \(p = 3\) it does not pay to spread it uniformly. The optimizer spreads the material differently: at \(p = 3\) it reaches \(C = 190{,}9\) (below), which is \(5{,}2\) times less than the uniform distribution at the same volume. Why does gathering the material pay? An element of density \(0{,}5\) uses half the material of a solid element, but contributes only one eighth of its full stiffness (the lowest point). Two such elements use as much material as one solid and one empty element, yet each contributes one eighth, while a solid element contributes all of its stiffness. The gap between the line and the curve \(p = 3\) is the stiffness that a grey element loses.

A near miss for lemma 29.68 are \(p = 1\) and \(p < 1\). At \(p = 1\) the ratio is exactly \(1\): grey is no worse than a blackwhite and whiteblack pattern, and the result \(0{,}703\) of grey at \(p = 1\) of the previous subsection is exactly this. At \(p < 1\) we have \(\rho^{\,p-1} > 1\) and the rule would reward intermediate values. So the rule is useful only at \(p > 1\). At \(p = 1\) the line is the diagonal of the square and the ratio of heights is \(1\) everywhere.

The problem at \(p > 1\) is no longer convex. CHK §9.3.2 (PDF p. 196) says so and adds that the algorithm can end in different local optima depending on the starting point. We cite this, we do not prove it. At \(p = 1\) it is convex and its optimum is a lower bound for all \(p \ge 1\). The reason is the curve: the stiffness is no longer a straight line in the density, so the matrix \(\mat K\) is no longer linear in \(\vek\rho\) and the convexity proof of this section does not carry over.

Lemma 29.69 A lower bound for SIMP (spodnja meja SIMP)

Let \(\mat K(\vek 1)\) be positive definite, \(\mat K_{\mathrm{p}}(\vek\rho) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\) with \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} \in (0, 1]\) and \(C_{\mathrm{p}}\) the compliance at the power \(p \ge 1\). Then \(C_{\mathrm{p}}(\vek\rho) \ge C_1(\vek\rho)\) for every \(\vek\rho\), and therefore for every feasible \(\vek\rho\) of problem (29.52)

\[C_{\mathrm{p}}(\vek\rho) \ge \min_{\vek\sigma}\,C_1(\vek\sigma) ,\]

where the minimum is over the feasible \(\vek\sigma\) of problem (29.52). The figure says the same: the curves for \(p = 2\) and \(p = 3\) lie below the line, so the stiffness is smaller and the compliance larger.

Proof

We have to show that a smaller stiffness means a larger compliance.

  1. For \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} \in (0, 1]\) we have \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p} \le \rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) at \(p \ge 1\): in figure 29.94 the curves for \(p = 2\) and \(p = 3\) lie everywhere below the line \(p = 1\) and reach it only at \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = 1\). With \(\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek v \ge 0\) (lemma 29.64), \(\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{p}}\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^p\,\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek v \le \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek v = \vek v^\T\mat K_1\vek v\) for every \(\vek v\).
  2. The matrices \(\mat K_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\mat K_1\) are positive definite: as in step 4 of lemma 29.64, \(\vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{p}}\vek v \ge \rho_{\min}^{\,p}\,\vek v^\T\mat K(\vek 1)\vek v > 0\) for \(\vek v \ne \vek 0\), where \(\rho_{\min} = \min_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\). By item 4 of lemma 29.33, \(C_{\mathrm{p}}(\vek\rho) = \max_{\vek{v}}[2\vek F^\T\vek v - \vek v^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{p}}\vek v] \ge \max_{\vek{v}}[2\vek F^\T\vek v - \vek v^\T\mat K_1\vek v] = C_1(\vek\rho)\) by step 1.
  3. Every feasible \(\vek\rho\) of problem (29.52) is also feasible for \(p = 1\), so \(C_1(\vek\rho) \ge \min_{\vek\sigma} C_1(\vek\sigma)\).

Source: The proof is not from the source.

This lemma is our own test. The compliance of no design with \(p = 3\) may be smaller than \(162{,}4\), if this is really the minimum at \(p = 1\). Our results are \(190{,}9\) and \(225{,}9\) (below), both larger. This is only a check, not a proof, because \(162{,}4\) is the value of a loop that stopped after \(14\) iterations with a change of \(0{,}0094\), not a proved minimum. At \(p < 1\) the inequality reverses: \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p} \ge \rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{p}} \le C_1\). The compliances are those of (a) and (b), and the lower bound is (c).

29.9.3 Sensitivity and the update (občutljivost in posodobitev)

For the loop of section 29.7.5 we need the derivative of the compliance with respect to the relative density. For the truss it was \(\partial C/\partial A_{\mathrm{e}} = -\vek u^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}\vek u\) (corollary 29.44). Here the dependence on \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) is a power, so the factor changes.

Lemma 29.70 Sensitivity of the compliance under SIMP (občutljivost podajnosti pri SIMP)

Let \(\mat K(\vek\rho) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\) be positive definite, \(\vek F\) independent of \(\vek\rho\) and \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} > 0\). Then

\[\frac{\partial C}{\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}} = -\,p\,\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{\,p-1}\,\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\,\vek u_{\mathrm{e}} \le 0 . \tag{29.56}\]

The factor \(p\,\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{p-1}\) is the slope of the stiffness curve at the density \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Proof

We have to show that \(\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = -\vek u^\T(\partial\mat K/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}})\vek u\), and compute \(\partial\mat K/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\).

  1. The solution \(\vek u = \mat K^{-1}\vek F\) is a differentiable function of \(\vek\rho\), because \(\mat K\) is differentiable and positive definite, hence invertible with a differentiable inverse (Cramer's rule).
  2. Differentiating the equation \(\mat K\vek u = \vek F\) with respect to \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(\vek F\) independent gives \((\partial\mat K/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}})\,\vek u + \mat K\,\partial\vek u/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\).
  3. From \(C = \vek F^\T\vek u = \vek u^\T\mat K\,\vek u\) and the symmetry of the matrix \(\mat K\) we get \(\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek F^\T\partial\vek u/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek u^\T\mat K\,\partial\vek u/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = -\vek u^\T(\partial\mat K/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}})\vek u\) by step 2.
  4. From \(\partial\mat K/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = p\,\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{p-1}\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\) and \(\vek u^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{e}}^0\vek u = \vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}\) follows (29.56). The sign is nonpositive by item 3 of lemma 29.64.

Source: SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 2, equation (4)): \(\partial c/\partial x_{\mathrm{e}} = -p(x_{\mathrm{e}})^{p-1}\,\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}\). The proof is ours, the same as for the truss in corollary 29.44.

The quantity \(\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}\) is twice the strain energy of the element at full thickness, so \(p\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{p-1}\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}\) measures how much the compliance decreases if we thicken the element a little. What remains is the updating rule. We write it in the form of SIGMUND2001, which is the same as the OC rule for the truss (definition 29.54). If we thicken the element, the compliance falls by that amount.

Definition 29.71 The OC update for SIMP (posodobitev OC za SIMP)

Let \(\vek\rho^k\) be a design with the equilibrium \(\mat K(\vek\rho^k)\vek u^k = \vek F\). Let \(\eta \in (0, 1]\) be the damping, \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} > 0\) the move limit, \(\lambda > 0\) the multiplier of the volume constraint, and

\[B_{\mathrm{e}}^k = \frac{-\,\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}}{\lambda\,\partial V/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}} = \frac{p\,(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^{p-1}\,\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}}{\lambda} , \tag{29.57}\]

where we used \(V = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\partial V/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = 1\). The update is

\[\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1} = \min\Big\{\,1,\ \rho_{\mathrm{e}}^k + \delta_{\mathrm{p}},\ \max\big\{\rho_{\min},\ \rho_{\mathrm{e}}^k - \delta_{\mathrm{p}},\ \rho_{\mathrm{e}}^k\,(B_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^{\eta}\big\}\Big\} , \tag{29.58}\]

and \(\lambda\) is chosen by bisection so that \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1} = \varphi N\). What the formula does is shown by the proposal and the window of width \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) on the number line below.

Source: SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 2, equations (2) and (3), \(\eta = 1/2\), "m" is the move limit, which we write \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) because \(m\) means a mass, bisection PDF p. 4) and CHK §9.1.2, §9.2.1 (PDF pp. 191-193). We write the three lines of formula (2) there as one min/max expression.

What formula (29.58) does with one element we draw on the number line of the density from \(0\) to \(1\) (figure 29.95, row (a)). The element has the density \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^k = 0{,}5\). The rule proposes the new density \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^k\,(B_{\mathrm{e}}^k)^{\eta}\). At \(B_{\mathrm{e}}^k = 2{,}89\) and \(\eta = 1/2\) this is \(0{,}5 \cdot 1{,}7 = 0{,}85\): an element with \(B_{\mathrm{e}}^k > 1\) lowers the compliance per unit of added material by more than \(\lambda\), so the rule thickens it. The proposal may stay only in the window from \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^k - \delta_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}3\) to \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^k + \delta_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}7\), which \(\rho_{\min}\) and \(1\) cut further at the ends of the line. The proposal \(0{,}85\) is outside the window, so the \(\min\) of the formula returns it to the edge of the window, \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1} = 0{,}7\).

Why the window, and why the power \(\eta\)? The sensitivity (29.56) is a derivative, so it describes only small changes of the density. Without a limit the design would change in one iteration so much that the computed derivatives would no longer hold for it: without the power the proposal would be \(0{,}5 \cdot 2{,}89 = 1{,}445\), which is beyond the upper bound \(1\). The price of both limits is a slower loop, the gain a calmer course (SIGMUND2001, PDF p. 2, calls \(\eta\) a numerical damping and \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) a move limit). On the line the proposal without the power would be outside the window, and the power and the window return it closer to the old density.

Formula (29.58) is the same as (29.46), except that \(B_{\mathrm{e}}\) is different and the volume of an element is \(1\). We find the number \(\lambda\) by bisection, because the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1}\) is continuous and does not increase with increasing \(\lambda\), as for the truss (section 29.7.5). This is exactly what the program in SIGMUND2001 does on PDF p. 4. We use \(\eta = 1/2\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}2\) and \(\rho_{\min} = 0{,}001\). In figure 29.96 the axes are \(\lambda\) and \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{k+1}\), and the sum is continuous and nonincreasing in \(\lambda\). The target \(\varphi N\) is the horizontal line, the intersection gives the wanted \(\lambda\), and bisection halves the interval until it is enclosed.

Lemma 29.72 Fixed points of the OC update for SIMP (negibne točke OC za SIMP)

Let \(\vek\rho\) be a design with \(\rho_{\min} \le \rho_{\mathrm{e}} \le 1\), \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = \varphi N\) and nonsingular \(\mat K(\vek\rho)\), and let \(\rho_{\min} < 1\). Then the update (29.58) with some \(\lambda > 0\) leaves \(\vek\rho\) unchanged exactly when for every \(e\) (the cases are the rows (b), (c) and (d) of the figure):

  1. if \(\rho_{\min} < \rho_{\mathrm{e}} < 1\), then \(p\,\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{p-1}\,\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}} = \lambda\) (row (b), the density is inside the window),
  2. if \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = \rho_{\min}\), then \(p\,\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{p-1}\,\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}} \le \lambda\) (row (c), the density is at the lower bound),
  3. if \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = 1\), then \(p\,\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}} \ge \lambda\) (row (d), the density is at the upper bound).
Proof

We have to show that the result of expression (29.58) agrees with \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) exactly under these conditions, separately in three cases.

  1. Let \(\rho_{\min} < \rho_{\mathrm{e}} < 1\). The lower bound is \(\max\{\rho_{\min}, \rho_{\mathrm{e}} - \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\} < \rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) and the upper \(\min\{1, \rho_{\mathrm{e}} + \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\} > \rho_{\mathrm{e}}\). The result \(\min\{\cdot\}\) is \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) exactly when \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} B_{\mathrm{e}}^\eta = \rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) (if \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}B_{\mathrm{e}}^\eta\) were outside the bounds, the result would be one of the bounds, which differs from \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\)). So \(B_{\mathrm{e}} = 1\), and this is item 1 by (29.57). In row (b) of figure 29.95 the density lies strictly inside the window, so only a proposal that falls exactly on it returns it.
  2. Let \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = \rho_{\min}\). The lower bound is \(\max\{\rho_{\min}, \rho_{\min} - \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\} = \rho_{\min}\). The result is \(\rho_{\min}\) exactly when \(\rho_{\min}B_{\mathrm{e}}^\eta \le \rho_{\min}\), that is \(B_{\mathrm{e}} \le 1\), which is item 2. In row (c) the proposal lies to the left of \(\rho_{\min}\) and the \(\max\) returns it to the bound.
  3. Let \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}} = 1\). The upper bound is \(\min\{1, 1 + \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\} = 1\). The result is \(1\) exactly when \(1\cdot B_{\mathrm{e}}^\eta \ge 1\), that is \(B_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 1\), which is item 3. In row (d) the proposal lies to the right of \(1\) and the \(\min\) returns it to the bound.

Source: The proof is ours, following lemma 29.55 for the truss. CHK §9.1.2 (PDF p. 191): at convergence the specific strain energy is constant in every element.

The conditions 1 to 3 have the same form as the conditions of theorem 29.37. At \(p = 1\) the problem is convex, and if we repeat the same calculations as there for \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\), then by theorem 29.30 the fixed point is a global minimum (as in item 3 of lemma 29.55). At \(p > 1\) the problem is not convex, so a fixed point is only a candidate for a minimum, and the third item of the lemma for the truss is missing here. This is a near miss for this lemma: the conditions hold, but the conclusion about the global minimum does not. At \(p = 1\) the stiffness is a line and the problem is convex, at \(p > 1\) the curve bends it, so a fixed point is only a candidate.

29.9.4 The sensitivity filter (filter občutljivosti)

If we run the loop of the previous section as it is, then on parts of the region the elements alternate between solid and empty like a chessboard (the orange frame in figure 29.99 below). CHK §9.3.2 (PDF p. 196) describes two difficulties that we see in such a problem, and says where each comes from. The first is mesh dependency (odvisnost od mreže): with a finer mesh the design does not improve but changes, more and ever thinner parts appear, one or two elements wide, and the structure is artificially stiff. The second is the checkerboard pattern (šahovnica), where the density alternates between \(0\) and \(1\). For a problem without a bound on the number of holes or on the smallest width of parts, a solution in general does not exist (CHK §9.3.1, PDF pp. 194-195): with thinner and more numerous bars the stiffness is always larger. We cite this, we do not prove it. The remedy is called restriction (omejitev), and one form of it is the filter (CHK §9.4.2, PDF pp. 199-200).

What is wrong with a checkerboard, one window of \(2 \times 2\) elements shows (figure 29.97, (a)). The solid elements lie on a diagonal, the empty ones have the density \(\rho_{\min}\) and carry almost nothing. The solid elements touch in one single node. A force passes through one point, a moment does not. In picture (b) the squares therefore turn about the common node from the original position, each in its own direction by the angle \(\alpha\), without deforming themselves. The contact is a hinge, as in a joint of a truss, and such a window does not resist the turn. A load-carrying part that holds at one point cannot be made, so we do not want a checkerboard in the design.

The sensitivity filter (filter občutljivosti) is the simplest. We replace the sensitivity of every element by a weighted average of the sensitivities of its neighbours within a circle of radius \(r_{\min}\) (SIGMUND2001, PDF p. 3). The circle is the circle of radius \(r_{\min}\) around the element in the filter figure.

Definition 29.73 The sensitivity filter (filter občutljivosti)

Let \(r_{\min} > 0\) be the filter radius (polmer filtra) in units of the element side and \(\mathrm{dist}(e, f)\) the distance between the centres of the elements \(e\) and \(f\). The weight is \(\hat H_{\mathrm{f}} = \max\{0,\ r_{\min} - \mathrm{dist}(e, f)\}\) (it also depends on \(e\)). The filtered sensitivity of the element \(e\) is

\[\widehat{\frac{\partial C}{\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}}} = \frac{1}{\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\sum_{\mathrm{f}=1}^{N}\hat H_{\mathrm{f}}}\ \sum_{\mathrm{f}=1}^{N}\hat H_{\mathrm{f}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{f}}\,\frac{\partial C}{\partial\rho_{\mathrm{f}}} . \tag{29.59}\]

In the update (29.58) we use \(\widehat{\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}}\) in place of \(\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\) in \(B_{\mathrm{e}}\). The weight is largest in the element itself and falls to the edge of the circle, as the numbers in the cells show.

Source: SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 3, equations (5) and (6) and the weight \(\hat H_{\mathrm{f}} = r_{\min} - \mathrm{dist}(e, f)\), "zero outside the filter area"), CHK §9.4.2 (PDF p. 200): "filtering the sensitivities in an OC or a convex approximation approach". We write the weight with \(\max\), which is the same as "zero outside the circle".

Let us look at the weights on a square mesh with \(r_{\min} = 1{,}5\) (a circle of radius \(r_{\min}\) around the element \(e\)). The central element has weight \(1{,}5 - 0 = 1{,}5\), the four neighbours at distance \(1\) have \(0{,}5\), the four diagonal ones at distance \(\sqrt 2 = 1{,}4142\) have \(0{,}0858\), and all others, at distance \(2\) or more from the centre, zero. The sum of these nine weights is \(1{,}5 + 4\cdot 0{,}5 + 4\cdot 0{,}0858 = 3{,}8431\) (num-09.out, F). In the weighted average the element itself counts \(1{,}5/3{,}8431 = 39{,}0\,\%\), each of the four neighbours \(13{,}0\,\%\) and each of the four diagonal ones \(2{,}2\,\%\).

Lemma 29.74 Properties of the filter (lastnosti filtra)

Let \(\rho_{\mathrm{f}} > 0\), \(s_{\mathrm{f}} = \partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{f}} \le 0\) for all \(f\) and \(r_{\min} > 0\). Then (the weights belong to the cells in the circle around the element):

  1. \(\widehat{\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}} \le 0\), so \(B_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) and the update (29.58) is defined (the numbers in the cells are nonnegative and positive in the central cell).
  2. The number \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\,\widehat{\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}}\) is a weighted average of the numbers \(\rho_{\mathrm{f}} s_{\mathrm{f}}\) over the elements \(f\) with \(\mathrm{dist}(e, f) < r_{\min}\), so it lies between the smallest and the largest of them (the weights are the numbers in the cells inside the circle).
  3. If \(r_{\min} \le 1\), then \(\widehat{\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}} = s_{\mathrm{e}}\): the filter does nothing (a circle with \(r_{\min} \le 1\) contains no neighbour except the element itself).
Proof

We have to show that the weights are nonnegative and that the weight of the element itself is positive.

  1. The weight \(\hat H_{\mathrm{e}} = r_{\min} - 0 = r_{\min} > 0\) is positive and all the others are nonnegative by definition (the largest from \(\max\)). The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{f}}\hat H_{\mathrm{f}} \ge r_{\min} > 0\), and \(\rho_{\mathrm{f}} s_{\mathrm{f}} \le 0\) for every \(f\), so the numerator of (29.59) is nonpositive and the denominator \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\sum_{\mathrm{f}}\hat H_{\mathrm{f}} > 0\) is positive (the cell weights are nonnegative and the central cell has \(r_{\min}\)).
  2. The weight \(\hat H_{\mathrm{f}}/\sum_{\mathrm{g}}\hat H_{\mathrm{g}}\) is nonnegative with sum \(1\), and from \(\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\widehat{\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{f}}\hat H_{\mathrm{f}}\rho_{\mathrm{f}} s_{\mathrm{f}}/\sum_{\mathrm{g}}\hat H_{\mathrm{g}}\) the claim follows (a weighted average lies between the smallest and the largest value, because \(\sum_{\mathrm{f}} w_{\mathrm{f}} a_{\mathrm{f}} \le \max_{\mathrm{f}} a_{\mathrm{f}}\sum_{\mathrm{f}} w_{\mathrm{f}} = \max_{\mathrm{f}} a_{\mathrm{f}}\) and similarly for the smallest) (all the cells of the circle together have weight \(1\) after dividing by the sum, like the percentages in the example above).
  3. At \(r_{\min} \le 1\) we have \(\mathrm{dist}(e, f) \ge 1\) for every \(f \ne e\) (the distance between the centres of two different squares of side \(1\) is at least \(1\)), so \(\hat H_{\mathrm{f}} = \max\{0, r_{\min} - \mathrm{dist}\} = 0\). Only \(f = e\) remains with weight \(r_{\min}\), and (29.59) gives \(\frac{1}{\rho_{\mathrm{e}} r_{\min}}\,r_{\min}\,\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\,s_{\mathrm{e}} = s_{\mathrm{e}}\) (inside the circle there is only the element itself).

Source: SIGMUND2001 (PDF p. 4): "By selecting rmin less than one ... the filtered sensitivities will be equal to the original sensitivities making the filter inactive." The proof is ours.

Item 3 is a near miss for what we expect from a filter: a filter with \(r_{\min} \le 1\) smooths nothing, because there are no other elements in the circle. Our case without a filter is exactly this (or equivalently \(r_{\min} < 1\)), and below it has \(51\) checkerboard patterns. In the filter figure the circle would be so small that it enclosed only the element.

The filter has a cost that we must state. It does not only change the course of the iteration, it also changes the conditions of the point that the iteration seeks. With filtered sensitivities, a fixed point satisfies condition 1 of lemma 29.72 with \(\widehat{\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}}\) in place of \(\partial C/\partial\rho_{\mathrm{e}}\), and this does not correspond to the condition for \(C\) alone. In our filtered computation the quotient of the largest and the smallest value of \(p\rho_{\mathrm{e}}^{p-1}\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_0\vek u_{\mathrm{e}}\) among the \(196\) elements with \(0{,}002 < \rho_{\mathrm{e}} < 0{,}998\) is \(2{,}5\cdot 10^5\) (num-09.out, D), so condition 1 of lemma 29.72 is not fulfilled for the true compliance. In the computation without a filter this quotient is \(1{,}060\) among two such elements. So the filter does not give a fixed point of the OC loop for the true compliance at \(p = 3\), hence not even a candidate for its minimum, but a design simplified so as to be acceptable for manufacture. The existence of a solution with the filter is not proved (SIGMUND2001, PDF p. 3: "It must be emphasized that this filter has not yet been proven to ensure existence of solutions"), and CHK (PDF p. 200) says that for this filter, in contrast to the two other ways of filtering, there is no mathematical proof that it gives a mesh independent design, but that all numerical experience points in this direction. The filter smooths the edges of the full parts in (b), while in (a) they stay sharp.

29.9.5 Example: the half beam (primer: polovica nosilca)

Now we put it all together. The same region, \(30 \times 10\) elements, \(\varphi = 0{,}5\), \(\rho_{\min} = 0{,}001\), initial density \(0{,}5\) everywhere, \(\eta = 1/2\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}2\), \(r_{\min} = 1{,}5\), by the procedure of SIGMUND2001 (PDF pp. 2-4), which we wrote in Python. The mesh is in each direction two times coarser than the \(60 \times 20\) mesh of the article, so that the computation stays light. What the coarse mesh does to the numbers we checked with one computation on the \(60 \times 20\) mesh, also with \(60\) iterations. The solid beam there has the compliance \(125{,}9\) instead of \(123{,}1\). With a filter of the same length (\(r_{\min} = 3\) sides of the smaller elements) the compliance is \(231{,}2\) instead of \(225{,}9\), which is \(2{,}3\,\%\) more. Without a filter it is \(203{,}2\) instead of \(190{,}9\), and there are \(129\) checkerboard windows instead of \(51\): without a filter the design changes with a finer mesh, which is the mesh dependency of section 29.9.4. Both approaches, without a filter and with a filter, run \(60\) iterations and stop because of the limit on the number of iterations. The stopping criterion of the article (a change below \(0{,}01\)) is not met, because the last change is \(0{,}0288\) without a filter and \(0{,}0121\) with a filter. So the numbers for the compliance are the values of iteration \(60\) and not proved minima, although the compliance without a filter is \(190{,}9\) to one decimal place from iteration \(30\) on.

Figure 29.99 shows three outcomes. In (a), \(p = 3\) without a filter, the compliance is \(190{,}9\), and the design is almost blackwhite and whiteblack: the share of elements with \(0{,}1 < \rho_{\mathrm{e}} < 0{,}9\) is \(0{,}003\), which is one element out of \(300\). The pattern is not healthy: in the orange frame in the middle of the region solid and empty elements alternate in rows, and among all the \(2 \times 2\) windows \(51\) are checkerboards, that is with two solid elements on a diagonal and two empty ones. In (b), \(p = 3\) with the filter, there is no checkerboard pattern at all, but the compliance is \(225{,}9\), which is \(18{,}4\,\%\) more than without the filter, and \(0{,}390\) of the elements are grey, because the filter smooths the edges. The edges of the solid parts are soft, with grey transitions. In (c), \(p = 1\), the compliance is \(162{,}4\) and \(0{,}703\) of the elements are grey (previous subsection). All three values agree with lemma 29.69: \(190{,}9\) and \(225{,}9\) are not below \(162{,}4\). The initial compliance at \(p = 3\) and density \(0{,}5\) is \(984{,}6\) (lemma 29.68), after ten iterations it drops to \(237{,}7\) and after thirty to \(190{,}9\) (without a filter), with the filter to \(298{,}9\) and \(230{,}9\) (num-09.out, D).

Why is the compliance without a filter smaller? The filter restricts the set of designs, so a worse optimum is expected even if the checkerboard were not artificial. The computation shows that without a filter a checkerboard appears (\(51\) patterns, none with the filter) and that the filter costs \(18{,}4\,\%\) of compliance. It does not show that this difference is artificial, that is, that a checkerboard in a real structure would not carry. CHK (§9.3.2, PDF p. 196) attributes the checkerboard to the choice of discretizations of the fields \(\rho\) and \(\vek u\), and calls slender parts one or two elements wide artificially stiff. We do not prove this. For comparison, one more number that we compute: a full checkerboard of solid elements and elements with \(\rho_{\min}\) (\(\varphi = 0{,}501\), \(p = 3\)) has compliance \(1{,}0\cdot 10^9\) (num-09.out, E), because the solid elements touch only at nodes and these contacts act as hinges (figure 29.97, (b)). So the optimizer does not find a whole checkerboard but local patterns in an otherwise connected structure.

Let us sum up what we showed and what we did not. We showed that the sheet problem is convex (corollary 29.66) and that at \(p = 1\) it does not penalize grey, while at \(p > 1\) it does (lemma 29.68). We showed the formula for the sensitivity (lemma 29.70), the fixed points of the OC loop (lemma 29.72) and the properties of the filter (lemma 29.74). We cited, without proof: the physical admissibility of SIMP at \(p \ge 3\), the nonexistence of a solution for a problem without a restriction (CHK §9.3.1, PDF pp. 194-195), the nonconvexity at \(p > 1\) (PDF p. 196) and the fact that the existence of a solution with the filter is not proved (SIGMUND2001, PDF p. 3). The convergence of the OC loop is not proved, and our computation on a \(30 \times 10\) mesh is no proof that the solutions on finer meshes would be like this. We cited the mesh dependency from CHK and checked it only with one computation on the \(60 \times 20\) mesh.

Section 29.10 connects this section with the other chapters of the book.

29.10 Connections and limits of the chapter (povezave in meje poglavja)

This is the last chapter of the book, so there is no list of chapters that are still to come. We say what optimization is built on, and then two questions that the chapter did not treat. The first: what changes if the design variable is not a cross-section area but the shape of a boundary (shape optimization). The second: what changes if one goal, for example weight, is not enough and we want several at once (multi-criteria optimization). For each we say what we derive and what we cite from the source. At the end is a list of what the book does not treat. The abbreviations of the courses are the same as in section 1.19.

29.10.1 What optimization stands on

  • Energy principles (VT, MK, chapter 4): the compliance (podajnost) \(C = \vek F\cdot\vek u\) equals \(2U\) by theorem 4.86, and by theorem 4.91 it is \(-2\Pi_{\min}\). From this theorem 29.34 gets the convexity of the compliance as a maximum of functions linear in the areas, theorem 29.37 gets the condition of equal energy density, and theorem 29.43 gets the sensitivity with one extra solve. The promise of chapter 4 that the least compliance follows from the least potential energy is kept by section 29.5.
  • Trusses and assembly (AK, chapter 7): the stiffness matrix \(K(A) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}} K_{\mathrm{e}}\) is linear in the areas by theorem 7.13. This is why the compliance is a maximum of linear functions (theorem 29.34). The promise about optimizing bar cross-sections from the same chapter is kept by sections 29.2, 29.5 and 29.7.
  • Lagrange multipliers and Taylor's formula (VT, chapter 8): theorem 8.37 is the basis of the necessary conditions 29.29, theorem 8.27 of the existence of an optimum (lemma 29.8) and theorem 8.68 of the error of finite differences (section 29.6).
  • Functionals and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (MK, chapters 5 and 6): a rod of variable cross-section is a function \(A(x)\), its compliance is a functional, and its least value is obtained by theorem 29.60 from lemma 6.19. The route through the variational condition, used by the source (CHK, PDF pp. 168-174), uses the same stationarity of a functional as theorem 5.70.
  • The Rayleigh quotient (VD, DSK, chapter 10): by theorem 10.43 the quotient is stationary at an eigenvector. Where the eigenvalue and the eigenvector are differentiable with respect to a design variable, the derivative of the eigenvalue therefore needs only the derivatives of the stiffness and mass matrices, not the derivative of the eigenvector. The book does not derive the expression for this derivative and does not use it.
  • When the chosen model is good enough: the optimum uses everything the model allows. In the truss of three bars of section 29.5 the optimum for a vertical force (\(\theta = 0\)) is a single middle bar with the area \(300\ \mathrm{mm}^2\). Its stiffness matrix is singular (\(\det = 0\)) and it carries no horizontal force. The model did not notice this, because it had no horizontal force. Checking a model and estimating its error are the subject of chapter 17 (AK).

29.10.2 Shape optimization (oblikovna optimizacija)

In section 29.1 we only named shape optimization (oblikovna optimizacija): the design variable here is the shape of the boundary of a body (plate edge in figure 29.100), not the area of a cross-section. Only what its first step needs remains here. For a surface (a plate in the plane) a change of shape changes the domain of every element, so the derivatives of the element stiffness matrix require the derivatives of the node positions with respect to the design variables (CHK, section 6.3.2.2, PDF p. 113). The first question is therefore how to describe the boundary with a few variables so that the nodes move consistently.

The simplest idea is to take the node coordinates as variables, as for bars. The source says that the boundary then usually becomes ragged and that the stresses are inaccurate because of this (CHK, section 7.1, PDF p. 122). The reason is that no condition ties neighbouring nodes to follow a smooth line, so the optimizer moves each of them on its own. In the right sketch of figure 29.100 every node has its own arrow and the edge becomes the orange broken line instead of the grey dashed smooth curve. So we describe the boundary with a few control vertices (nadzorna oglišča) and the mesh follows them. The smooth curve that the control vertices determine is a spline (zlepek), because it is composed of polynomial pieces of low degree (CHK, section 7.1, PDF p. 122). Its simplest case is the quadratic Bézier spline (CHK, equation (7.7), PDF p. 124), which we draw in the left sketch of figure 29.100.

First we draw the edge of the plate over the length \(100\) mm and its end points \(\vek V_0\) and \(\vek V_2\), which do not move in the optimization (this is their role, not a property of the curve). Then we take the control vertex \(\vek V_1\), which pulls the edge upward, and let it move along the span (razpon), the segment between \(\vek V_1^{\min}\) and \(\vek V_1^{\max}\). The span gets a variable: \(\vek V_1 = \vek V_1^{\min} + \alpha\,\vek L\) with \(0 \le \alpha \le 1\) and the vector \(\vek L = \vek V_1^{\max} - \vek V_1^{\min}\) (CHK, equation (7.1), PDF p. 122). Here \(\vek L = (0, 40)\) mm, the span is vertical and \(40\) mm long. One variable \(\alpha\) thus determines a whole curve and not only one point. Three are drawn: the thin grey one at \(\alpha = 0\), the grey dashed one at \(\alpha = 0{,}5\), when \(\vek V_1\) is at the middle of the span, and the orange one at \(\alpha = 1\), when \(\vek V_1\) is at \(\vek V_1^{\max}\). The curve is

\[\vek r(u, \alpha) = (1-u)^2\,\vek V_0 + 2u(1-u)\,\vek V_1 + u^2\,\vek V_2 , \qquad 0 \le u \le 1 , \tag{29.60}\]

and the parameter \(u\) runs along it from \(\vek V_0\) to \(\vek V_2\). A mesh node that lies at the value \(u\) moves when \(\alpha\) changes. The lemma says by how much.

Lemma 29.75 Displacement of a point on a quadratic spline (premik točke na kvadratnem zlepku)

Let \(\vek V_0\), \(\vek V_2\) and \(\vek L\) be fixed vectors of the plane, \(\vek V_1 = \vek V_1^{\min} + \alpha\,\vek L\) and \(\vek r(u, \alpha)\) the curve (29.60) (in figure 29.100, \(\vek L\) is the span and the curves are \(\vek r\)).

  1. \(\vek r(0, \alpha) = \vek V_0\) and \(\vek r(1, \alpha) = \vek V_2\) for every \(\alpha\) (in the figure the end points).
  2. For every \(u \in [0, 1]\), every \(\alpha\) and every \(h \ne 0\), \(\big(\vek r(u, \alpha + h) - \vek r(u, \alpha)\big)/h = 2u(1-u)\,\vek L\). The derivative with respect to \(\alpha\) is therefore \(\partial\vek r/\partial\alpha = 2u(1-u)\,\vek L\), zero at the end points and equal to \(\vek L/2\) at \(u = 1/2\) (in the figure the distances between the curves).
  3. \(\partial\vek r/\partial u\,(0, \alpha) = 2(\vek V_1 - \vek V_0)\) and \(\partial\vek r/\partial u\,(1, \alpha) = 2(\vek V_2 - \vek V_1)\) (in the figure the thin segments).
Proof

We must show three points, all from equation (29.60). In the second the curve is linear in \(\alpha\), so the difference quotient is exact for every \(h\) and not only in the limit.

  1. At \(u = 0\), \((1-u)^2 = 1\) and \(u(1-u) = u^2 = 0\), at \(u = 1\), \((1-u)^2 = u(1-u) = 0\) and \(u^2 = 1\). What remains is \(\vek V_0\) and \(\vek V_2\) respectively. This is why all three curves in figure 29.100 pass through the same end points.
  2. The variable \(\alpha\) appears only in \(\vek V_1\). The difference \(\vek r(u, \alpha + h) - \vek r(u, \alpha)\) therefore contains only the term \(2u(1-u)\big(\vek V_1(\alpha + h) - \vek V_1(\alpha)\big) = 2u(1-u)\,h\,\vek L\), since \(\vek V_1(\alpha + h) - \vek V_1(\alpha) = h\,\vek L\). Dividing by \(h\) gives the claim, and the limit \(h \to 0\) gives the derivative. The function \(2u(1-u)\) is zero at \(u = 0\) and \(u = 1\) and \(1/2\) at \(u = 1/2\). In the figure these are the blue distances between the dashed and the orange curve: shorter at \(u = 1/4\), longest at \(u = 1/2\), none at the end points.
  3. The derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(-2(1-u)\,\vek V_0 + 2(1-2u)\,\vek V_1 + 2u\,\vek V_2\) (the rule for the derivative of a product and of a polynomial). At \(u = 0\) this is \(-2\vek V_0 + 2\vek V_1\), at \(u = 1\) it is \(-2\vek V_1 + 2\vek V_2\). The curve therefore leaves \(\vek V_0\) in the direction of \(\vek V_1\) and arrives at \(\vek V_2\) from the direction of \(\vek V_1\). At \(\alpha = 1\) these directions are the thin orange segments from the end points to \(\vek V_1^{\max}\), and the orange curve touches them at the end points.

Source: The spline is CHK equation (7.7) (PDF p. 124), the span variable equation (7.1) (PDF p. 122), the tangent at the end points equation (7.6) (PDF p. 124, there in general for degree \(n\)). The proof for degree \(n = 2\) is not from the source.

In figure 29.100 we see what the lemma says. The displacement of the point at \(u = 1/4\) is \(2\cdot\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac34\cdot 40 = 15\) mm per unit of \(\alpha\), so \(7{,}5\) mm when \(\alpha\) changes from \(0{,}5\) to \(1\) (heights \(11{,}25\) and \(18{,}75\) mm). At \(u = 1/2\) it is \(20\) mm per unit of \(\alpha\), which is half of \(\vek L\): the middle point rises by \(10\) mm, from \(15\) to \(25\) mm. A mesh whose nodes are assigned fixed values of \(u\) therefore moves consistently and the edge stays smooth: neighbouring nodes have nearly the same \(u\) and so nearly the same displacement \(2u(1-u)\,\vek L\), unlike in the right sketch, where each gets its own. The derivatives \(\partial\vek r/\partial\alpha\) are exactly what the derivatives of the stiffness matrix, cited by the source, need.

A case where the lemma says nothing: by point 2 the end points at \(u = 0\) and \(u = 1\) stay where they are, whatever \(\alpha\) is. If we wanted the edge to move there as well, \(\vek V_0\) or \(\vek V_2\) must also get its own span and variable. The move of an end point is not a consequence of the move of \(\vek V_1\). The source extends the same idea to splines of higher degree, to B-splines and to the computation of the derivatives of node positions for an arbitrary mesh (CHK, chapter 7, PDF pp. 122-151). We do not derive this and do not use it. The idealization that remains: the edge is a smooth curve with a few variables, and the optimum is the best among these curves, not among all edges. Here, with the one variable \(\alpha\), this is a family of symmetric arches with the top in the middle and a height from \(5\) to \(25\) mm. An edge with its top elsewhere, or higher than \(25\) mm, cannot come out of this description, however good it might be. More control vertices give more shapes and more variables.

29.10.3 Several goals at once (več ciljev hkrati)

In the chapter we always had one goal and the others were constraints: the least volume at a limited stress or displacement (sections 29.2 and 29.6), the least compliance at a given volume (section 29.5). A designer, however, often wants both, a light and a stiff structure, and cannot fix the volume in advance: every volume has its least compliance, and figure 29.101 shows the curve of these. The source calls such problems multi-criteria (večciljne, vector optimization) and leaves them entirely to other sources (CHK, section 1.3, PDF pp. 13-14). We say what we derive about them with the tools of this chapter.

Definition 29.76 Pareto optimality (Paretova optimalnost)

Let \(f_1, \dots, f_{\mathrm{l}}\) be objective functions (ciljne funkcije) on the feasible set \(S\) (definition 29.5), each a real function on \(S\) that we want to make as small as possible. A design \(\vek x^* \in S\) is Pareto optimal if there is no design \(\vek x\) in \(S\) for which \(f_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \le f_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\) for all \(i = 1, \dots, l\) and \(f_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) < f_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\) for at least one \(i\). In figure 29.101 this means that the square below and to the left of the point is empty.

Source: CHK section 1.3 (PDF pp. 13-14, the inequalities on p. 14). The name "optimal" is there because no other feasible design can be improved in all goals at once.

Take the wall of chapters 4 and 7 with the force \(F = 10\) kN, two bars (called AC and BC below) and the goals volume \(V\) and compliance \(C\) (section 29.5). Is the design of chapter 7 with \(100\ \mathrm{mm}^2\) per bar Pareto optimal? We get the answer if we know all the designs that can be made. The wall is statically determinate: the bar forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13{,}33\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16{,}67\) kN are fixed by the equilibrium of the loaded joint alone, so they do not depend on the areas. This is the assumption of the computation that follows. In a statically indeterminate truss (the three bars of section 29.5) the forces change with the areas, so \(K\) below no longer follows from forces known in advance, and the least compliance must be sought by optimization. For the wall, however, by theorem 4.86 and definition 4.2 \(C = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}^2 L_{\mathrm{i}}/(E A_{\mathrm{i}})\) with lengths \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m and \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m. By lemma 6.19 for the vectors \(\big(|N_{\mathrm{i}}|\sqrt{L_{\mathrm{i}}/A_{\mathrm{i}}}\big)_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\big(\sqrt{A_{\mathrm{i}} L_{\mathrm{i}}}\big)_{\mathrm{i}}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\),

\[\Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} |N_{\mathrm{i}}|\,L_{\mathrm{i}}\Big)^2 \le \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{N_{\mathrm{i}}^2 L_{\mathrm{i}}}{A_{\mathrm{i}}}\ \sum_{\mathrm{i}} A_{\mathrm{i}} L_{\mathrm{i}} , \qquad\text{so}\qquad C \ge \frac{K}{V} , \quad K = \frac{(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} |N_{\mathrm{i}}|\,L_{\mathrm{i}})^2}{E} , \tag{29.61}\]

with equality exactly for areas proportional to \(|N_{\mathrm{i}}|\) (equality in the lemma). The same conclusion for a rod of variable cross-section is theorem 29.60. Here \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} |N_{\mathrm{i}}| L_{\mathrm{i}} = 136\,667\) N m and \(K = 0{,}0953\) J m\(^3\). All designs therefore lie on the curve \(C = K/V\) or above it, and on the curve are those with stresses of equal magnitude in both bars (AC is in compression, BC in tension). At \(V = 900\ \mathrm{cm}^3\), (29.61) gives the lower bound \(105{,}88\) J, and the design with \(100\ \mathrm{mm}^2\) has \(107{,}14\) J. It is not Pareto optimal: the same compliance can be reached with \(889{,}4\ \mathrm{cm}^3\), which is \(1{,}18\) % less. The curve is shown by figure 29.101 on the left.

We draw the axes \(v\) and \(c\) and the curve \(c = 1/v\) that (29.61) requires. We divide both quantities by those of the fully stressed design (section 29.2, \(V_0 = 621{,}2\ \mathrm{cm}^3\), \(C_0 = 153{,}4\) J), so that they are free of units. The design with \(100\ \mathrm{mm}^2\) is the orange dot at \(v = 1{,}449\), \(c = 0{,}698\), just above the curve: at the same \(v\) the curve has a \(c\) smaller by \(1{,}18\) %. At the scale of the figure this difference is thinner than the line, so the magnified frame shows it, with the blue distance between the orange dot and the curve. Definition 29.76 reads in the figure like this: designs better in both goals than the point \(v = 1\), \(c = 1\) on the curve would lie in the light square to its lower left. Since all designs lie on the curve or above it, the square is empty and the point is Pareto optimal. The square of the orange dot, however, is cut by the curve, as the magnified frame shows. How do we choose a point on the curve? The most common way is the weighted sum: with weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) and \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) we solve the problem with the single goal \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}} f_{\mathrm{i}}\) (CHK, equation (1.2), PDF p. 14). The lemma proves that the solution is Pareto optimal.

Lemma 29.77 A weighted sum gives a Pareto optimal design (utežena vsota da Paretovo optimalno zasnovo)

Let \(f_1, \dots, f_{\mathrm{l}}\) be objective functions on the set \(S\), \(w_1, \dots, w_{\mathrm{l}} > 0\) and \(\vek x^*\) a minimum of \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}} f_{\mathrm{i}}\) on \(S\). Then \(\vek x^*\) is Pareto optimal (definition 29.76), again the empty square below and to the left of the point.

Proof

We argue by contradiction: if \(\vek x^*\) is not Pareto optimal, there is a design with a smaller weighted sum, a point in the square below the line of equal sum.

  1. Let \(\vek x \in S\) be such that \(f_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) \le f_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\) for all \(i\) and \(f_{\mathrm{j}}(\vek x) < f_{\mathrm{j}}(\vek x^*)\) for some \(j\) (definition 29.76), in the figure a point in the square.
  2. Multiply every inequality by \(w_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\), which keeps its direction, and add. Since \(w_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\), the inequality at \(j\) is strict, so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}} f_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x) < \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}} f_{\mathrm{i}}(\vek x^*)\), and the point lies below the line.
  3. This contradicts that \(\vek x^*\) is a minimum of the weighted sum. Therefore no such \(\vek x\) exists: the square is empty.

In figure 29.101 on the left this is the proof for two goals and \(w = 0{,}5\). Designs with the same weighted sum lie on a line parallel to the dashed line \(v + c = 2\), and a smaller sum means a line closer to the origin. The design \(\vek x\) of step 1 would lie in the light square to the lower left of the point of contact. Except for its upper right corner the square is entirely below the dashed line, which is step 2.

Source: The claim is CHK section 1.3 (PDF p. 14: "the solution of which is a Pareto optimum"). The proof is not from the source.

The condition \(w_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) is needed. The source also allows weights \(w_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0\) (CHK, PDF p. 14), but with a zero weight the claim fails. On the axes \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) take the designs \((f_1, f_2) = (1, 4)\) and \((1, 5)\) and the weights \(w_1 = 1\), \(w_2 = 0\). The weighted sum is just \(f_1 = 1\), so both lie on the same line of equal value and both are a minimum. The second is not Pareto optimal: the arrow shows that the first is equally good in \(f_1\) and better in \(f_2\). In the proof step 2 fails: at \(j = 2\), \(w_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) and the sum is no longer strict.

On the wall we carry this through. Let \(v = V/V_0\) and \(c = C/C_0\), then by (29.61) \(c = 1/v\) on the curve. At a given \(v\) the least weighted sum \(w\,v + (1-w)\,c\) belongs to the design with the least \(c\), which is the design on the curve, so we seek the minimum only on the curve. There the weighted sum is \(f_{\mathrm{w}}(v) = w\,v + (1-w)/v\). Its derivative \(w - (1-w)/v^2\) is zero at \(v = \sqrt{(1-w)/w}\), and the second derivative \(2(1-w)/v^3\) is positive, so this is a minimum. The weights \(w = 0{,}8\), \(0{,}5\) and \(0{,}2\) give \(v = 0{,}5\), \(1\) and \(2\), so \(V = 310{,}6\), \(621{,}2\) and \(1242{,}4\ \mathrm{cm}^3\) and \(C = 306{,}8\), \(153{,}4\) and \(76{,}7\) J. Conversely, for every \(v > 0\) the weight \(w = 1/(1 + v^2)\) is a proper one. On the wall we thus reach every point of the curve with the weighted sum: the grey dashed line \(v + c = 2\) is the line of equal weighted value at \(w = 0{,}5\) and it touches the curve, because the curve lies above it and is convex. Caution: the weight \(0{,}5\) has this meaning only at these scales \(V_0\) and \(C_0\). At other units the same \(w\) gives another point.

The conclusion that the weighted sum reaches every Pareto point is not general, and the source warns about it (CHK, PDF p. 14: "in general not every Pareto optimal point may be obtained"). A small example suffices, three designs \((f_1, f_2) = (1, 4)\), \((3, 3)\) and \((4, 1)\). None improves another in both goals, so all three are Pareto optimal: for the middle one this is shown by the light square to the lower left of \((3, 3)\), which holds no other design. For every weight \(w \in [0, 1]\) the value \(w f_1 + (1-w) f_2\) at \((3, 3)\) is \(3\), and at the better of the two outer ones it is smaller than \(3\) by at least \(0{,}5\): \(\min_{\mathrm{w}}\big(3 - \min(w + 4(1-w),\ 4w + (1-w))\big) = 0{,}5\) at \(w = 1/2\). This least difference is the blue distance \(0{,}5\): at \(w = 1/2\) the value \((f_1 + f_2)/2\) is \(2{,}5\) on the dashed line and \(3\) at the point \((3, 3)\). The middle design wins at no weight, because it lies above the line through the outer two, so the set of attainable values is not convex. For the wall with continuous areas there are no such holes, since above we reached every point of the curve with the weighted sum. For the choice "the bar is there or it is not" (the nonconvex set of section 29.3), however, there can be.

29.10.4 What the book does not treat (kar knjiga ne obravnava)

  • Optimization without derivatives: design of experiments, response surfaces, surrogate models, genetic algorithms and neural networks. The chapter uses only first-order methods, which the sensitivities of section 29.6 make possible, and the source says that these methods (zero order methods, metode ničtega reda) solve other kinds of problems and that another source must present them (CHK, preface, PDF p. 6). None of the books we use treats them. Computationally the difference is this: in the nested form every value of the objective is one whole solve of the model (CHK, section 1.3, PDF p. 15). With \(n\) variables the finite differences of section 29.6 require \(n + 1\) solves, and the adjoint method one extra per constraint.
  • Cited, not proved (this is said beside the theorems that use them): Lagrangian duality (CHK, section 3.4, PDF pp. 55-64), the convergence of sequential linear and convex approximations and MMA (CHK, chapter 4, PDF pp. 65-83), the limit \(\varepsilon \to 0\) for bars of zero area (CHK, PDF p. 92) and the relaxation of the topology problem (CHK, section 9.5, PDF pp. 202-204).
  • Idealizations of the chapter: a linearly elastic truss with small displacements, an allowable stress without a safety factor and a single load case. If the load is not single, the optimum for one can be useless for another, like the middle bar that carries no horizontal force at a vertical load (above).
